title: Japanese versatility list
orderingVariable: Course order: 4 stages interleaving all categories; within a category, chunks run simple -> complex.
whyThatVariable: Versatility = spoken frequency (jiten.moe drama subtitles) x spread across topics x reach x speaking need. Casual is the default form; the polite (desu/masu) counterpart sits next to it.

conventions.romaji: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei); wa/o/e particles
conventions.register: romaji = casual (default); polite = desu/masu counterpart or null
conventions.freqSource: jiten.moe drama frequency list (3,030 live-action dramas), CC BY-SA 4.0

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Greet, thank and apologise, ask what, who and where, and say what you do, have and where you're going today or did yesterday, linked with but and because.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Ask favours, say what you want, like, saw, know, said and think, react with e?, hee and sou, and say how often and how soon things happen.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Check things with someone, guess and make plans and choices, talk about food, mood and difficulty, use fillers to hold the floor, and say how sure you are.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Suggest things, pass on what you heard or what seems true, compare, soften what you say and give advice, and talk about before, after and until.

categories.name: Time & sequence
categories.scope: relative time, aspect/timing adverbs, frequency, time clauses

blocks.label: Now and nearby days
blocks.rationale: The anchor words for the present moment and the days on either side of it. Plans and catch-ups start here.
blocks.interference: kyou and kinou sound alike: listen for the 'no' in ki-no-u. kinou pairs with past tense, ashita with non-past, and kyou with either.

items.use: Places anything at the present moment, and builds ima kara (from now), ima made (until now) and ima sugu (right now).

examplePolite.ja: 今どこですか？

items.use: Names the current day, and kyou wa makes it the topic for plans and small talk.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は休みですか？

items.freqNote: 今日(きょう) #86
items.notes: Shop and office staff say honjitsu. Recognise it, but you don't need to say it.

items.use: The default word for the next day, used in plans, deadlines and goodbyes (jaa ashita).

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよ。

items.freqNote: 明日(あした) #367; formal あす #10447
items.notes: Shop and office staff say myounichi, and asu is the news reading. Recognise both; ashita is fine in your own polite speech.

items.use: Names the day before today. Pair it with past tense to report what happened.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は休みでした。

items.freqNote: 昨日(きのう) #319
items.notes: To tell kinou from kyou, listen for the 'no'. Shop and office staff say sakujitsu.

blocks.label: Already, still, finally
blocks.rationale: These say where an event stands: done, not yet, ongoing all along, or done after a long wait.
blocks.interference: mou + negative means 'not anymore' and mada + negative means 'not yet'. zutto is an unbroken stretch, and yatto is the moment that stretch finally ends.

items.use: Marks something as done (mou tabeta), or as over for good when the verb is negative (mou ikanai). 'mou ...?' asks whether it has happened yet.

examplePolite.ja: ご飯はもう食べましたか？

items.freqNote: もう #36, all senses (already / anymore / more / exasperated 'mou!')
items.notes: Before an amount, mou means 'more, another': mou ichido (once more), mou sukoshi (a bit more). 'mou!' said alone with a sigh is exasperation, not a time word.

items.use: Says something hasn't changed yet. mada + negative means 'not yet', mada + -teru means 'still doing', and mada alone answers a 'mou ...?' question.

examplePolite.ja: ご飯はまだ食べてません。

items.freqNote: まだ #92
items.notes: 'Haven't X yet' is mada + -te nai (mada tabetenai), or just mada (desu). Not mada tabenakatta (= I didn't eat) and not mada tabenai (= I won't eat yet).

items.use: Stretches a state or action unbroken across time: zutto matteta (waited the whole time), zutto suki (have always liked).

example.english: I've been waiting the whole time.

examplePolite.ja: ずっと待ってましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I've been waiting the whole time.

items.freqNote: ずっと #142, includes the 'by far' comparison sense
items.notes: In comparisons it means 'by far' (zutto ii = much better).

items.use: Shows relief that something long awaited has happened, usually with past tense (yatto owatta).

examplePolite.ja: やっと仕事が終わりました。

items.notes: tsuini is the more dramatic 'at last', the climax of a long build-up, and it can mark a bad end (tsuini kowareta = it finally broke). yatto always sounds relieved, and can also mean 'only just' (yatto ma ni atta = only just made it).

blocks.label: How often
blocks.rationale: The frequency scale for habits. Every one of these goes before the same verb.
blocks.interference: Keep them on one scale: itsumo > yoku > tokidoki > tama ni. mainichi literally means every day, not 'always'.

items.use: Says something happens every single day. It is the backbone of talk about routines.

examplePolite.ja: 毎日歩いて帰ります。

items.notes: The same mai- gives maiasa (every morning), maiban (every night) and maishuu (every week).

items.use: The default word for habits and for doing things as usual. It sits at the top of the frequency scale.

examplePolite.ja: いつも歩いて帰ります。

items.freqNote: いつも #172
items.notes: itsumo no means 'the usual' (itsumo no mise = our usual place).

items.use: The everyday word for 'often', used before any verb to describe a habit (yoku iku).

examplePolite.ja: よく歩いて帰ります。

items.freqNote: よく #143, includes the 'well / thoroughly' sense
items.notes: It is the same word as 'well' (yoku dekita = well done), and yoku wakaranai means 'I'm not really sure'. yoku nai (not good) and yokatta (that's good) come from ii, not from this 'often'.

items.use: The middle of the frequency scale, for things that happen now and then.

examplePolite.ja: 時々歩いて帰ります。

items.use: The low end of the scale, one step below tokidoki. Very common in casual talk about habits and treats.

example.english: I walk home once in a while.

examplePolite.ja: たまに歩いて帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I walk home once in a while.

items.freqNote: たまに #724
items.notes: tama ni wa means 'for a change, every once in a while' (tama ni wa ii ne = nice for a change; tama ni wa renraku shite = get in touch once in a while).

blocks.label: Soon and suddenly
blocks.rationale: How soon something happens, from right away to 'it's about time', plus out of the blue.
blocks.interference: sugu = right after, mou sugu = the event is close, sorosoro = it's time (mostly to leave), kyuu ni = without warning, usually in past tense.

items.use: Makes an action immediate or close at hand (sugu iku, sugu kaeru). It also builds ima sugu and mou sugu.

examplePolite.ja: すぐ行きます。

items.notes: ima sugu means 'right this minute'. sugu can also mean 'easily' (sugu okoru = gets angry easily) and 'very near' (sugu soko = right over there, eki kara sugu = right by the station).

items.use: Says that a time or event is about to arrive, before a verb (mou sugu tsuku) or a noun (mou sugu natsu = summer's nearly here).

examplePolite.ja: もうすぐ着きます。

items.freqNote: もうすぐ #691
items.notes: It is about time only. 'Almost' as in nearly all is hotondo, and 'a little more' is mou sukoshi.

items.use: Signals that it's time to move on, most often to leave (sorosoro kaeru). It softens wrapping things up.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ帰りますね。

items.freqNote: そろそろ #413
items.notes: The polite way to excuse yourself is sorosoro shitsurei shimasu.

items.use: Marks an abrupt, unexpected change or action. kyuu ni dou shita no? means 'what's got into you?'

example.english: It's suddenly turned cold, hasn't it?

examplePolite.ja: 急に寒くなりましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's suddenly turned cold, hasn't it?

items.freqNote: 急に #345; synonyms 突然 #573, いきなり #723
items.notes: kyuu ni gomen ne = sorry for the short notice; kyuu na youji ga dekite = something came up (the standard excuse). totsuzen (stronger) and ikinari (casual, abrupt) are near-synonyms.

blocks.label: Later and next time
blocks.rationale: These push something to a later point: later today, the next occasion, next in line, or again.
blocks.interference: English 'next time' is usually kondo. tsugi is the next in order, ato de stays within the same occasion, and mata just means 'again'.

items.use: Says something happens again (mata kita), and closes goodbyes and invitations (mata ne, mata kite ne).

examplePolite.romaji: mata watashi ga harau n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: また私が払うんですか？

items.freqNote: また #91, includes the 'also' connector sense
items.notes: mata ne and mata ashita are the everyday goodbyes. The 'also' sense belongs to connectors. Men say ore here in casual talk (mata ore ga harau no?).

items.use: Puts something off until later, usually the same day (ato de ne). After a -ta verb, -ta ato de means 'after doing'.

examplePolite.ja: 後で払いますね。

items.freqNote: 後で #1484; kana あとで #3950
items.notes: Business speech uses nochi hodo. ato de is fine in ordinary polite talk. ato + an amount means 'X more, X left' (ato go-fun = five more minutes).

items.use: Points to the next occasion or some future one. It is how people float plans and soft invitations (kondo nomi ni ikou).

examplePolite.ja: 今度払いますね。

items.notes: mata kondo ('another time') is often a polite no. kondo no + a day means 'this coming' (kondo no doyoubi). After an earlier try, kondo wa can mean 'this time' (kondo wa umaku itta).

items.use: Points to the next item in a sequence or line (tsugi no eki, tsugi wa?). tsugi ni marks the next step.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi wa doko ni ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 次はどこに行きますか？

items.notes: tsugi wa also means 'next time' for a definite next occurrence (tsugi wa ki o tsukete = be careful next time). kondo is vaguer and is the word for invitations.

blocks.label: Earlier and lately
blocks.rationale: These point back into the past, from a moment ago to long ago, and all fit the same 'sore ... kiita' frame.
blocks.interference: kono aida = one recent occasion; saikin = the recent stretch up to now; mae ni = some earlier time; mukashi = long ago, often for old habits.

items.use: Refers back to something earlier today, anywhere from seconds to a few hours ago.

example.english: I heard that a minute ago.

examplePolite.ja: それはさっき聞きました。
examplePolite.english: I heard that a minute ago.

items.freqNote: さっき #253; formal 先ほど(さきほど) #1337
items.notes: Staff and business speech say sakihodo. sakki is fine with desu/masu.

items.use: Points to one recent past occasion, days or weeks ago (kono aida itta mise = the place we went the other day).

example.english: I heard that the other day.

examplePolite.ja: それはこの間聞きました。
examplePolite.english: I heard that the other day.

items.freqNote: この間 #883; casual こないだ #1644; synonym この前 #800; formal 先日 #1182
items.notes: Casually it is often squeezed to konaida (sore konaida kiita). kono mae means the same, and senjitsu is the formal version. kono aida wa arigatou thanks someone again for last time, and Japanese speakers expect it.

items.use: Covers the recent stretch up to now, for trends, current life and recent news (saikin isogashii).

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa saikin yoku kikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは最近よく聞きますね。

items.notes: saikin dou? is the stock 'how have you been?'.

items.use: Refers to an earlier time: mae ni (before, once before), mae wa (used to), and a time span + mae for 'ago' (ni-nen mae).

examplePolite.ja: それは前に聞きました。

items.freqNote: 前 #80, all senses including spatial 'front'
items.notes: The same word means 'in front'. -mae ni after a verb has its own card.

items.english: long ago; in the old days
items.use: Frames the distant past and old habits (mukashi wa yoku itta = I used to go a lot). mukashi kara means 'for ages'.

example.english: I used to listen to that a lot.

examplePolite.ja: それは昔よく聞きました。
examplePolite.english: I used to listen to that a lot.

items.notes: mukashi mukashi opens folk tales ('once upon a time').

blocks.label: First and last
blocks.rationale: Positions in a sequence plus first-ever experiences. These are the words for explaining steps and telling stories.
blocks.interference: saisho and saigo differ only in the ending (sho = start, go = end). hajimete means first-ever, not first in order, and mazu opens a plan.

items.use: Opens a series of steps or names the top priority (mazu wa ...). Later steps follow with tsugi ni and saigo ni.

examplePolite.ja: まずこれを食べましょう。

items.notes: It can also mean 'almost certainly' (mazu daijoubu, mazu muri). Don't confuse it with mazui (bad, uh-oh): mazu kore = this first; mazui na = uh-oh.

items.use: Names the start of something. saisho ni = first, before anything else; saisho wa = at first, in contrast to later.

example.ja: これ、最初は嫌いだった。
example.english: I didn't like this at first.

examplePolite.ja: これ、最初は嫌いでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't like this at first.

items.notes: hajime (ni / wa) is a softer synonym.

items.use: Names the end of a sequence or the final one: saigo ni = lastly, saigo no = the last (saigo no hi).

examplePolite.ja: 最後にこれを食べましょう。

items.notes: 'Finally' after a long wait is yatto, not saigo ni.

items.use: Marks a first-ever experience (hajimete kita = my first time here). It is the root of hajimemashite.

example.english: This is my first time eating this.

examplePolite.ja: これ、初めて食べました。
examplePolite.english: This is my first time eating this.

items.freqNote: 初めて #237; kana はじめて #12742; #2670 is 始めて ('starting'), a different word
items.notes: It does not mean first in an order. For 'first, do X' use mazu or saisho ni. nihon wa hajimete? / nihon wa hajimete desu ka? (first time in Japan?) is a stock small-talk question.

blocks.label: When, before, after, while
blocks.rationale: Clauses that time one action against another: when, before, after and at the same time.
blocks.interference: Each takes a different verb form: -mae ni is always non-past (deru mae ni); -toki takes a plain verb in either tense, and the tense shows the order (deru toki = as I leave, deta toki = once I'd left); -te kara takes the -te form (dete kara); -nagara takes the masu-stem, with one person doing both actions (arukinagara).

items.use: Makes a 'when X' clause after a plain verb, an adjective, or noun + no (kodomo no toki). The verb's tense shows whether X has happened yet.

example.english: I'll call you when I leave.

examplePolite.ja: 出るとき電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you when I leave.

items.freqNote: 時(とき) #293, includes the noun 'time'; kana とき #633
items.notes: The verb before toki stays plain even in polite speech. Tense sets the order: iku toki katta = bought it on the way there; itta toki katta = bought it there. For 'once X happens, then Y', use -tara: tsuitara denwa suru.

items.use: Means 'before X' after a dictionary-form verb or noun + no (neru mae ni, shigoto no mae ni). The verb stays non-past even when talking about the past.

example.romaji: deru mae ni denwa suru ne.
example.english: I'll call you before I leave.

examplePolite.romaji: deru mae ni denwa shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 出る前に電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you before I leave.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits 前に (#183446 is the tail floor); 前 #80 covers every sense incl. spatial 'front'. No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: Always use the dictionary form: deru mae ni, never deta mae ni.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to put one action after another (tabete kara deru) or to mark a starting point, 'since' (nihon ni kite kara).

example.english: I'll call you after I leave.

examplePolite.ja: 出てから電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you after I leave.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; から #14 counts every kara (mostly 'because / from'). No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: -ta ato de (deta ato de) is the other 'after' and means much the same here.

items.use: Joins two actions one person does at once, using the masu-stem (arukinagara hanasu). The main action comes last.

example.romaji: eki made arukinagara denwa suru ne.
example.ja: 駅まで歩きながら電話するね。
example.english: I'll call you on my walk to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made arukinagara denwa shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで歩きながら電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you on my walk to the station.

items.notes: It only works with one person. 'While you were out' needs -aida or -toki.

blocks.label: Busy right now
blocks.rationale: Ways to say whether you're free right now: whether there's time, whether you're in the middle of something, or whether you're about to act.
blocks.interference: -chuu attaches to nouns (denwa-chuu) and -tokoro to verbs. With -tokoro the verb form picks the stage: suru tokoro = about to, shiteru tokoro = in the middle of, shita tokoro = just did.

items.use: Time as something you have or lack (jikan aru? = got a minute?, jikan nai = no time). It also counts hours (ni-jikan).

examplePolite.ja: 今お時間いいですか？

items.freqNote: 時間(じかん) #181
items.notes: Asking about someone else's time, say ojikan (ojikan ii desu ka?). Your own time is always jikan.

items.use: Attaches to an activity noun to say you're busy with it right now (shigoto-chuu, kaigi-chuu, denwa-chuu).

examplePolite.ja: すみません、今電話中です。

items.freqNote: 中(ちゅう) #417; じゅう reading #9118; なか reading #133 is 'inside'
items.notes: Read -juu, the same kanji means 'throughout': ichinichi-juu = all day.

items.english: about to / in the middle of / just did
items.use: Pins down the exact stage of an action, depending on the verb form before it: taberu tokoro (about to eat), tabeteru tokoro (eating right now), tabeta tokoro (just ate).

example.ja: 今電話するところだった。
example.english: I was just about to call you.

examplePolite.ja: 今電話するところでした。
examplePolite.english: I was just about to call you.

items.freqNote: ところ #187, includes 'place'; casual とこ #280
items.notes: Casual speech often clips it to toko (ima deru toko). For 'on the way', say tochuu (ima mukatteru tochuu), not itteru tokoro. tabeta tokoro = just finished eating; tabeta bakari = only recently ate (could be hours or weeks).

blocks.label: Until, by, while still
blocks.rationale: Clauses that mark the edges of a time window: until, by, and while the window is still open.
blocks.interference: 'Until' is -made (the action lasts up to X) and 'by' is -made ni (it happens once before X). -uchi ni means acting while a state still holds.

items.use: Means 'until' after a dictionary-form verb or a time word (kuru made matsu, ashita made). It pairs with kara for ranges and also means 'as far as' a place.

example.english: I'll wait until you get back.

examplePolite.ja: 帰るまで待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wait until you get back.

items.freqNote: まで #64, all senses including spatial 'as far as'
items.notes: The action fills the whole span. For a deadline, use -made ni.

items.use: Sets a deadline: the action happens once, some time before X (ashita made ni okuru).

example.romaji: kaeru made ni wa owaru yo.
example.ja: 帰るまでには終わるよ。
example.english: It'll be done by the time you're back.

examplePolite.romaji: kaeru made ni wa owarimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 帰るまでには終わりますよ。
examplePolite.english: It'll be done by the time you're back.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits (までに not listed); まで #64 covers every made. No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: Quick test: if English says 'until', use made; if it says 'by', use made ni.

items.use: Says to act while a condition still holds (atsui uchi ni, wakai uchi ni). With a negative, -nai uchi ni means 'before X happens'.

examplePolite.ja: 熱いうちに食べてください。
examplePolite.english: Please eat it while it's hot.

items.freqNote: うち #113 is mostly 'home / we'. No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: Don't hear it as uchi ni ('to home'). Here it follows a verb, an adjective, or noun + no. ima no uchi ni = while you still can. -teru uchi ni = while doing X, before you knew it (hanashiteru uchi ni kuraku natta).

changelog.change: Every statement example (both registers) now ends in '.' and '。', matching kotoba and category J. Questions are unchanged.
Interference rewritten: listen for the 'no' in ki-no-u; kinou takes past, ashita non-past, kyou either.
Examples changed to ima doko? / ima doko desu ka? (no textbook 'ni iru/imasu').
Polite example keeps yo (ashita wa yasumi desu yo.). Notes name myounichi as staff speech and asu as the news reading.
Notes add sakujitsu as the staff-speech form, to match kyou's honjitsu.
Notes add the 'more, another' sense (mou ichido, mou sukoshi). freqNote lists 'more' among the senses.
Notes spell out 'not yet' = mada + -te nai, and contrast it with mada tabenakatta and mada tabenai.
freqNote drops the cryptic '(B)'. Notes drop the claim that 'by far' has its own card: no zutto-by-far appears in either keep list.
Notes: tsuini is spelled as one word and is not written-style. It is the dramatic 'at last' and can mark a bad end. Adds yatto = 'only just' (yatto ma ni atta).
Notes add yoku wakaranai and the trap that yoku nai / yokatta come from ii.
Notes correct tama ni wa to 'for a change, every once in a while'. The 'nice' comes from ii ne.
Example is now sugu iku ne / sugu ikimasu ('I'll be right there'). Notes add the 'very near' sense (sugu soko, eki kara sugu). contrastGroup renamed to how-soon.

English is now 'very soon, any minute now'. Example is mou sugu tsuku yo / mou sugu tsukimasu ('I'm almost there'). use covers verb and noun uses, and notes say it is about time only (not hotondo / mou sukoshi). contrastGroup renamed to how-soon.
contrastGroup renamed to how-soon (kyuu ni left the group).

Example is now the weather remark kyuu ni samuku natta ne / narimashita ne, replacing the reproach-like line. use no longer repeats that example. contrastGroup set to null. Notes add kyuu ni gomen ne and kyuu na youji ga dekite.
Polite English now matches the casual ('I'm paying again?'). Notes add that men say ore in casual talk.
Notes add ato + amount = 'X more, X left' (ato go-fun).
English adds 'this time'. Notes add kondo no + day = 'this coming' and kondo wa = 'this time'.

Example is now tsugi doko iku? / tsugi wa doko ni ikimasu ka? ('Where to next?'), so it no longer duplicates kondo's 'next time I'll pay'. Notes explain that tsugi wa = a definite 'next time', while kondo is vaguer.
Rationale names the shared 'sore ... kiita' frame. Items reordered nearest to farthest: sakki, kono aida, saikin, mae, mukashi.
Notes add the casual konaida and kono aida wa arigatou. freqNote adds こないだ #1644 (tool-verified).
Casual example adds ne (sore saikin yoku kiku ne.) to match the polite pair.
English is now 'long ago; in the old days'. 'back then' is ano koro.
Notes add the mazu / mazui audio trap.
Polite example drops the contrastive wa (kore, hajimete tabemashita.). freqNote corrected: kana はじめて is #12742, and #2670 is 始めて. Notes add the stock question nihon wa hajimete (desu ka)?
Label is now 'When, before, after, while'. Interference rewritten: toki takes either tense and only mae ni is locked to non-past.
ja fields now spell the conjunction in kana (〜とき, 出るとき). Notes add the tense-order trap (iku toki / itta toki katta) and -tara for 'once X happens'. alsoIn adds 13-list-exit-battery #1.
freqRank is now null so it doesn't double-count 前 #80. freqNote explains the tokenizer split.
prereqs changed to the slug 'te-and' (the -te form is E-te-and). 'nihon' is lowercase in use. freqNote phrasing standardised.
Example adds 'eki made' for a natural on-my-way call. alsoIn drops the 05-acquisition-order pointer, which leads to a gap report, not an item.
polite / politeJa set to null: ojikan is an honorific for the other person's time, not a register swap. Notes reworded; examplePolite kept.

Fatal fix: use now teaches the stages with taberu / tabeteru / tabeta, replacing itteru = 'on the way'. prereqs are the slugs teru and ta-past. Notes add tochuu for 'on the way' and the -ta tokoro vs -ta bakari contrast.

Example is now made ni wa (kaeru made ni wa owaru yo / owarimasu yo). prereqs changed to the slug 'made'. alsoIn drops 13-list-exit-battery #79, a -nakereba naranai item. freqNote phrasing standardised.
Notes add ima no uchi ni and -teru uchi ni. freqNote phrasing standardised.

Not applied, because adding items is forbidden: the coverage suggestions (tochuu, -aida / -aida ni, ato + amount, hisashiburi, ima made, ichido, kekkyoku, toriaezu, raishuu / kotoshi-type relative periods) and the 'Free or busy right now' relabel that came with tochuu. Points that fit a note were folded into existing notes (ato in ato-de, tochuu in tokoro, -tara in toki).

reviewSummaries: natural: Overall the category is solid: almost every casual example is something a Tokyo speaker would actually say, the shared frames (aruite kaeru, ... kiita, denwa suru ne) make good minimal pairs, and all the spot-checked ranks match the tool. The real problems are a few polite versions that nobody says to a coworker or clerk (sugu/mou sugu 'kaerimasu', kyuu ni sounding like a reproach), the tsugi example contradicting its own kondo/tsugi contrast, and a wrong gloss on tama ni wa. The rest is polish: particle drops, konaida, the myounichi note, one bad pointer, and a few missing relative-time words.

nuance: The category is solid overall. Glosses, register pairs and examples are mostly accurate and natural, and the draft already catches several good traps: mada vs the past negative, non-past before mae ni, made vs made ni, uchi ni misheard as 'home', and mata kondo as a soft no. Every freqRank checked against the tool and the vocab-trainer and research pointers resolve, except made-ni's exit-battery #79. The real errors are the itteru tokoro = 'on the way' gloss (fatal); the toki interference line and the missing -tara trap; ojikan used as a register counterpart; the tama ni wa gloss; and mou missing its 'more' sense. Two blocks have only 3 items; adding tochuu and -aida (ni) fills them, and ato + amount is a clear gap. Nothing needs cutting.

form: The form is clean overall. Every romaji string follows the convention (no macrons, wa/o particles, doubled consonants, verbs joined, hyphenated patterns), every kana reading and conjugation is correct, the example romaji matches its ja word for word, and polite/politeJa always agree. I spot-checked all 42 freqRank values with the tool and they match; the one wrong freqNote is hajimete's kana rank. I checked 18 alsoIn pointers and 16 resolve correctly; the 13-list #79 pointer and the 05 'i-stem tails' pointer are wrong. Blocks have 3–5 items and no slugs repeat. The real defects: prereqs written as romaji ('-made', '-te', '-teru', '-ta') instead of slugs; the tokoro example 'itteru tokoro' teaching iku-teru as progressive; and the block interference saying toki takes only the dictionary form, which contradicts the item's own use field.

categories.name: Degree, amount & limits

blocks.label: A bit / more
blocks.rationale: The small-degree dials and their 'more' partners, needed in almost every request or comment.
blocks.interference: chotto and sukoshi share the 'a little' sense; chotto is the spoken default and sukoshi sounds more careful. Only chotto does the social jobs: softening (chotto ii?), getting attention (chotto!) and the soft refusal (chotto…). motto is 'more' and mou chotto is 'a bit more', which makes a softer request.

items.use: Turns a degree or amount down to 'a bit'. It is the everyday spoken default and also softens complaints, requests and refusals.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと高いですね
examplePolite.english: It's a bit pricey, isn't it.

items.freqNote: whole word; rank includes softener and 'excuse me' uses
items.notes: Said alone with a trailing tone ('chotto…'), it is a soft no (see G).

items.use: Means the same 'a little' as chotto but sounds more careful. It is safe in polite speech and also measures amounts (sukoshi dake).

examplePolite.ja: 少し高いですね
examplePolite.english: It's a little expensive, isn't it.

items.notes: Casual talk prefers chotto. Reach for sukoshi with strangers or when chotto might sound evasive.

items.use: Adds 'more' to any adjective, adverb or verb (motto yukkuri, motto hoshii, motto ganbaru).

examplePolite.ja: もっと頑張ります

items.notes: For 'one more' of something use mou (mou hitotsu, mou ikkai), never motto. In a request to a stranger, mou chotto or mou sukoshi sounds softer. For 'too much' the ending is -sugiru (see I).

items.use: Asks for or offers 'a bit more' of anything, and is softer than motto. With de it means 'almost' (mou chotto de owaru).

example.ja: もうちょっとゆっくり話して

examplePolite.ja: もうちょっとゆっくり話してください
examplePolite.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

items.freqNote: kept whole by the tokenizer; もう少し is split and shows only #41735
items.notes: With strangers, mou sukoshi is the slightly more careful version.

blocks.label: Really / very
blocks.rationale: The intensity dial: five words that each go before the same adjective and set how strong it is.
blocks.interference: kekkou and kanari sit below sugoku: kekkou adds 'more than I expected', and kanari is matter-of-fact. honto ni stresses that it is true rather than how big it is. metcha is casual only.

items.use: The everyday spoken 'very'. It goes before an adjective or verb and works in both casual and polite speech.

examplePolite.ja: これ、すごくおいしいです

items.freqNote: tokenizer lemmatises すごく under すごい (#114, includes adjective uses); すごく as its own entry is a residual #40036
items.notes: Casual speech often uses sugoi as the adverb (sugoi oishii). Natives say it, but it counts as sloppy and slangy: recognise it, produce sugoku, and never use sugoi + adjective in desu/masu speech.

items.use: Adds 'really / truly' to an adjective, verb or thanks (honto ni arigatou). It stresses sincerity more than size.

example.ja: これ、ほんとにおいしい

examplePolite.ja: これ、本当においしいです

items.freqNote: rank of 本当に (all registers); casual spelling ほんとに separately #3240
items.notes: The bare reaction 'honto?' (really?) is a separate item in G.

items.use: Means 'pretty / quite', and signals that the degree is higher than you expected.

examplePolite.romaji: asoko no mise, kekkou oishii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: あそこの店、結構おいしいですよ
examplePolite.english: That place is actually pretty good, you know.

items.freqNote: rank includes the 'kekkou desu' (no thanks / fine) senses
items.notes: Trap: 'kekkou desu' on its own (often with a small hand wave) is a polite 'no thanks' (see G), so never use it to accept an offer; say 'onegai shimasu'. 'Kore de kekkou desu' means 'this will do'. Before an adjective (kekkou oishii) it never means 'no', but never say kekkou oishii to the person who made or chose the food: it implies you expected worse. Use sugoku or hontou ni instead.

items.use: A strong but measured 'considerably'. It sits between kekkou and sugoku and sounds factual rather than excited.

examplePolite.ja: これ、かなりおいしいです

items.use: Casual 'super / so', the strongest everyday intensifier among younger speakers. Switch to totemo or sugoku in polite speech.

example.ja: これ、めっちゃおいしい

examplePolite.ja: これ、とてもおいしいです

items.freqNote: めっちゃ #1170; stronger sibling めちゃくちゃ #1297
items.notes: Kansai in origin, now used nationwide. vocab-trainer spells it meccha. The polite pair totemo sounds stiff among friends (use sugoku there), and with a negative it means 'no way': totemo muri = can't possibly.

blocks.label: Also / only
blocks.rationale: Particles that widen (mo) or fence off (dake, shika, bakkari) whatever comes before them.
blocks.interference: dake, shika and bakkari all mean 'only'. dake is neutral with any verb, shika needs a negative and sounds like 'and that's all', and bakkari complains that it is too much or too often.

items.use: Takes the place of wa, ga or o to mean 'too / also'. After a number it stresses 'as many as' (mittsu mo tabeta).

examplePolite.ja: 私も行きたいです

items.notes: mo replaces wa, ga and o (watashi mo, never watashi wa mo) but follows other particles (nihon ni mo, tomodachi to mo). A mo B mo = both A and B; with a negative, neither. In casual speech men usually say ore mo or boku mo.

items.use: Means 'only / just' after a noun, number or clause (sore dake, chotto dake). Any verb can follow, positive or negative.

example.romaji: kyou wa geemu dake shite owatta
example.ja: 今日はゲームだけして終わった
example.english: Today was just games, and that was it.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa geemu dake shite owarimashita
examplePolite.ja: 今日はゲームだけして終わりました
examplePolite.english: Today was just games, and that was it.

items.notes: 'Kore dake?' (just this?) and 'chotto dake' (just a little) are everyday chunks.

items.use: Means 'nothing but / only' and must be followed by a negative verb. It sounds emphatic or regretful: 'and that's all'.

example.ja: 今日ゲームしかしなかった
example.english: All I did today was play games.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa geemu shika shimasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 今日はゲームしかしませんでした
examplePolite.english: All I did today was play games.

items.notes: Trap: shika with a positive verb is wrong. Say hitotsu shika nai, never hitotsu shika aru.

items.use: Means 'nothing but', with a sense of too much or too often. It is the complaining 'only' (geemu bakkari).

example.ja: 今日ゲームばっかりしてた
example.english: I did nothing but game all day.

examplePolite.ja: 今日はゲームばかりしてました
examplePolite.english: I spent all day just playing games.

items.freqNote: ばっかり #511; neutral/polite ばかり #448, clipped ばっか #1180
items.notes: It carries judgement, so use dake for a neutral 'only'. bakka is the clipped casual form you'll hear constantly (geemu bakka shiteru). -te bakari and -ta bakari belong to I.

blocks.label: All / a lot
blocks.rationale: Words for how much there is: the whole lot, or plenty of it.
blocks.interference: takusan and ippai both mean 'a lot', but ippai is chattier and also means 'full'. zenbu means 'all of it', not 'a lot'.

items.use: Means 'all / everything' for things and amounts. zenbu de means 'in total' (zenbu de ikura?).

examplePolite.ja: 全部食べましたよ

items.notes: For people use minna, not zenbu. subete (#732) is the formal, written-leaning variant. Trap: zenbu + negative usually means 'not all of it': zenbu wa tabenakatta = I didn't eat all of it (some is left). For 'none at all' say nani mo tabenakatta or zenzen tabenakatta.

items.use: The neutral 'a lot / many' for amounts and counts. It goes straight before the verb with no particle (takusan aru).

examplePolite.ja: まだたくさんありますよ

items.freqNote: たくさん #418; kanji 沢山 #15969

items.use: Chatty 'loads'. It also means 'full' (onaka ippai) and 'at my limit' (ippai ippai).

examplePolite.ja: まだいっぱいありますよ

items.freqNote: いっぱい #512; 一杯 #2892 includes the 'one cupful' sense
items.notes: 'Onaka ippai' means 'I'm full'. Ippai is a bit more colloquial than takusan. Ear trap: flat ippai = lots / full; ippai with the pitch high on the first i and falling after it = one cup, a drink (ippai nomi ni ikou = let's go for a drink). Before a noun both ippai and takusan take no (takusan no hito).

blocks.label: Not at all / not much
blocks.rationale: The negative-degree scale: each sets how strong a 'no' is before a negative verb or adjective.
blocks.interference: zenzen means 'not at all', hotondo 'hardly' and anmari 'not very'. Without a negative, hotondo flips to 'almost all'.

items.use: Means 'not at all' before a negative verb or adjective. With a few words like daijoubu, ii, heiki and chigau it means 'totally' (zenzen daijoubu, zenzen chigau).

example.english: I don't get it at all.

examplePolite.ja: 意味が全然わかりません
examplePolite.english: I have no idea what it means.

items.notes: 'Zenzen ii' or 'zenzen daijoubu (desu)' means 'totally fine' and is the stock reply to an apology ('no worries at all'). It's heard all the time, in desu/masu speech too, though sticklers object. zenzen + other positive adjectives (zenzen oishii) is slangy, so don't produce it. imi wakannai on its own is also a casual 'that makes no sense'.

items.use: Means 'not very / not much' before a negative. It is the soft, hedged no, gentler than zenzen.

example.ja: 意味あんまりわかんない

examplePolite.ja: 意味があまりわかりません
examplePolite.english: I don't really get what it means.

items.freqNote: あんまり #603; the neutral/polite form あまり #871
items.notes: 'Anmari…' said alone, trailing off, is a polite 'not really'. Without a negative it means 'too much': anmari da yo! = that's going too far; amari ni takakute kaenakatta = it was so expensive I couldn't buy it. For 'not that …' (sonna ni takakunai) see J.

items.use: Before a negative it means 'hardly / barely' (hotondo nai). With a positive it means 'almost all' (hotondo owatta).

example.ja: 意味ほとんどわかんない

examplePolite.ja: 意味がほとんどわかりません
examplePolite.english: I barely understand what it means.

items.notes: Its meaning flips with the verb: hotondo shitteru = know almost all, hotondo shiranai = know hardly any. As a noun: hotondo no hito = most people; hotondo ga = most of them.

blocks.label: About / exactly
blocks.rationale: Hedging an amount or pinning it down exactly.
blocks.interference: gurai goes after the number and daitai goes before it, and they can stack (daitai ichijikan gurai). choudo is the opposite pole: exactly.

items.use: Goes after a number or word to mean 'about' (gofun gurai) or 'to that extent' (sore gurai, onaji gurai).

examplePolite.ja: 1時間ぐらいかかりますよ

items.freqNote: ぐらい #342; the same particle spelled くらい is #299 (adjective 暗い is listed separately, #1480)
items.notes: kurai and gurai are interchangeable. 'Onaji gurai' means 'about the same'. sore gurai also means 'that much at least': sore gurai wakaru yo = I know that much.

items.use: Goes before a number or claim to mean 'roughly / mostly' (daitai wakatta). It hedges any amount or statement.

example.ja: 大体1時間ぐらいかかるよ

examplePolite.ja: 大体1時間ぐらいかかりますよ

items.freqNote: 大体 #1240; kana-spelled だいたい separately #3197
items.notes: Opening a complaint, it means 'in the first place' (daitai, nande…).

items.use: Means 'exactly / just right' for amounts, sizes and timing (choudo ii, choudo ima).

example.ja: ちょうど1時間かかった

examplePolite.ja: ちょうど1時間かかりました

items.notes: 'Choudo ii' (just right) and 'choudo yokatta' (perfect timing) are the most common chunks.

blocks.label: Comparing
blocks.rationale: The frames that rank things: most, more, than, than expected, and not as.
blocks.interference: The thing before yori loses and the thing before no hou ga wins. In a comparison hodo needs a negative and means 'not as … as', which an English ear can mishear as a positive comparison.

items.use: Makes any adjective superlative ('the most'). kono naka de ('out of these') sets the range.

example.english: Today's the coldest day of the year, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kotoshi ichiban samui desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日は今年一番寒いですね
examplePolite.english: Today's the coldest day of the year, isn't it.

items.notes: 'Ichiban suki' (my favourite) is the chunk you will use most.

items.use: Goes after the winning item to say 'X is more …' (kocchi no hou ga ii). It is the standard answer to 'docchi?'.

example.romaji: kyou no hou ga samui ne

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no hou ga samui desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日の方が寒いですね

items.freqNote: rank of 方 (ほう) across all uses, including -ta hou ga ii advice; kana ほう also #639
items.notes: The full frame is A yori B no hou ga …, but in speech either half usually stands alone. no goes only after a noun (kocchi no hou ga ii). Adjectives and verbs take hou ga directly (yasui hou ga ii, iku hou ga hayai); never yasui no hou ga.

items.use: Goes after the item being beaten to mean 'than' (kinou yori samui). In speech it usually stands alone; the full frame adds no hou ga to the winner.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日より寒いですね
examplePolite.english: It's colder than yesterday, isn't it.

items.freqNote: rank includes the formal 'from' sense and adverbial yori
items.notes: Trap: the thing before yori is the one that loses (has less of the quality). Kinou yori samui = today is colder.

items.use: Says that something was more (or less) than you expected, and works with any adjective (omotta yori takai, omotta yori hayakatta).

examplePolite.ja: 思ったより寒いですね

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits 思ったより and 思ってたより (both not found); components より #132, 思う #33
items.notes: Two pool items used as one chunk. Casual speech often uses omotteta yori (思ってたより) with the same meaning. The let-down version is omotta hodo … nai.

items.use: With a negative it means 'not as … as' (kinou hodo samukunai). It also marks extreme extent (shinu hodo, 'to death'). After an amount in polite or service speech it simply means 'about' (juppun hodo kakarimasu = it takes about ten minutes), with no negative and no comparison.

example.english: It's not as cold as yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日ほど寒くないですね
examplePolite.english: It's not as cold as yesterday, is it.

items.freqNote: ほど #288; kanji 程 #9747
items.notes: Trap: in a comparison, hodo always means NOT as … as, never 'as … as'. -ba … hodo means 'the more … the more'.

changelog.change: Block 'A bit / more' interference rewritten: chotto and sukoshi share only the 'a little' sense, and only chotto softens, gets attention and refuses. alsoIn trimmed to the Intensifiers pointer; 12 #3 and 13 #62 only used it in an example.

reviewSummaries: natural: Nearly all casual and polite sentences are things a Tokyo speaker would actually say. The shared frames (kore, X oishii; imi ... wakannai; ... samui ne) make the contrasts audible, and all freq ranks check out against the tool. The real problems: dake's example uses the one context where natives pick shika or bakkari; the polite kekkou example can insult whoever made or chose the food; totemo (and possibly -sugiru and sonna ni) is missing. The rest is translationese in some polite English glosses, a few overstated notes, and hyphenated counters (ichi-jikan) that break kotoba's joined spelling.

nuance: Glosses, register pairs (anmari/amari, bakkari/bakari, honto ni/hontou ni, metcha/totemo) and flags are mostly accurate, the shared-frame examples contrast well, and every freqRank checks against the tool. No item needs cutting. The main weaknesses: a category named 'limits' has no 'too much' (-sugiru) or 'enough / not enough' (juubun/tarinai); three blocks hold only 3 items; and several high-cost traps are missing or mis-stated (kekkou desu = no thanks, zenbu + negative = partial, no hou ga only after nouns, hodo = 'about' in service speech, zenzen's limited positive use, sugoi + adjective unflagged). omotta-yori borrows yori's rank, and the particle hyphens and 'ichi-jikan' don't match kotoba's stored spelling.

form: The mechanics are mostly solid. I checked all 27 freqRanks with the tool and every number matches. Kana readings, polite/politeJa pairs, conjugations, っ spelling (metcha) and long-vowel spelling (sou-style: kekkou, choudo, hontou) are correct. Every example's romaji matches its ja word for word, and all blocks have 3–6 items with no duplicate slugs. The real defects are convention breaks. Counters are hyphenated (ichi-jikan; kotoba stores ichijikan). Particles are inconsistent: gurai, yori and hodo have a hyphen and 〜, while mo, dake, shika and bakkari are bare. Prereqs cite romaji ('-yori', '-nai', '-kunai / ja nai') instead of slugs. About ten alsoIn pointers into 13-list-exit-battery point to items that only mention the word in an example sentence.

categories.name: Stance, attitude & manner
categories.scope: how the speaker feels about what they say; manner adverbs

blocks.label: Fast, slow, properly, well
blocks.rationale: Everyday manner adverbs that go straight before a verb to say how it's done: speed, care, and whether it works.
blocks.interference: hayaku shite ne (hurry up) and yukkuri de ii yo (no rush) are the opposite pair. yukkuri shite ne on its own means relax, make yourself at home, not 'do it slowly', and the opposite of hayaku in its 'early' sense is osoku. chanto means doing it the right way; umaku means it came out well.

items.use: The adverb form of hayai: before any verb it means fast or early (hayaku kaeru, hayaku okiru), and 'hayaku!' on its own means hurry up.

examplePolite.ja: 早くしてくださいね。

items.freqNote: 早く #144; 速く ('fast') #6275 is counted separately
items.notes: Spoken hayaku covers both 早く (early) and 速く (fast); the sound is the same. To a clerk or coworker, hayaku shite kudasai sounds impatient, so soften it: sumimasen, chotto isoide iru n desu ga... (sorry, I'm in a bit of a hurry).

items.use: A manner adverb for slow, unhurried action: yukkuri de ii (yo) means no rush, take your time, and mou sukoshi yukkuri asks someone to slow down. yukkuri shite ne / yukkuri shitette ne is different: a host's 'relax, make yourself at home'.

examplePolite.ja: ゆっくりでいいですよ。

items.freqNote: ゆっくり #515; set phrase ごゆっくり #1875 counted separately
items.notes: Survival line: mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai (please speak a little more slowly), or simply yukkuri onegaishimasu. goyukkuri douzo (enjoy, take your time) is the shop and host set phrase.

items.use: Says something is done the right, responsible way (chanto tabete, chanto kiite), and 'chanto shita hito' is a proper, reliable person.

examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと食べてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please make sure you eat properly.

items.notes: kichinto is a stiffer synonym. chanto is fine in polite speech too.

items.use: Says something works out or is done skilfully. It is used mostly in 'umaku iku' (go well) and in negatives that describe trouble (umaku ienai = can't put it well).

examplePolite.ja: 試験、うまくいきましたか？

items.freqNote: rank of うまくいく #761 (うまく行く #10741 and 上手くいく #16573 counted separately); the bare うまく token is only #45903, probably because the tokenizer lemmatises the adverb to うまい #246 (unverified)
items.notes: Learner lifeline: umaku ienai kedo... (I can't put it well, but...).

blocks.label: How sure
blocks.rationale: The certainty dial runs from a soft guess to full commitment, and 'of course' takes the point for granted.
blocks.interference: tabun, kitto and zettai share one frame (___ daijoubu da yo), so only the strength changes. kitto is mostly for confident guesses about others or the future, and rarely for your own firm plans.

items.use: The default hedge: it commits softly to any claim and is often closed with deshou, kamo or to omou.

examplePolite.ja: 多分大丈夫ですよ。

items.freqNote: 多分 #1323 and kana たぶん #1598 are counted separately, so real use is well above either rank
items.notes: osoraku is the stiffer, more formal 'probably'; tabun is fine in desu/masu speech.

items.use: A confident guess about something you can't check, such as someone else's feelings, an outcome or the future.

examplePolite.ja: きっと大丈夫ですよ。

items.notes: To commit to your own plan, say zettai iku (or kanarazu iku); kitto iku sounds like a heartfelt promise rather than a plan. kitto kite ne (be sure to come) is fine.

items.use: The strongest commitment either way, as in zettai iku (definitely going) and zettai dame (absolutely not). It is constant in promises and refusals.

examplePolite.ja: 絶対大丈夫ですよ。

items.notes: zettai ni is the same word; casual speech usually drops the ni. For polite commitments, kanarazu (without fail) is safer, but it doesn't do 'never' the way zettai ikanai does.

items.use: Says something goes without saying, either before a statement or alone as a warm 'of course!' reply.

examplePolite.ja: もちろん行きますよ。

items.freqNote: もちろん #264 (kanji 勿論 #46156)
items.notes: As a reply to a request, mochiron! means 'sure, happy to'.

blocks.label: Together, alone, as is
blocks.rationale: Set phrases that give the circumstances of an action (with others, by yourself, or leaving things as they are), and all fit before a verb like iku.
blocks.interference: issho ni and hitori de share the casual question frame (___ iku?). kono mama is the current situation, often 'if things go on like this'; sono mama is that thing as it stands, or carrying straight on without a further step.

items.use: Says an action is shared, with 'X to issho ni' meaning with X. It is the core of every invitation (issho ni ikou, issho ni iku?).

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come along?

items.notes: issho without ni means 'the same': issho da ne = same here. Polite invitations use -masen ka (issho ni ikimasen ka); casual can be iku? or ikanai?

items.use: Says you do something on your own, either without company or without help (hitori de dekiru).

examplePolite.ja: 一人で行きますか？

items.freqNote: 一人で #913; kana ひとりで #7320 and 独りで #9339 counted separately
items.notes: Two people is futari de.

items.use: Keeps the current situation unchanged, as in 'kono mama de ii' (fine like this) and 'kono mama ja dame' (can't go on like this).

examplePolite.romaji: kono mama de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このままでいいですよ。

items.notes: kono mama ja... warns where things are heading if nothing changes.

items.english: as is; just like that; straight on
items.use: Leaves something as it is (sono mama de ii = leave it as is, no need to change anything), or carries straight on without a further step (sono mama kaetta = went straight home; sono mama mattete = just wait there).

examplePolite.ja: そのまま帰りました。

items.notes: To a clerk offering a bag or wrapping, sono mama de ii desu means 'it's fine as it is'. Said to a person, sono mama de ii also reassures: you're fine as you are. sono mama omachi kudasai (please hold) is the fixed phone and shop line.

blocks.label: Expected or not
blocks.rationale: Reactions to how things match expectations: confirmed, admirably confirmed, flatly refused, or tentatively suspected.
blocks.interference: yappari (turned out as I thought) and sasuga (praise: just what you'd expect of them) share '___ kenta da ne', but yappari kenta da ne can be a sigh (late again) while sasuga kenta da ne is praise. masaka (surely not!) and moshikashite (could it be?) share '___ wasureta no?'.

items.use: Confirms that something turned out as you thought, restates a settled opinion (yappari natsu wa biiru da ne = summer means beer, after all), or marks a change of mind (yappari yameru = actually, I'll skip it).

example.english: Typical Kenta, just as I thought.

examplePolite.ja: やっぱり健太さんですね。
examplePolite.english: Typical Kenta, just as I thought.

items.freqNote: やっぱり #150; clipped やっぱ #576; formal やはり #979
items.notes: Casual speech clips it to yappa. yahari is the formal, written-leaning form (meetings, news); in desu/masu speech yappari is normal.

items.english: impressive; as expected (of you); that's X for you
items.use: Praise that someone lives up to their reputation, either alone ('sasuga!') or as 'sasuga X da ne'. With ni, it means 'understandably, as you'd expect': sasuga ni tsukareta (I'm tired, understandably), sasuga ni sore wa muri (that's really too much).

examplePolite.ja: さすが健太さんですね。
examplePolite.english: Just what you'd expect from Kenta.

items.freqNote: さすが #463; さすがに #1098 counted separately
items.notes: Bare sasuga is praise; for bad news you expected, use yappari. sasuga ni is the separate 'understandably, even so' sense. Said flatly, sasuga da ne can be sarcastic.

items.use: Expresses disbelief, either alone as 'no way!' or to open a guess you hope is wrong (masaka ... ja nai yo ne).

examplePolite.ja: まさか忘れたんですか？

items.notes: masaka! alone is a full reaction: no way!

items.use: Floats a guess or a tentative question, usually ending in no?, kana or kamo.

example.english: Did you forget, by any chance?

examplePolite.ja: もしかして忘れたんですか？
examplePolite.english: Did you forget, by any chance?

items.freqNote: もしかして #431; variant もしかしたら #988 counted separately
items.notes: moshikashitara is the 'if by any chance' variant (moshikashitara kuru kamo). Polite-safe opener for a sensitive guess: moshikashite, tanaka san desu ka? (Are you Mr. Tanaka, by any chance?)

blocks.label: Honestly, actually
blocks.rationale: Openers that flag how real or how frank the next thing said is.
blocks.interference: jitsu wa (reveals something new) and shoujiki (gives a frank opinion) share one frame. maji de is slang for 'seriously', so swap in hontou ni outside friends.

items.use: Opens a confession, a piece of news or a favour, and signals that something real or unexpected is coming.

example.romaji: jitsu wa anmari suki ja nai.
example.ja: 実はあんまり好きじゃない。
example.english: Actually, I don't really like it.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa amari suki ja nai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 実はあまり好きじゃないです。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I don't really like it.

items.notes: Often stretched as jitsu wa ne... to buy a moment before the news.

items.use: Goes at the start of a sentence to mark a frank opinion, often a negative one; shoujiki ni iu to means 'to be honest'.

example.ja: 正直、あんまり好きじゃない。
example.english: Honestly, I'm not a big fan.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, amari suki ja nai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、あまり好きじゃないです。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I'm not a big fan.

items.freqNote: rank includes adjectival 'honest' uses of 正直
items.notes: As a na-adjective it means 'honest' (shoujiki na hito).

items.use: A casual intensifier ('really, seriously') among friends. Said alone with a rising tone, it means 'seriously?'.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, hontou ni oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、本当においしいですね。

items.freqNote: マジで is not a token; rank of マジ
items.notes: Never with superiors or strangers; use hontou ni instead (often clipped to honto ni in speech). maji? alone works too; maji ka is rough and male-coded.

blocks.label: Softeners
blocks.rationale: Words that take the edge off: downplaying, hedging an action, and softening a request.
blocks.interference: betsu ni denies something the listener might assume ('it's not that...'), while toku ni just says nothing stands out; a bare 'betsu ni.' sounds curt and toku ni doesn't. ichiou (just in case) is not toriaezu (for now).

items.english: not particularly; not really; it's not that...
items.use: Denies something the listener might assume ('it's not that...'), usually with a negative (betsu ni okotte nai, betsu ni mondai nai). betsu ni ii yo / betsu ni ii kedo means 'I don't mind' but can sound grudging, and a bare 'betsu ni.' is a curt 'whatever'.

examplePolite.romaji: betsu ni okotte nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 別に怒ってないですよ。

items.notes: A bare 'betsu ni.' as a reply sounds cold; say toku ni nai instead. Exceptions to the negative rule: betsu ni ii (I don't mind) and the bare curt reply.

items.use: Singles one thing out (toku ni kore ga suki), and with a negative it is the neutral, polite-safe 'nothing in particular'.

examplePolite.romaji: toku ni mondai nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 特に問題ないですよ。

items.notes: toku ni nai (desu) is the safe answer to 'any questions?'.

items.use: Hedges an action done to be safe (ichiou kakunin suru) or a claim that is only technically true (ichiou dekita).

example.english: I'll take an umbrella just in case.

examplePolite.ja: 一応傘持っていきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll take an umbrella just in case.

items.notes: It also works as modesty: ichiou eigo hanaseru = I speak English, sort of.

items.use: Goes at the front of a request or preference and softens it by making it conditional.

example.ja: できれば明日がいいな。

examplePolite.romaji: dekireba ashita ga ii n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: できれば明日がいいんですけど。

items.notes: Literally 'if it can be done': dekiru + -ba.

blocks.label: Getting through
blocks.rationale: Words for handling a situation: start somewhere, push past the details, manage somehow, and say how it ended.
blocks.interference: toriaezu (for now, as a first step) and tonikaku (anyway, whatever else) share '___ yatte miyou'. nantoka is about managing despite trouble; kekkyoku is about the final outcome.

items.use: Marks a first step or a temporary choice made before deciding the rest (toriaezu biiru, toriaezu yatte miru).

example.ja: とりあえずやってみよう。
example.english: Let's just try it for now.

examplePolite.ja: とりあえずやってみましょう。

items.freqNote: とりあえず #864; 取りあえず #5786 counted separately
items.notes: toriaezu biiru (beer to start) is the classic first order at an izakaya.

items.use: Cuts past details or doubts to the main point or action (tonikaku ikou, tonikaku tsukareta).

example.ja: とにかくやってみよう。
example.english: Never mind the details, let's just try it.

examplePolite.ja: とにかくやってみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Never mind the details, let's just try it.

items.notes: It also pivots a story to its point: tonikaku, sugokatta (anyway, it was amazing).

items.use: Says something gets handled despite difficulty, as in nantoka naru (it'll work out), nantoka dekita and nantoka shite (do something!).

examplePolite.ja: 何とかなりますよ。

items.freqNote: 何とか #1078; kana なんとか #2646 counted separately
items.notes: It also stands in for a forgotten name: nantoka san (Mr. So-and-so).

items.use: Sums up how things finally turned out, often against the plan, which makes it key for telling stories.

example.english: In the end, it didn't work out.

examplePolite.ja: 結局ダメでした。
examplePolite.english: In the end, it didn't work out.

items.notes: kekkyoku reports the final outcome; yappari says it matched what you expected.
