reviewSummaries: natural: The block is strong: almost every casual example is what a Tokyo speaker actually says, the polite pairs keep the meaning, and all freqRanks match the tool output. The real problems are 'yukkuri shite ne' glossed as 'take your time' (it means 'make yourself at home', which breaks the hayaku/yukkuri pair), 'issho ni ikimasu ka' used where the invitation is 'ikimasen ka', yahari set as an over-formal polite pair, and maji de with no polite example. The rest is polish: casual 'motteku', 'toku ni' spelling, kono/sono mama glossed identically, and the 'sasuga ni' sense missing.

nuance: Strong draft overall. Every freqRank I spot-checked matches the tool output, all alsoIn pointers resolve, register pairs are true counterparts (yappari→yahari and maji de→hontou ni are handled well), and the slang flag on maji de is right. One fatal error: sasuga is called 'only for admiration' despite the frequent sasuga ni sense. The major problems are polite issho ni using ikimasu ka instead of the invitation form ikimasen ka; contrast pairs that can't be heard apart (kono/sono mama, betsu ni/tokuni); yappari and betsu ni each missing their most common conversational sense; maji de missing its polite example; and a 3-item 'Honestly, actually' block. No item needs cutting.

form: The data is clean overall. All 27 freqRanks match the tool exactly, every freqNote figure checks out, and all 10+ alsoIn pointers I grepped resolve (11-list-adjectives #8, 13-list-exit-battery #101/#113, learner-phrases expr_yukkuri_onegai, core-vocab Intensifiers/Intensifiers (extended)/na-adjectives (extended), utility-vocab counter-people, kotoba particles de, 05 response tokens majide). Kana, polite/politeJa pairs, masu forms and example romaji/ja agree word for word, with no duplicate slugs and 3–4 items per block. The real defects: tokuni breaks the particle-spacing convention its sibling betsu ni follows; maji-de has a polite value with no polite example and a prereq that isn't a slug (betsu-ni '-nai' and dekireba '-ba' have the same problem); yappari's polite 'yahari' contradicts its own note; and tashika-ni (#230) from the C selection was silently dropped.

categories.name: Versatile adjectives
categories.scope: i-/na-adjectives that apply across almost any topic

blocks.label: Good or no good
blocks.rationale: The four basic verdicts (good, OK, no good, bad) that answer 'is this all right?' about anything.
blocks.interference: ii and daijoubu both mean 'OK' and both turn down offers (ii desu / daijoubu desu = no thanks). The shared frame keeps them apart: kore de ii? asks for approval, kore de daijoubu? asks if anything is wrong, and dame flips the frame to kore ja dame?

items.use: The default positive verdict on anything, and 'fine, acceptable' when checking (kore de ii?). When choosing, X ga ii = I'd like X, and X de ii = X will do. It is also the core of -te mo ii (may) and -ta hou ga ii (should).

examplePolite.ja: これでいいですか？

items.freqNote: いい #24; includes reply and -te mo ii uses; formal 良い #1474
items.notes: Only the dictionary form is ii; every other form uses yo-: yokatta, yokunai, yokute. As a reply, ii yo = sure, go ahead, but ii desu to an offer usually means no thanks; accept with onegaishimasu. Choosing a gift or dish, say kore ga ii: kore de ii sounds like settling.

items.use: Says someone or something is OK, safe or not a problem; it is how you check on people (daijoubu?), and daijoubu desu politely declines an offer.

examplePolite.ja: これで大丈夫ですか？

items.freqNote: 大丈夫 #76; rank includes the reply use (daijoubu desu = no thanks)
items.notes: To an offer it usually means 'no thanks' (fukuro wa? / daijoubu desu), but it can also mean 'yes, that's fine', so clerks may check again. To accept clearly, say onegaishimasu.

items.use: Says something is no good, won't work or isn't allowed (rules, plans, broken things, hopeless efforts), and is the base of -cha dame (must not).

examplePolite.ja: これじゃダメですか？

items.freqNote: spelling split: ダメ #596, 駄目 #1901, だめ #3328; combined it is far higher than any one row
items.notes: In the 'is this OK?' frame, de ii becomes ja dame: kore de ii? / kore ja dame?

items.use: Bad in quality, weather, health (guai ga warui) or behaviour, and 'to blame' (X ga warui); the opposite of ii.

example.romaji: kyou, chotto guai warui n da
example.ja: 今日、ちょっと具合悪いんだ

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto guai ga warui n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと具合が悪いんです

items.freqNote: 悪い #139; includes the casual apology 'warui'
items.notes: Casual apology: warui! or warui ne (mostly male), and warui kedo... (sorry, but...), which everyone uses. The polite equivalent is sumimasen / sumimasen ga..., never warui desu.

blocks.label: Like & dislike
blocks.rationale: The three ways to say how you feel about a thing; all can take the X ga ___ frame.
blocks.interference: kirai is a settled dislike of a thing or person; iya is a gut rejection, 'I don't want this / this is unpleasant', usually about what is happening now. Drill 'ame no hi, kirai' (rainy days in general) against 'mata ame? iya da naa' (the rain today). iya also sounds like the interjection iya ('no / well', G): the interjection is soft and opens a reply (iya, chigau yo), while the adjective is emphatic and stands alone or ends the sentence (iya!, iya da, iya na yokan).

items.use: Says you like something or someone (X ga suki); suki na X means 'the X I like, my favourite X'.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga suki desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が好きです

items.notes: Ends in -i but is a na-adjective: suki ja nai, suki datta (never sukikunai). About a person, suki usually means romantic interest, and 'suki desu' to someone's face is a confession; for friendly liking say ii hito da ne or yasashii ne.

items.use: Says you dislike something or someone (X ga kirai); it sounds strong about people, so polite speech often softens it to amari suki ja nai.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga kirai desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が嫌いです

items.notes: A na-adjective despite ending in -ai: kirai ja nai, kirai datta.

items.use: A gut rejection of a situation or action, 'I don't want this / this is unpleasant' ('iya!', iya da, iku no iya da = I don't want to go); more immediate and emotional than kirai. iya na X = unpleasant X (iya na yokan = a bad feeling).

example.english: Rain again? Ugh, I hate this.

examplePolite.romaji: mata ame desu ne. iya desu ne
examplePolite.ja: また雨ですね。嫌ですね

items.freqNote: 嫌 #304; いや #54 is mostly the interjection 'no / well' (G); casual contraction やだ #777
items.notes: Casually iya da is usually yada: mou yada (I've had enough), yada yo (no way). Polite iya desu in reply to a request is a blunt, childish-sounding refusal; refuse with chotto... or kekkou desu instead. About things like the weather, iya desu ne is fine small talk.

blocks.label: Want & need
blocks.rationale: What you want, what you need and what matters, all said with X ga ___.
blocks.interference: hoshii (want) and hitsuyou (need) share the same sentence, so only the word changes (casual hitsuyou adds da na). Remember hoshii is an adjective, not a verb (X ga hoshii, never X o hoshii).

items.use: Says you want a thing (X ga hoshii); it is an adjective, and for wanting to do something use -tai, for wanting someone else to do it -te hoshii.

example.ja: 新しいパソコンがほしい

examplePolite.ja: 新しいパソコンがほしいです

items.freqNote: ほしい #195 (欲しい #420); includes the -te hoshii auxiliary
alsoIn: vocab-trainer core-vocab: Intensifiers (in example of motto)
items.notes: Only for your own wants. Asking a superior 'X ga hoshii desu ka?' sounds too direct. To ask for something in a shop, say X o kudasai or X onegaishimasu, not X ga hoshii desu.

items.use: Says something is needed (X ga hitsuyou) or not needed (hitsuyou nai), for documents, money, time, skills and steps.

example.romaji: atarashii pasokon ga hitsuyou da na
example.ja: 新しいパソコンが必要だな
example.english: I'm going to need a new computer.

examplePolite.ja: 新しいパソコンが必要です

items.freqNote: 必要 #271; casual verb 要る (iru, need) #2729
items.notes: Casual 'need' is usually the verb iru (要る): kore iru? / iranai (no need). It sounds like iru (be there), but the negatives differ: iranai = don't need, inai = isn't here.

items.use: Says something or someone is important or precious (daiji na hanashi = an important matter), and odaiji ni means 'take care' to someone who is ill.

example.romaji: kazoku ga ichiban daiji da yo

examplePolite.romaji: kazoku ga ichiban daiji desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 家族が一番大事ですね

items.freqNote: 大事 #262; synonym 大切 (taisetsu) #578
items.notes: taisetsu is a synonym that sounds warmer and a little more formal; daiji is the everyday spoken choice.

blocks.label: Amazing & awful
blocks.rationale: Strong reactions at both ends of the scale: amazing, best, worst, terrible, and yabai, which can mean either.
blocks.interference: saikou and saiaku both start with sai- and mean opposite things, so learn saikou first and add saiaku once it is solid. sugoi and yabai share a sentence: same feeling, but yabai is casual only.

items.use: The all-purpose impressed reaction ('sugoi!') to people, skills, views and news; it also marks sheer intensity, good or bad (sugoi ame = torrential rain), and as sugoku it becomes 'really, very' (B).

examplePolite.ja: この歌、すごいですね

items.freqNote: すごい #114; masculine-rough variant すげえ #1510 (noted, not carded)
items.notes: The rough male sugee is heard all the time in dramas; recognise it, but say sugoi. Casually, bare sugoi also works as 'really' (sugoi oishii = really tasty); with desu, use sugoku or totemo.

items.use: The top-end enthusiastic verdict on a day, meal, person or experience ('saikou!'); it takes da or datta like a noun.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は最高でした

items.use: The top-end complaint about a day, event, person or situation; said alone, 'saiaku!' is the standard 'ugh, terrible' reaction to bad luck.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は最悪でした

items.notes: sai-kou and sai-aku only differ after sai-, so hear the whole word before you react.

items.use: Says something is terrible (weather, a cold, traffic) or that someone is mean or unfair; 'hidoi!' is the reaction to being treated badly, and 'sore wa hidoi' is sympathy for someone's story.

examplePolite.ja: それはひどいですね

items.notes: Said to someone's face, 'hidoi!' means 'that's mean!'

items.politeJa: すごいです / まずいです
items.use: Casual intensity word with two senses, 'uh-oh, I'm in trouble' (the original) and 'insanely good' (younger speakers); tone and context decide which.

examplePolite.ja: この歌、すごいですね

items.freqNote: spelling split: ヤバい #1166, やばい #2058, やべえ #4269
items.notes: The 'uh-oh' sense: 'yabai, okureru!' = Oh no, I'm going to be late! Don't use it with clerks or strangers: politely, say sugoi desu for the good sense and mazui desu for the uh-oh sense (mazui desu ne, okuremasu).

blocks.label: Fun, tasty, cute
blocks.rationale: The positive comments you make about food, things, activities and shows, plus boring as the let-down.
blocks.interference: tanoshii (fun to do) and omoshiroi (interesting or entertaining in itself) are the classic mix-up, and the shared job sentence keeps the difference to one word. kawaii (ka-wa-i-i) is easily misheard as kowai (ko-wa-i, scary, in a later block).

items.use: Says food or drink tastes good, at nearly every meal; often a one-word reaction ('oishii!') or the past oishikatta as thanks to the cook.

examplePolite.ja: これ、おいしいですね

items.freqNote: おいしい #302 (美味しい #5867)
items.notes: umai is a blunter casual 'tasty' (more common from men, but not male-only) and also means 'good at'; oishii is safe for everyone and the safe choice with desu.

items.use: A reaction to anything cute or charming (animals, babies, clothes, design, people), used much more widely and freely than English 'cute'.

examplePolite.ja: その服、かわいいですね

items.notes: Don't confuse it with kowai (scary): ka-wa-i-i has four beats, ko-wa-i has three. kawaisou is a different word meaning 'poor thing, what a shame', not 'looks cute'.

items.use: Says an activity or time is fun for the people taking part, most often in the past after an event (tanoshikatta).

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa tanoshii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は楽しいですね

items.freqNote: 楽しい #283
items.notes: It doesn't mean 'happy': that is ureshii (glad about something).

items.use: Says something is interesting or entertaining (shows, ideas, people, places) and also 'funny' (a joke, a person); it is the default praise for content.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa omoshiroi desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は面白いですね

items.freqNote: 面白い #558 (おもしろい #3445)
items.notes: tanoshii is about the fun of doing something; omoshiroi is about the thing itself being interesting or entertaining. For a game, show or book, omoshiroi is the normal praise ('it's good').

items.use: Says something is boring or dull (a show, a job, a person, a day); the opposite of omoshiroi, and in fast speech often tsumannai.

example.ja: この仕事、つまんないね

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa tsumaranai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事はつまらないですね

items.freqNote: つまらない #2645; contracted つまんない #2662 is roughly equal
items.notes: The -nai is part of the word, not a negative. Its own negative is tsumaranakunai. Casual speech mostly says tsumannai; use the full tsumaranai with desu.

blocks.label: How you're doing
blocks.rationale: The small-talk status words for checking in and making plans: well, busy, free.
blocks.interference: isogashii and hima are opposites that fill the same casual invitation slot (ashita no yoru, ___?), so learn isogashii first and then swap in hima. Politely, ask oisogashii desu ka? or aitemasu ka?, not hima desu ka?

items.use: The check-in word ('genki?' = how are you doing?) for someone you haven't seen in a while; it also describes good health, good spirits and lively people.

example.english: Long time no see. How have you been?

examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気でしたか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time. How have you been?

items.notes: When you ask about someone else politely, add o- (ogenki desu ka?); about yourself it stays genki desu.

items.use: Says a person is busy; it is the standard small-talk status (saikin isogashii) and the polite excuse for turning something down.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no yoru wa oisogashii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日の夜はお忙しいですか？

items.freqNote: 忙しい #447
items.notes: Describes people, days and workplaces (kyou wa isogashii, isogashii jiki), but not a crowded street: that is hito ga ooi or konderu. Asking about someone else politely, add o-: oisogashii desu ka? The opener oisogashii tokoro sumimasen = sorry to bother you when you're busy.

items.use: Says someone has free time ('hima?' is the standard opener before an invitation) or is bored with nothing to do (hima da naa).

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no yoru nara hima desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 明日の夜なら暇ですよ
examplePolite.english: If it's tomorrow night, I'm free.

items.notes: Asking a coworker, clerk or stranger 'hima desu ka?' can sound like 'got nothing to do?'. To ask politely, say ashita no yoru, aitemasu ka? or jikan arimasu ka?; hima desu is fine about yourself.

blocks.label: Easy & hard
blocks.rationale: The difficulty scale for tasks and situations, from easy through hard and tough to impossible.
blocks.interference: muzukashii (hard to do or understand), taihen (hard to go through, lots of work) and muri (can't be done) blur together. The shared 'kono shigoto' sentence isolates the nuance, and kantan anchors the easy end.

items.use: Says a task, recipe, explanation or test is easy or simple; kantan ni means 'simply, briefly'.

example.english: This job is easy, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa kantan desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は簡単ですね
examplePolite.english: This job is easy, isn't it?

items.notes: A na-word: before ne or yo it takes da (kantan da ne), and its past is kantan datta, never kantankatta.

items.use: Says something is hard to do or understand (tasks, questions, languages, decisions); chotto muzukashii is also a soft way to say no.

example.english: This job is difficult, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa muzukashii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は難しいですね
examplePolite.english: This job is difficult, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 難しい #468
items.notes: 'Sore wa chotto muzukashii desu' usually means a polite no, not just 'difficult'.

items.use: Says a situation is tough, a lot of work or a real problem; 'taihen da ne' is the stock sympathy reply to anyone's hard time, and 'taihen!' alone means 'oh no, trouble!'.

example.english: This job is tough, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa taihen desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は大変ですね
examplePolite.english: This job is tough, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 大変 #224; includes the formal 'very' sense
items.notes: In formal speech taihen also means 'very' (taihen moushiwake arimasen).

items.use: Says something is impossible or too much for you; 'muri!' or 'kyou wa muri' is the everyday casual refusal, and muri shinaide means 'don't overdo it'.

example.english: No way we can do this job.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa muri desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は無理ですね
examplePolite.english: No way we can do this job.

items.freqNote: 無理 #217; includes muri suru / muri shinaide
items.notes: Blunt to a superior; chotto muzukashii desu refuses more politely. Everyday casual refusal: ashita? gomen, muri.

blocks.label: Price & speed
blocks.rationale: The two everyday scales for errands and plans: what something costs and how early, late, fast or slow it is.
blocks.interference: Antonym pairs get swapped, so learn takai before yasui and hayai before osoi, then mix them; per 11-list-adjectives note 9(d), keep yasui at least 15 items after takai in drill order even though they share a block. takai also means tall or high, and its opposite there is hikui, not yasui.

items.use: Expensive (the daily shopping sense), and also high or tall for buildings, people, voices and levels; the opposite is yasui for price and hikui for height.

examplePolite.ja: このお店、高いですね

items.notes: se ga takai = tall (of a person).

items.use: Says something is cheap or good value (prices, shops, deals); it is the opposite of takai only in the price sense.

examplePolite.ja: このお店、安いですね

items.freqNote: 安い #1315; やすい #1141 is mostly the -yasui suffix (easy to ...), which is not carded
items.notes: It is a different word from the suffix -yasui (easy to ...): tabeyasui = easy to eat.

items.use: Early in time ('mou? hayai!') and fast in speed or progress; it is one word by ear but has two kanji in writing (早い early, 速い fast).

examplePolite.ja: 今日は早いですね

items.freqNote: 早い #396; 速い #2346 (two kanji, one word by ear)
items.notes: The adverb hayaku (quickly, early) is its own item in C.

items.use: Late in time or slow in speed; 'mou osoi' means it's too late now, and 'osoi!' is the complaint to someone who kept you waiting.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は遅いですね

items.notes: 'Late for something' uses the verb okureru (densha ni okureta), not osoi.

blocks.label: Glad, let down, worried
blocks.rationale: Your own emotional reactions to news and to what's coming: glad, disappointed, scared, worried.
blocks.interference: kowai (scared) and shinpai (worried) share the exam-results sentence so only the feeling changes, and ureshii and zannen are paired replies to news. kowai also sounds like kawaii (cute, earlier block): three beats against four.

items.use: Says you are glad about something specific (a gift, news, a compliment), either as 'ureshii!' or as -te ureshii; it describes your own feeling, not a general state of happiness.

examplePolite.ja: それはうれしいです

items.notes: 'Happy in life' is shiawase; ureshii is for one good thing that happened. About someone else, say ureshisou (looks happy).

items.use: The reaction to disappointing news, a cancellation or a missed chance ('zannen!', 'sore wa zannen'), and the base of -te zannen (it's a shame that ...: aenakute zannen = shame we couldn't meet).

examplePolite.ja: それは残念ですね

items.notes: Use it for let-downs; for real hardship the sympathy line is taihen da ne. It is not an apology: for 'I'm sorry' use gomen or sumimasen.

items.use: Says something is scary or that you are scared (films, heights, people, the future); about a strict person it means 'intimidating'.

example.english: I'm scared to see my exam results.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no kekka ga kowai desu
examplePolite.ja: 試験の結果が怖いです
examplePolite.english: I'm scared to see my exam results.

items.notes: The same word covers 'scary' (the thing) and 'scared' (you); context decides.

items.use: Says you are worried about someone or something (X ga shinpai), and shinpai shinaide means 'don't worry'; it is na-class even though it ends in -ai.

example.english: I'm worried about my exam results.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no kekka ga shinpai desu
examplePolite.ja: 試験の結果が心配です
examplePolite.english: I'm worried about my exam results.

items.freqNote: 心配 #210; includes the verb shinpai suru
items.notes: Also a verb, shinpai suru; the form you'll use most is shinpai shinaide (don't worry).

blocks.label: Size & amount
blocks.rationale: How big something is and how much of it there is: the two size-and-quantity scales.
blocks.interference: ookii (big) and ooi (many) both start with oo-: hito ga ooi means 'crowded', while ookii hito is 'a big person'. Within each pair, learn the first word before adding its opposite.

items.use: The size of things and people, loudness (ookii koe = a loud voice) and how big a matter is; before nouns, ookina is just as common.

example.ja: この靴、ちょっと大きい
example.english: These shoes are a bit big.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa chotto ookii desu
examplePolite.ja: この靴はちょっと大きいです
examplePolite.english: These shoes are a little big.

items.freqNote: 大きい #536; the prenominal 大きな #538 is counted separately
items.notes: For 'a lot of', use ooi or takusan, not ookii.

items.use: The size of things, quiet voices (chiisai koe) and childhood (chiisai koro = when I was little); before nouns it is also chiisana.

example.ja: この靴、ちょっと小さい
example.english: These shoes are a bit small.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa chotto chiisai desu
examplePolite.ja: この靴はちょっと小さいです
examplePolite.english: These shoes are a little small.

items.freqNote: 小さい #879; prenominal 小さな #1079
items.notes: chiisana goes only before a noun (chiisana mise); at the end of a sentence it is always chiisai.

items.use: Says there are many or a lot of something, or that something happens often (machigai ga ooi); it works after the noun (hito ga ooi) and not normally in front of it.

example.english: There are a lot of people today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hito ga ooi desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日は人が多いですね
examplePolite.english: There are a lot of people today.

items.notes: Not 'ooi hito' for 'many people'; say takusan no hito instead.

items.use: Says there are few or not much of something; the opposite of ooi, with the same after-the-noun pattern (hito ga sukunai).

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hito ga sukunai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日は人が少ないですね

items.notes: Not sukoshi (a little, B): sukunai describes an amount, sukoshi gives one.

blocks.label: Same & different
blocks.rationale: Comparing and sorting: the same, another one, weird, normal, all sorts.
blocks.interference: onaji takes a noun directly (onaji iro) but betsu needs no (betsu no iro), and the shared sentence makes that the only difference. futsuu and hen are opposites on the same 'sore, ___ da yo' sentence.

items.use: Says things are the same (X to onaji) for comparisons on any topic; it goes straight before a noun with no na or no (onaji iro).

examplePolite.ja: 同じ色がいいです

items.notes: watashi mo onaji (same here) is the easy everyday reply.

items.use: Means another or a separate one: betsu no X (a different X) and betsubetsu (separately), for choices, payments, plans and people.

examplePolite.romaji: betsu no iro ga ii desu
examplePolite.ja: 別の色がいいです

items.freqNote: 別 #500; includes the adverb betsu ni (C)
items.notes: Paying separately is betsubetsu de (onegaishimasu). betsu ni (not really) is its own item in C.

items.use: Says something is strange or off (a taste, a sound, a person, a situation); hen na X goes in front of any noun.

examplePolite.ja: それは変ですよ

items.notes: About a person (hen na hito) it is a real criticism; about a taste or a noise it is neutral.

items.use: Says something is normal, usual or average and serves as the baseline in comparisons (futsuu wa = usually); futsuu ni means 'normally' and, in casual speech, 'honestly, genuinely' (futsuu ni oishii = it's actually really good).

examplePolite.ja: それは普通ですよ

items.freqNote: 普通 #344; includes adverbial futsuu ni
items.notes: As an answer to 'how was it?', futsuu means 'just OK, nothing special'. It is lukewarm, not praise.

items.use: Means many different things without listing them: iroiro na X (all sorts of X), iroiro atta (a lot happened), iroiro arigatou (thanks for everything).

example.ja: 今日はいろいろあった

examplePolite.ja: 今日はいろいろありました

items.notes: As a reply, iroiro desu ne means 'it varies, it depends'.

reviewSummaries: natural: Solid block: the right 44 adjectives, accurate notes on register traps, and every freqRank verified against the tool (all match). Most minimal-pair frames sound natural to a native ear. The main problems come from forcing a word into a shared frame where it doesn't fit (kowai with an exam, iya as a general dislike, omoshiroi translated as 'interesting'). Two polite examples contradict their own guidance (hima desu ka?) or the register (bare mise). Two casual forms aren't what people actually say (tsumannai, yada).

nuance: Solid draft overall. All 44 freqRanks match the tool, the glosses are mostly accurate, and many good traps are already flagged (daijoubu as 'no thanks', the lexical -nai on tsumaranai, ooi only after its noun, chotto muzukashii as a soft no). The main weaknesses are pragmatic:
- iya's interference note gives a wrong rule (fatal).
- ii lacks the ga/de choosing sense and the ii yo vs ii desu reply split.
- Three shared frames undercut the contrasts they're meant to teach (iya/kirai, tanoshii/omoshiroi on a game, kowai/shinpai on an exam).
- Some polite glosses change meaning.
- Three blocks have only 3 items, and jouzu/heta/nigate, daisuki, itai, atarashii and the weather pair are missing without a recorded reason.
No item needs cutting.

form: The data is accurate. I checked all 44 freqRank values and about 20 secondary ranks in freqNote with the frequency tool, and every one matches its output. All 47 alsoIn pointers resolve to the right entry, except daiji's two, which point to its synonym taisetsu. Romaji, kana, politeJa, conjugations and the word-for-word example ja/romaji are all correct, every block has 3–5 items, and slugs are unique within D. The real problems are a slug collision ('iya' is also G's interjection), a kantan note that contradicts the bare na-adjective examples elsewhere, cross-tags such as (G) and (I) pointing to items that are not in the keep list, the betsubetsu spacing, particle prereqs that are not list items, and a few English glosses that drift from the Japanese.

categories.name: Connectors & conditionals
categories.scope: what links one idea to the next

blocks.label: But
blocks.rationale: Three ways to say 'but', from neutral to complaining, learned on one rain sentence.
blocks.interference: demo starts a new sentence, -kedo ends the first clause, -noni adds surprise or complaint and can't lead into a request or plan; the shared 'ame ... iku' sentence keeps only the connector changing.

items.use: Opens a sentence or a turn that pushes back against what was just said; works the same in every register.

example.romaji: ame da ne. demo, iku yo.
example.english: It's raining, huh. But I'm going.

examplePolite.romaji: ame desu ne. demo, ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 雨ですね。でも、行きますよ。

items.freqNote: でも #32 (also counts noun + demo 'even / or something')
items.notes: Same sound as noun + demo ('ocha demo' = tea or something); sentence-initial position tells them apart.

items.politeJa: ですけど / ますけど
items.use: Ends the first clause and contrasts it with the second. Left trailing, it softens a statement ('chotto takai kedo...') or sets up a request ('chotto kikitai n da kedo...'). Fuller keredo; formal ga.

examplePolite.ja: 雨ですけど、行きますよ。

items.freqNote: けど #37; fuller けれど #1376
items.notes: A trailing kedo ('sumimasen kedo...') is a soft opener, not a contrast.

items.use: Contrast with surprise, complaint or regret: the result isn't what the first clause should lead to. Nouns and na-adjectives take na noni. Left trailing it's a complaint ('itta noni!' = 'but I told you!'); after -tara / -ba it means 'if only' ('motto hayaku ittara, maniatta noni').

example.english: You're going, even though it's raining?

examplePolite.romaji: ame na noni, iku n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨なのに、行くんですか？
examplePolite.english: You're going even though it's raining?

items.freqNote: のに #95 (also counts purpose noni); sentence-initial なのに #274, それなのに #1791
items.notes: Can't end in a request or plan ('...noni, ikou' is wrong); use kedo there.

blocks.label: Because / so
blocks.rationale: The reason family: two clause linkers, two sentence openers and the reason-stacker.
blocks.interference: -kara vs -node differ in softness, not meaning: node sounds objective and suits strangers, and in polite speech it still follows the plain form ('isogashii node, ikemasen'). dakara points forward to the result while datte points back to the reason; kara, dakara and datte share the 'isogashii' reason so only the linker changes.

items.politeJa: ですから / ますから
items.use: Reason clause + kara + result; also ends a sentence as a bare excuse ('isogashii kara'). Nouns and na-adjectives take da kara.

example.english: I'm busy, so I can't go.

examplePolite.romaji: abunai desu kara, ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 危ないですから、気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous, so please be careful.

items.freqNote: から #14 (also counts 'from')
items.notes: Reason comes first, then kara, then the result: the reverse of English 'because'. As a polite refusal desu kara sounds pointed; use node there ('isogashii node, ikemasen').

items.use: Same reason-then-result order as kara, but sounds objective and softer; the standard choice for explanations and excuses to strangers. Nouns and na-adjectives take na node.

example.romaji: ashita hayai node, mou neru ne.
example.ja: 明日早いので、もう寝るね。
example.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'm heading to bed.

examplePolite.ja: 忙しいので、行けません。
examplePolite.english: I'm busy, so I can't go.

items.freqNote: ので #156; casual contraction -n de
items.notes: With friends kara is the default; node, when used, often clips to -n de ('isogashii n de'). In polite speech node still follows the plain form; desu node / -masu node is business-formal.

items.use: Starts a sentence that states the result of what came before; said sharply ('dakara!') it means 'like I said'.

example.ja: 忙しいんだ。だから、行けない。
example.english: I'm busy. So I can't go.

examplePolite.ja: 忙しいんです。なので、行けません。
examplePolite.english: I'm busy. So I can't go.

items.freqNote: だから #58; polite なので #652; ですから #269 (can sound insistent)
items.notes: Points forward to the result; datte points back to the reason. In polite speech, desu kara at the start of a sentence can sound insistent ('as I said'); nanode is the softer opener.

items.use: Starts a sentence that justifies yourself or pushes back, usually answering 'why?' or a complaint; the reason follows, often ending in n da (yo / mon).

examplePolite.ja: でも、忙しいんですよ。

items.freqNote: だって #79, also counts 'even / too' datte
items.notes: Sounds sulky to a coworker; there, open with demo and give the reason with ...n desu (yo). Don't confuse it with noun + datte 'even X' or hearsay '...n datte' ('I hear').

items.english: and what's more; since ... and all
items.use: Stacks reasons ('yasui shi, oishii shi'); a single trailing -shi hints there are more, like 'and all'. Nouns and na-adjectives take da shi.

example.english: It's late and all, let's head home.

examplePolite.ja: もう遅いですし、帰りましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's late and all, so let's head home.

items.notes: A trailing -shi gives a reason softly ('mou osoi shi'); it isn't a neutral 'and' for listing facts, use -te for that.

blocks.label: And then
blocks.rationale: Ways to carry on to the next thing: -te inside a sentence; de, jaa and ato at the start of one.
blocks.interference: Sentence-initial de is not the place / means particle de; ato alone means 'also' while ato de means 'later'; jaa overlaps with dattara (If-openers block).

items.use: The te-form chains clauses: one action then the next, or a cause and its result ('tsukarete, neta'). Adjectives join with -kute, nouns and na-adjectives with de.

examplePolite.ja: うちに帰って、寝ました。

items.freqNote: て #458, heavily undercounted: tokenizer usually fuses -te into the verb
items.notes: Tense and politeness go only on the last verb, in polite speech too: 'kaette, nemashita', not 'kaerimashite' (that sounds formal). A -te reason can't lead into a request or invitation ('isogashikute, tetsudatte' is wrong); use kara there.

items.use: Starts a sentence that moves a story to the next step, or prompts the speaker to go on ('de?' = 'and?'). Clipped casual form of sorede.

examplePolite.ja: それで、どうなりましたか？

items.freqNote: rank of それで; sentence-initial で is not separable from particle で (#8); slangy んで #3821
items.notes: Comes first, after a pause; that's how to hear it apart from the particle de. Bare 'de?' can sound impatient; 'de, de?' or 'sorede?' with rising pitch sounds keen.

items.use: Draws a conclusion from what was just said and moves to the next step: deciding, ordering, wrapping up, saying goodbye. Short form ja.

example.english: Okay then, I'll go with this.

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、これにします。
examplePolite.english: Okay then, I'll go with this one.

items.notes: To a clerk or coworker, jaa + masu is normal ('jaa, kore ni shimasu'); dewa is the formal version for meetings, announcements and shop staff.

items.use: Starts a sentence that adds one more item to a list, order or request, often as an afterthought.

examplePolite.ja: あと、これもお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Oh, and this one too, please.

items.freqNote: あと #135, also counts 'after / later / remaining'
items.notes: Ato de = 'later'; ato + amount = 'more / left' ('ato gofun' = five more minutes); bare ato at the start, then a pause = 'oh, and'.

blocks.label: Or / for example
blocks.rationale: Offering choices and examples instead of one definite thing.
blocks.interference: -toka lists things and can trail anything, -tari ... -tari lists actions and closes with suru; both use the same 'eiga' sentence. -tari is not -tara ('if').

items.use: A ka B offers a choice between nouns or clauses; B can take a second ka. Clause + ka dou ka = 'whether or not' ('kuru ka dou ka wakannai').

example.english: Are you free tomorrow or the day after?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ka asatte, jikan arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日か明後日、時間ありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have time tomorrow or the day after?

items.freqNote: か #11, also counts the question particle; sentence-initial それとも #892
items.notes: To offer the second option as its own question, use soretomo ('kocchi? soretomo acchi?').

items.use: Names examples without a full list ('A toka B toka'), or hedges one item so it sounds less blunt ('eiga toka'). '...toka itteta' = 'said something like'.

example.english: I'd like to see a movie or something.

examplePolite.ja: 映画とか見たいですね。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to see a movie or something.

items.freqNote: とか #70
items.notes: In careful speech nado replaces a listing toka ('eiga nado'); the hedging toka can sound vague or young there.

items.use: Introduces an example or a hypothetical; also buys a second to think.

example.english: How about this one, for example?

examplePolite.romaji: tatoeba, kore wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 例えば、これはどうですか？
examplePolite.english: How about this one, for example?

items.freqNote: 例えば #790

items.use: Lists sample actions without claiming the list is complete; built on the -ta form and closed with suru ('mitari, kaimono shitari suru'). A single -tari softens an invitation or plan ('gohan tabetari shinai?'); casually the closing suru is sometimes dropped.

example.ja: 映画見たり、買い物したりしたい。
example.english: I want to see a movie, go shopping, that kind of thing.

examplePolite.romaji: eiga o mitari, kaimono o shitari shitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 映画を見たり、買い物をしたりしたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to see a movie, do some shopping, things like that.

items.freqNote: たり #2470; tokenizer often fuses it into the verb
items.notes: The last -tari normally takes suru (shita, shitai, shiteru); one -tari alone is common too ('eiga mitari shitai'). Verbs whose -ta is -da give -dari (nondari, asondari). Don't mix it up with -tara.

blocks.label: Talking about talk
blocks.rationale: Words for handling what's said: quoting it, raising a related topic, naming the subject, summing it up.
blocks.interference: sou ieba jumps to something new, tsumari restates what was just said; -tte reports someone's words, -ni tsuite names the topic.

items.use: Spoken quote marker after anything said, thought, heard or asked, followed by iu, omou, kiku and the like ('kuru tte itta'). Works the same in desu/masu speech; to is the written/formal quote marker. Sentence-final, it reports hearsay: 'ashita ame da tte' = 'I hear it'll rain'.

examplePolite.ja: 来るって言ってましたよ。

items.freqNote: って #18, also counts topic tte and hearsay tte
items.notes: After n it shrinks to te: 'nan te itta?' (nan + tte) = 'what did he say?'

items.english: oh yeah; come to think of it
items.use: Brings up something that just came to mind, linked to the conversation or not; the natural way to switch topics mid-chat.

example.english: Oh yeah, are you off tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: sou ieba, ashita wa yasumi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そういえば、明日は休みですか？
examplePolite.english: By the way, are you off tomorrow?

items.freqNote: そういえば #607 (+ そう言えば #8072)
items.notes: For a deliberate change of subject with no reminder, tokorode ('by the way').

items.use: Attaches to a noun to name the topic of talking, thinking, asking or knowing ('nihon ni tsuite kiku'); small talk often uses no koto instead.

example.ja: それについて、なんか聞いてる？
example.english: Have you heard anything about that?

examplePolite.romaji: sore ni tsuite, nanika kiitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それについて、何か聞いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Have you heard anything about that?

items.freqNote: について #426
items.notes: Before a noun it takes no: 'nihon ni tsuite no hon'.

items.use: Rephrases or sums up what was said; with '...tte koto?' it checks that you understood.

example.ja: つまり、来ないってこと？

examplePolite.romaji: tsumari, konai tte koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: つまり、来ないってことですか？
examplePolite.english: So you mean you're not coming?

items.freqNote: つまり #499

blocks.label: If / even if
blocks.rationale: The four 'if' endings plus 'even if', all on one 'jikan aru' sentence so only the ending changes.
blocks.interference: English gives all five as 'if/when': -tara is the default, -nara picks up what was just said, -te mo flips to 'even if', -ba means 'that's all it takes', -to is automatic and never takes a request or plan after it.

items.use: Conditional built on the -ta form: 'if' for hypotheticals, 'when / once' for things sure to happen, and 'when I did X, I found Y' in stories. The safe default when unsure which 'if' fits.

example.english: If you've got time, come by.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga attara, kite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 時間があったら、来てくださいね。
examplePolite.english: If you have time, please come by.

items.freqNote: たら #2818, misleadingly low: tokenizer fuses most -tara into the verb token (cf. だったら #207, よかったら #938)
items.notes: Polite speech keeps plain -tara; -mashitara sounds very formal.

items.use: Takes up something just said or known and builds on it: 'if it's X / if you're going to X'. Attaches to nouns and plain forms ('sushi nara, ii mise shitteru').

example.ja: 時間あるなら、手伝ってよ。
example.english: If you've got time, help me out.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga aru nara, chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 時間があるなら、ちょっと手伝ってもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: If you've got time, could you give me a hand?

items.freqNote: なら #77
items.notes: English speakers overuse nara for every 'if'; save it for picking up what was said. Timing trap: with nara the main action can come first ('nihon ni iku nara, kore yonde' = read this before you go), while 'nihon ni ittara, ...' = once you're there.

items.use: Te-form + mo: the result holds anyway ('ame ga futte mo iku'). Adjectives take -kute mo, nouns and na-adjectives de mo; casual alternative -tatte.

example.ja: 時間あっても、行かない。
example.english: Even if I have time, I'm not going.

examplePolite.ja: 時間があっても、行きません。
examplePolite.english: Even if I have time, I won't go.

items.freqNote: ても #13684, misleadingly low: tokenizer splits -te + mo; casual たって #1142
items.notes: Listen for what follows: 'tabete mo ii?' = 'can I eat it?', while 'tabete mo, ...' = 'even if I eat'. Don't treat -te mo as a kind of -tara; it flips the meaning ('even if' vs 'if').

items.use: Conditional on the e-stem (areba, ikeba, yasukereba): 'if X, then Y', often with the sense that X is all it takes. Also inside -ba ii, -nakereba and dou sureba.

example.english: If I have time, I'll go.

examplePolite.ja: 時間があれば、行きます。
examplePolite.english: If I have time, I'll go.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; ば alone unusable (#183446); rank of できれば, cf. なければ #1873, よければ #2273
items.notes: Casually -nakereba shrinks to -nakya; -kerya / -rya (yokerya, arya) sound rough and male: recognise, don't produce. After an action verb, -ba can't lead into a request or invitation; use -tara ('tsuitara, denwa shite').

items.use: Plain form + to: Y always or automatically follows X; used for directions, how things work and habits ('migi ni magaru to, eki ga aru'). The main clause can't be a request, invitation or plan.

example.ja: 時間あると、いつも寝ちゃう。
example.english: Whenever I have time, I end up sleeping.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga aru to, itsumo nechaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 時間があると、いつも寝ちゃいます。
examplePolite.english: Whenever I have time, I end up sleeping.

items.freqNote: と #7, counts every と (and, with, quote), not just the conditional
items.notes: '...to, kite' (a request) is wrong; use -tara for that.

blocks.label: If-openers
blocks.rationale: Sentence-starting words that set up a condition or follow from one, all built around -tara.
blocks.interference: dattara overlaps with jaa (And then block): dattara explicitly builds on what was just said; moshi never stands alone, it still needs the conditional ending.

items.use: Opens a sentence to flag a hypothetical, so the -tara / -ba / -nara / -te mo at the end is expected.

example.ja: もし雨だったら、やめよう。
example.english: If it rains, let's call it off.

examplePolite.ja: もし雨だったら、やめましょう。
examplePolite.english: If it rains, let's call it off.

items.notes: Moshi alone doesn't make an 'if'; the ending still has to be -tara, -ba, -nara or -te mo.

items.use: Starts a reply that builds a plan on what the other person just said.

example.ja: だったら、明日にしよう。
example.english: In that case, let's make it tomorrow.

examplePolite.ja: でしたら、明日にしましょう。
examplePolite.english: In that case, let's make it tomorrow.

items.freqNote: だったら #207 (also counts noun + dattara mid-sentence); polite でしたら #3192; near-synonym それなら #1552

items.use: Softens an offer or invitation so it's easy to say no; goes at the start of the sentence.

example.ja: よかったら、一緒に行く？
example.english: If you're up for it, want to come along?

examplePolite.ja: よかったら、一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come along?

items.freqNote: よかったら #938; よければ #2273
items.notes: Same word in desu/masu speech; yokereba is a touch more formal, yoroshikereba is keigo.

blocks.label: Depends / without / for
blocks.rationale: Linkers that do the job of an English preposition: depends on X, without doing X, in order to / for X.
blocks.interference: -naide (without) vs -nakute (because not); -tame ni (purpose, an action you choose) vs -you ni (so that, after potential, -nai or non-volitional verbs).

items.use: Noun + ni yoru: the answer depends on X; the all-purpose hedge when yes or no would be too strong ('hito ni yoru', 'toki ni yoru').

example.romaji: sore wa hito ni yoru ne.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa hito ni yorimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは人によりますね。

items.freqNote: による #1018; によって #939; near-synonym 次第 #1911
items.notes: Mid-sentence it becomes ni yotte: 'hito ni yotte chigau' = varies by person. 'X ni yoru to' = 'according to X' ('yohou ni yoru to, ame da tte').

items.use: -nai form + de: you do the main action without doing X, or instead of X ('nenaide benkyou shita').

example.ja: 朝ごはん食べないで来た。

examplePolite.ja: 朝ごはんを食べないで来ました。

items.freqNote: ないで #3426 (also counts the request 'don't'; tokenizer often fuses with the verb)
items.notes: For a negative reason use -nakute ('wakaranakute komatta'), not -naide. At the end of a sentence it's a request: 'ikanaide' = 'don't go'.

items.use: Plain verb + tame ni = in order to; noun + no tame ni = for X's sake ('kenkou no tame ni'). The 'because of' reading is news/written; in chat use de or kara.

example.romaji: ryokou suru tame ni, chokin shiteru.
example.ja: 旅行するために、貯金してる。

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou suru tame ni, chokin shitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 旅行するために、貯金してます。
examplePolite.english: I'm saving up so I can travel.

items.freqNote: ために #124 (purpose and cause together); ため #203
items.notes: Tame ni needs an action you choose to do; with potentials, -nai forms and verbs you don't control (maniau, wakaru), use -you ni instead ('mieru you ni', 'maniau you ni', 'wasurenai you ni').

Every block has at least 3 items, so no re-chunk was required. Prereqs were kept as romaji forms; the form reviewer's idea of using slugs instead depends on the list-wide convention.

reviewSummaries: natural: Casual examples are mostly natural Tokyo speech. The main fault is the polite pairs. Several swap in formal or business-only forms where everyday desu/masu speech keeps the same word or a contracted form: dewa, yokereba, to-quote, desu node, desu kara as an opener, to iu no mo. These need polite null or the real everyday pair (nanode, demo ...n desu yo). A few polite examples are uncontracted and read aloud (-te shimaimasu, -te imasu), and the noni 'if only' gloss is wrong. Nothing needs cutting. Worth checking that other categories cover tokorode (#581), nanode and the temporal linkers (-te kara, -mae ni, -ato de, -nagara).

nuance: Strong draft: glosses, intent descriptions, contrast groups and shared-sentence drills are mostly accurate, and every alsoIn pointer checks out against the research and vocab-trainer files. The serious problems are noni's 'if only' gloss, datte's fake polite pair (to iu no mo), and two missing audio traps (nara before/after ordering; -te mo vs -te mo ii). Nothing needs cutting, but three blocks are under 4 items, and the category has no time-clause linkers (-toki, -mae ni, -ato de, -te kara) unless another category covers them.

form: The data is clean. All 31 freqRanks match the tool's output, and every alsoIn pointer I checked (12-list #1/10/35/38/40, 13-list #1–12/23/63/67/108/111/112/124, 11-list #1, vocab-trainer conjunctions and greetings, kotoba kara/ka/tte/to) resolves to a real entry. The ja, kana and romaji fields match sound for sound, the conjugations are correct, slugs are unique, and every block has 3–5 items.
The real problems are three content errors: -tari's headline form drops the closing suru, tame-ni's -you ni rule uses a verb that doesn't fit it (maniau), and yokattara/yokereba is listed as a polite pair though both are the same register.
The rest is spelling: -naide and the -te imasu / -te shimau polite forms should be written as one word to match kotoba's stored spellings. One gap: the -you ni contrast is cited but not an item in this category.

categories.name: Sentence endings & intent

blocks.label: Basic enders
blocks.rationale: The plain copula, the three core sentence-final particles (ka, ne, yo) and their most common combination, yo ne. They share one base sentence so that only the ending changes.
blocks.interference: yo and ne get mixed up. yo tells the listener something they don't know, ne treats it as shared, and yo ne checks that it's shared. In a casual question ka sounds blunt or rough, so drop it and use a rising tone.

items.use: Plain 'is' after nouns and na-adjectives. A bare final da is mostly self-talk or a sudden realisation and can sound blunt, so to tell someone, drop it (ashita yasumi) or add yo or ne (ashita yasumi da yo). It stays before ne, yo and kedo. Polite speech has no self-talk, so the polite pair is a plain statement.

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みです

items.notes: It becomes na before n da and no (yasumi na n da) and never follows an i-adjective (takai, not *takai da). Dropping da before yo or ne (yasumi yo, kirei ne) is common but feminine-leaning; da yo / da ne is the neutral form.

items.use: Turns a polite sentence into a question when said with a rising tone. Said falling, polite desu ka is a realisation instead (sou desu ka = I see). Casual questions drop ka and rise, so bare casual ka is mostly heard in musing realisations (sokka, ashita yasumi ka).

example.english: Oh, tomorrow's a day off, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: a, ashita wa yasumi desu ka
examplePolite.ja: あ、明日は休みですか
examplePolite.english: Oh, tomorrow's a day off, I see.

alsoIn: vocab-trainer learner-phrases: ○○ wa nihongo de nan desu ka
items.notes: For a casual question, drop ka and raise the pitch: ashita yasumi? The real polite question is ashita wa yasumi desu ka? with a rising tone. A casual rising ...ka? (daijoubu ka?) sounds rough and masculine. Neutral casual ka appears in musing (sokka), in jaa iku ka (let's get going, then) and inside sentences (nani ga ii ka wakaranai = I don't know what would be good).

items.use: Invites the listener to share or agree with what you say. It softens statements, comments on things you both see, and confirms details.

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですね
examplePolite.english: So tomorrow's a day off, then.

items.notes: A drawn-out nee at the start of a sentence means hey. Mid-sentence ne (ano ne, kinou ne...) just holds the listener's attention. Don't add ne to facts only you know, such as your name or your plans; yo or nothing fits there.

items.use: Marks something the listener doesn't know or needs reminding of, such as news, warnings, corrections or recommendations. Without it, a statement can sound flat.

example.english: Tomorrow's a day off, you know.

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよ
examplePolite.english: Tomorrow's a day off, you know.

items.notes: When correcting a superior, yo can sound like lecturing.

items.use: Checks that the listener shares something you believe, either to confirm it or to agree emphatically (sou da yo ne).

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yasumi desu yo ne?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよね？

items.notes: The order is fixed: always yo ne, never *ne yo.

blocks.label: Explaining: n da
blocks.rationale: The n/no explanatory frame in four forms: statement, question, soft lead-in and conclusion. All four share one base sentence.
blocks.interference: n da gives the reason and wake da draws the conclusion from it. no? is the question form, and the answer usually comes back with n da. After nouns, all four take na (yasumi na n da, yasumi na no?).

items.use: Frames a statement as the explanation or background to the situation: giving reasons, sharing news, or showing you're personally involved.

examplePolite.ja: 頭が痛いんです
examplePolite.english: I have a headache, you see.

items.freqNote: #20 んだ (polite んです #23)
items.notes: After nouns and na-adjectives it becomes na n da (yasumi na n da). As a question, use no? (casual) or n desu ka (polite); casual n da? sounds rough. n desu ka about someone's actions can sound like a challenge (nani shite iru n desu ka?).

items.use: The everyday casual question that asks about the situation or for an explanation (doushita no?, doko iku no?). It is said with a rising tone and used by everyone.

examplePolite.romaji: atama ga itai n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 頭が痛いんですか？

items.freqNote: rank of なの (na no?); bare の #1 is mostly possessive
items.notes: With a falling tone (atama itai no), it is a soft, feminine-leaning statement version of n da.

items.use: Sets out the background and trails off so the listener can offer help. It is the soft way to open a request, a question or a new topic.

example.romaji: chotto atama itai n da kedo
example.ja: ちょっと頭痛いんだけど
example.english: My head kind of hurts, so...

examplePolite.romaji: chotto atama ga itai n desu kedo
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと頭が痛いんですけど
examplePolite.english: I have a bit of a headache, so...

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of けど #37, the rarer component (んだ #20)
items.notes: Leave the request unsaid, because the listener fills it in. The polite form is the classic opener with clerks.

items.use: Draws the conclusion once the reason is known ('no wonder', 'which means'). It is common as sou iu wake (so that's how it is). dou iu wake? demands an explanation (what's going on here?!); the neutral question is dou iu koto?

example.english: So that's why your head hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: dakara atama ga itai wake desu ne
examplePolite.ja: だから頭が痛いわけですね
examplePolite.english: So that's why your head hurts.

items.freqNote: わけ #272 (all uses; わけじゃない #535 and わけない #449 are separate tokens); わけだ not found
items.notes: Don't confuse it with wake ja nai (it's not that...), which is a separate item.

blocks.label: Thinking aloud
blocks.rationale: Endings for talking half to yourself: exclaiming, wondering, trying to remember, and summing things up loosely.
blocks.interference: kana wonders about something you don't know, while kke tries to recall something you once knew. naa is said to yourself, where ne would draw the listener in (samui naa vs samui ne). tte kanji loosely sums up your own impression; it is not tte koto?, which checks what the other person meant.

items.use: Exclaims or muses to yourself, for envy, admiration or wishes (ii naa, samui naa, ikitai naa). Unlike ne, it isn't aimed at the listener. Polite speech has no self-talk; drawn-out desu nee is the nearest.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は寒いですねえ
examplePolite.english: It's really cold today, isn't it.

items.freqNote: #387 なあ (なー #934); bare な #16 merges prohibitive and attributive na
items.notes: Short na works after adjectives and -tai (samui na, ikitai na). After a dictionary-form verb, short na is a rough prohibition (iku na = don't go!), so stretch it: ame furu naa. Short na aimed at someone in place of ne (sou da na, jaa na) is masculine-leaning.

items.use: Wonders aloud about something you don't know, or softens a guess or request (ii kana? = is it okay?). Because it is half to yourself, the listener can answer or not.

example.english: Is the meeting tomorrow, I wonder?

examplePolite.romaji: kaigi wa ashita desu ka ne
examplePolite.ja: 会議は明日ですかね
examplePolite.english: Is the meeting tomorrow, I wonder?

items.freqNote: #90 かな (polite でしょうか #341)
items.notes: No da before it: ashita kana, not *ashita da kana. deshou ka is the more formal polite option, right for clerks and superiors. kana is common even with coworkers as a soft hedge: ...kana to omoimasu. The feminine kashira is dated and heard mostly in dramas.

items.politeJa: でしたっけ／〜ましたっけ
items.use: Asks someone to confirm something you once knew but have half-forgotten, like a name, time or plan. It attaches to da / datta or a past verb (nan datta kke?, itta kke?); with a non-past verb, use n da kke (iku n da kke?). It can also be nostalgic self-talk: yoku asonda kke (we used to play a lot).

example.english: Wait, is the meeting tomorrow again?

examplePolite.ja: 会議は明日でしたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, remind me, is the meeting tomorrow?

items.notes: deshita kke is fine with coworkers but a little casual for superiors.

items.use: Sums up a feeling or situation loosely ('it's like...'), so you can approximate when you lack the exact words. sonna kanji means 'something like that', and konna kanji desu (it's like this) is fine at work.

example.english: Eh, it's kind of just okay.

examplePolite.ja: まあ普通って感じです

items.freqNote: rank of 感じ (all uses); って感じ and そんな感じ not found
items.notes: A sentence-final X tte kanji is youthful and sounds vague when overused; sonna / konna kanji is the neutral all-purpose core.

blocks.label: Asking someone
blocks.rationale: Ways to get the listener to do something: asking for a thing, the bare -te and the softer favour forms, then the 'don't' form.
blocks.interference: -te is blunt; -te kureru? and -te moraeru? are plain asks, and the negatives -te kurenai? and -te moraenai? are softer still. onegai (polite kudasai) asks for a thing, and kudasai also makes -te polite. -naide is the 'don't' of -te.

items.use: The bare te-form is the everyday casual request to friends and family (matte, mite, kiite). Add chotto or ne to soften it.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待って

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってください

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (bare て #458 is mostly connective; ください #350)
alsoIn: vocab-trainer learner-phrases: mou ichido itte kudasai
items.notes: -te kudasai is polite but still direct; with strangers, -te moraemasu ka is safer.

items.use: A softer request for a favour, asked as a negative question. It is one step up from bare -te and fine with friends and family.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待ってくれない？
example.english: Sorry, could you wait a sec?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってくれませんか
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you wait a moment?

items.freqNote: rank of くれる; くれない alone #78901 undercounts (tokenizer splits)
items.notes: The negative question makes it softer than -te kureru?, and it is not a refusal. Rising, it's a request; flat, it's a complaint: tetsudatte kurenai = they won't help me.

items.use: Asks for a favour framed as something you would receive. It is about as soft as -te kureru?, and its polite form -te moraemasu ka is the safe choice with clerks and strangers.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待ってもらえる？
example.english: Sorry, could you wait a bit?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってもらえますか
examplePolite.english: Sorry, would you mind waiting a moment?

items.freqNote: rank of もらえる (all uses)
items.notes: The negative is softer: -te moraenai? casually, and -te moraemasen ka, the softest of the set, politely.

items.use: Asks someone not to do something. It is built on the -nai form (wasurenai → wasurenaide) and often softened with ne.

examplePolite.ja: これを忘れないでくださいね

items.freqNote: rank of ないで (includes 'without doing')
items.notes: In the middle of a sentence, -naide means 'without doing' (nenaide benkyou shita).

blocks.label: Checking with you
blocks.rationale: Tags that pull the listener into agreement, plus tte koto? to check you've understood what they said.
blocks.interference: desho? means 'surely you agree' (often 'told you'), ja nai? offers your view as a rising question, and jan states it with a falling tone, not as a question. tte koto? restates the other person's words to check you understood.

items.use: A rising tag that expects agreement, meaning 'see, I told you' or 'you know what I mean'. Everyone uses it in casual speech.

examplePolite.ja: これいいでしょう？

items.freqNote: tokenizer files でしょ under でしょう #147 (bare でしょ #43859); includes polite 'probably'
items.notes: With a falling tone, polite deshou means 'probably' (ame deshou). In casual speech, guess with tabun, kamo or to omou. A bare final darou and the tag daro? lean masculine, while nan darou / dou darou (I wonder) are used by everyone. With people above you, a rising deshou? can sound pushy; desu yo ne? (kore ii desu yo ne?) is the safer check.

items.use: Offers your view softly as a rising question (ii ja nai? = that's nice, no?). It attaches directly to nouns and adjectives (tanaka-san ja nai?, kirei ja nai?, ii ja nai?). After verbs, use n ja nai? (ame furu n ja nai?).

example.romaji: are, ano hito tanaka-san ja nai?
example.ja: あれ、あの人田中さんじゃない？
example.english: Wait, isn't that Tanaka over there?

examplePolite.romaji: are, ano hito tanaka-san ja nai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あれ、あの人田中さんじゃないですか？
examplePolite.english: Oh, isn't that Tanaka-san over there?

items.freqNote: rank of じゃない, which merges plain negation; じゃないか #202
items.notes: Tone decides the meaning: rising ame ja nai? = isn't it rain?, while flat ame ja nai = it isn't rain. After an i-adjective it is always this tag, never negation, because the negative is -kunai.

items.use: Contracted ja nai said with a falling tone. It presents something as obvious or newly noticed (ii jan = hey, that's nice) and isn't a real question.

examplePolite.romaji: kore ii ja nai desu ka
examplePolite.ja: これいいじゃないですか

items.freqNote: #363 じゃん (Kansai やん #1690)
items.notes: It spread to Tokyo from Yokohama and the surrounding region and is now heard nationwide; Kansai speakers say yan. With verbs it means 'I told you': datte itta jan (I told you so!). In polite speech, asserting ...ja nai desu ka about things the listener can't know sounds presumptuous.

items.use: Restates what the other person said to check you understood, which is vital for a learner. It attaches to the plain form.

example.english: So you mean tomorrow's no good?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa muri tte koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は無理ってことですか？
examplePolite.english: So you mean tomorrow's no good?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (ってこと and ということ not found; こと #26 too generic)
items.notes: sou iu koto? (is that what you mean?) works as a reply on its own. to iu koto desu ka is the more formal polite option, for meetings and email.

blocks.label: How sure
blocks.rationale: A ladder of certainty from 'maybe' to 'should be', all on one base sentence.
blocks.interference: From least to most sure: kamo (could go either way), to omou (my opinion), n ja nai (I'd guess), hazu (should, by reasoning). hazu is about what you expect: not your own plans, which take tsumori, and never advice, which takes -ta hou ga ii.

items.use: Marks something as possible but uncertain. It attaches to any plain clause, with no da after nouns (ame kamo).

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くかもしれません

items.freqNote: #240 かも (かもしれない #219, polite かもしれません #665)
items.notes: kamo desu is common among younger coworkers but sounds a bit loose; with superiors or customers, use kamo shiremasen.

items.use: Presents a statement as your own opinion or guess so it doesn't sound blunt. It attaches to the plain form, with da after nouns (ame da to omou).

example.english: I think they'll be here soon.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くと思います
examplePolite.english: I think they'll be arriving soon.

items.freqNote: rank of 思う (all uses)
items.notes: Use it for your own thoughts only; for someone else, say to omotteru. The casual variant is tte omou. For 'I don't think...', negate the clause: konai to omou (I don't think they'll come), not kuru to omowanai.

items.use: Gives a soft but fairly confident guess or opinion, either as a rising question or as a flat statement. After nouns, use na n ja nai.

example.ja: そろそろ着くんじゃない？
example.english: They'll probably be here soon, no?

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro tsuku n ja nai desu ka
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くんじゃないですか
examplePolite.english: I'd say they'll be here soon.

items.freqNote: んじゃない not found (split); rank of じゃない (んじゃ #32265)
items.notes: A sharp, falling ...n ja nai! is a scolding 'don't!' (sawaru n ja nai!). Flat, it can also deny an explanation: asobi ni iku n ja nai = it's not that I'm going to play.

items.use: States what you expect on good grounds, such as a schedule, what someone said, or how things normally work. After nouns it is no hazu; after na-adjectives, na hazu.

example.english: They should be here any minute.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くはずです
examplePolite.english: They should be arriving any minute.

items.notes: hazu ga nai means 'can't possibly'; hazu datta means 'was supposed to (but didn't)'. It is never advice: 'you should rest' is yasunda hou ga ii.

blocks.label: Let's, suggestions & plans
blocks.rationale: The volitional -ou family for inviting and offering, the softer -nai? invitation and -tara? advice, then tsumori and -ou to omou for your own plans.
blocks.interference: -ou proposes outright, -ou ka asks for agreement or offers help, and -nai? leaves room to say no; -tara? advises the listener rather than inviting them. tsumori is a settled plan, while -ou to omou is a decision you're still making.

items.use: The volitional form proposes doing something together (ikou, tabeyou, shiyou). Godan verbs change the final u to ou (iku → ikou, kaeru → kaerou); ichidan verbs swap ru for you (taberu → tabeyou).

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きましょう

items.freqNote: tokenizer folds the volitional into the verb; rank of いこう (ikou) alone
items.notes: The irregulars are suru → shiyou and kuru → koyou.

items.use: Asks whether to do something together, or offers to do it for the listener (mado akeyou ka? = shall I open the window?).

example.english: Want me to come with you?

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きましょうか？

items.freqNote: casual 行こうか not found (volitional folded into verb); rank of polite ましょうか
items.notes: With a falling tone it can be self-directed: jaa, kaerou ka (well, guess I'll head home).

items.use: Invites the listener with a rising negative question (issho ni ikanai?), which leaves room to decline. It is softer than -ou.

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come along?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (ない #43 merges all negation; ませんか #111176 tokenizer-split)
items.notes: The rising tone is what makes it an invitation; flat ikanai just means 'I'm not going.'

items.use: Suggests, with a rising tone, something the listener could do for their own good (yasundara?, kiite mitara?). The fuller form is -tara dou?. -ba? (sureba?) is curter and can sound dismissive (katte ni sureba? = suit yourself).

example.english: Why don't you take a break?

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休んだらどうですか
examplePolite.english: Why don't you take a little break?

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of たら alone
items.notes: With superiors -tara dou desu ka can sound pushy; -ta hou ga ii kamo is gentler.

items.use: States a plan you've already decided on. It attaches to the plain form (iku tsumori, ikanai tsumori).

example.ja: 今日は早く寝るつもり
example.english: I'm planning to go to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hayaku neru tsumori desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は早く寝るつもりです
examplePolite.english: I plan to go to bed early tonight.

items.freqNote: #208 つもり
items.notes: After a past verb it means 'I thought I had': itta tsumori = I thought I'd said it. Asking others about their tsumori can sound like a challenge (dou iu tsumori? = what do you think you're doing?), so ask about plans with ...suru no? / ...n desu ka. For loose plans, -ou to omotteru is softer.

items.use: Shares a plan you're deciding on now or are still considering. It is softer than tsumori.

example.romaji: kyou wa hayaku neyou to omou
example.ja: 今日は早く寝ようと思う
example.english: I think I'll go to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hayaku neyou to omoimasu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は早く寝ようと思います
examplePolite.english: I think I'll go to bed early tonight.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (volitional folded into verb; 思う #33 covers all uses)
items.notes: Polite speech keeps the plain volitional (neyou to omoimasu, never *nemashou to omoimasu); -ou to omotteru = I've been thinking of it.

blocks.label: Seems / I heard
blocks.rationale: Endings that show where your information comes from: what you see, what you infer, and what you heard. All four share one base sentence.
blocks.interference: -sou is how something looks right now. mitai is the everyday 'seems', from what you see or from what you've heard; rashii and tte clearly mark it as secondhand. Polite hearsay oishii sou desu is easy to confuse with oishisou desu (looks tasty).

items.use: Says how something looks right now, before you know for sure (oishisou). On verb stems it means something is about to happen (furisou = looks like rain).

example.ja: このケーキおいしそう

examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、おいしそうですね
examplePolite.english: This cake looks delicious, doesn't it?

items.freqNote: tokenizer glues -sou to stems; rank of おいしそう alone (なさそう #2362; bare そう #31 is mostly 'so')
items.notes: It attaches to the stem (oishii → oishisou); the irregulars are ii → yosasou and nai → nasasou. It is not for what's plainly visible: a red car is akai, not *akasou. kawaisou means 'poor thing', not 'looks cute'.

items.use: Says something seems so, either from what you see yourself (dare mo inai mitai) or from what you've heard (oishii mitai da yo). It is the everyday catch-all; rashii is a bit more detached. It also means 'like a' (kodomo mitai, kodomo mitai na hito).

example.ja: このケーキおいしいみたい
example.english: This cake seems to be good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki, oishii mitai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、おいしいみたいですよ
examplePolite.english: This cake's supposed to be good.

items.freqNote: #99 みたい (みたいな #951)
items.notes: No da before it: ame mitai, not *ame da mitai.

items.use: Ends a sentence to pass on what someone said or what you heard (ashita ame da tte). It attaches to the plain form and keeps da after nouns.

example.ja: このケーキおいしいって
example.english: They say this cake is good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki, oishii sou desu yo
examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、おいしいそうですよ
examplePolite.english: I hear this cake is good.

items.freqNote: rank of って, which merges quotative and topic uses
items.notes: Polite oishii sou desu (I hear it's good) and oishisou desu (it looks good) differ only in the i. Also very common: oishii tte kikimashita (I heard it's good).

items.use: Passes on secondhand information you believe but didn't witness, with a little more distance than mitai or tte. No da after nouns (ame rashii).

example.ja: このケーキおいしいらしい

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki wa oishii rashii desu
examplePolite.ja: このケーキはおいしいらしいです

items.freqNote: #218 らしい
items.notes: Directly after a noun it can instead mean 'typical of' (otokorashii = manly).

changelog.change: Rationale now says three core particles plus the yo ne combination, not 'four most frequent particles' (nuance, form). Interference now says casual ka sounds 'blunt or rough'.
Interference uses 'wake da' with no hyphen.
tte-kanji moved in, so the block has 4 items (nuance). Rationale and interference updated, and interference now separates tte kanji from tte koto?.

tara-suggest moved out (nuance). Reordered kudasai, -te, -te kurenai?, -te moraeru?, -naide so -naide no longer splits the ladder. Interference rewritten so the negatives are the softer step (nuance), and it uses onegai/kudasai.
tte-kanji moved out, leaving 4 items. Rationale and interference updated and the tte koto / tte kanji sentence dropped.
Interference: n ja nai is 'I'd guess', not 'I'd bet'. Added that hazu is never advice.
Renamed from 'Let's & plans'. Took in tara-suggest (6 items; a separate Plans block would have had only 2). Rationale and interference cover -tara? advice.
Interference: mitai is the everyday 'seems' from evidence or hearsay, and rashii/tte mark it as secondhand (natural, nuance).

Example is now the self-talk realisation 'a, ashita yasumi da' / 'Oh right, I'm off tomorrow!'. Use explains how to tell someone and why the polite pair is a plain statement. Notes add that dropping da before yo/ne is feminine-leaning.

Casual and polite examples are now the same falling realisation ('a, ashita (wa) yasumi (desu) ka'). Use covers falling vs rising desu ka and sokka. Notes add that rough casual ...ka? is masculine, plus neutral casual ka (jaa iku ka, embedded questions). Removed the tangential pointer 13-list-exit-battery #27.
Polite now 'desu ne / -masu ne'. Notes add mid-sentence ne and say not to use ne on facts only you know.
English is now 'you know (new info for you)'. Polite now 'desu yo / -masu yo'.
Notes add that casual n da? sounds rough and that n desu ka about someone's actions can sound like a challenge.
English is now 'is it that...? (casual question)'. Prereq is the slug n-da. alsoIn changed to 13-list-exit-battery #93 (#124 and #26 were tangential).
freqRank 37 (けど, the rarer component) and freqNote updated. Prereqs are slugs n-da and kedo. Added pointer vocab-trainer utility-vocab: conjunctions (verified).

Romaji/ja/polite no longer take a hyphen or 〜 (wake da, わけだ, wake desu). Use now says dou iu wake? demands an explanation and dou iu koto? is the neutral question. freqNote corrected (わけじゃない and わけない are separate tokens). Prereq is the slug n-da.

Polite now 'desu nee' / ですねえ, with examplePolite 'kyou wa samui desu nee'. Use notes that polite speech has no self-talk. Notes explain short na: fine after adjectives and -tai, a rough prohibition after a dictionary-form verb, masculine-leaning when aimed at someone.
Polite now 'desu ka ne / deshou ka', with examplePolite 'kaigi wa ashita desu ka ne'. Notes add no da before kana, deshou ka as the formal option, and dated feminine kashira.
Polite now 'deshita kke / -mashita kke'. Use adds n da kke for non-past verbs and the nostalgic self-talk use. Both English glosses now carry the half-forgotten nuance.

Moved to Thinking aloud. Romaji/ja no longer take a hyphen or 〜 (tte kanji). Flagged slang. Use adds konna kanji desu for work. Prereq changed from hearsay -tte to quotative -tte iu. Notes reworded. Polite kept as 'tte kanji desu', not form's 'to iu kanji desu', because the natural view keeps the contraction in polite talk.

English and use rewritten. freqRank 258 (お願い, verified) with a sourced freqNote. Notes cover onegaishimasu and choudai (soft, childlike, family). Added pointer vocab-trainer utility-vocab: politeness.
English is now 'do... (casual request)'. freqRank null with judgement note (the bare て token is mostly connective). examplePolite English is now 'Sorry, just a moment, please.'
examplePolite English starts 'Sorry,'. Notes add that flat -te kurenai is a complaint. Prereqs are te-request and -te kureru.

Use now says it is about as soft as -te kureru?, not more distant (nuance). examplePolite English is now 'Sorry, would you mind waiting a moment?'. Notes add casual -te moraenai?. Prereq slug is te-kurenai.
English is now 'don't... (casual request)'. Prereq slug is te-request.

Notes: kamo desu is loose and for younger coworkers; use kamo shiremasen with superiors and customers.
