reviewSummaries: natural: Strong block overall: the shared base sentences (ashita yasumi, atama itai, sorosoro tsuku, kono keeki) are natural Tokyo speech, the request ladder and certainty ladder are accurate, and the freq ranks checked out against the tool. The main fixes are the bare-da example (it reads as a realisation, not a statement), the ka pair (it changes speech act), ja-nai-q (verbs need n ja nai, and its polite example duplicates jan's), and mitai being wrongly limited to your own inference. The rest are stiff polite examples (wa with no ne on reactions, to iu koto desu ka, deshou ka for kana) and small register notes (darou, choudai, sureba?, kamo desu).

nuance: The core distinctions are accurate: ne / yo / yo ne, kana vs kke, -sou vs hearsay sou desu, the invitation ladder and the n da frame. Shared base sentences per block, honest freqNotes and true register pairs are strong, and nothing needs cutting. The main problems are missing gender/roughness flags (darou, short na, casual ka?, dropping da), a few misleading glosses (no? 'what's up', hazu as advice-should, -ba? as a 'fuller variant', ja nai? with verbs, dou iu wake?) and one polite example whose meaning differs from its casual pair (ka). kudasai breaks the casual default. The chunking needs a reshuffle: blocks of 3 and 6 items, with tte kanji and -tara? in the wrong blocks. darou/deshou (probably) is a notable gap in the certainty ladder.

form: The data is mechanically clean. I checked 31 freqRanks against the tool and all match. Every example's romaji matches its ja word for word, long vowels and っ follow the convention, there are no duplicate slugs, every block has 3–6 items, and about 30 alsoIn pointers resolve. The real defects are these: kudasai puts a polite form in the casual field; the volitional items omit -you from the romaji and teach a -ru rule that breaks on godan verbs; prereqs use romaji names instead of slugs, so the two tte items point at the hearsay item. Smaller problems are inconsistent hyphens and 〜 on wake and the tte items, plus a few tangential battery pointers. Nothing needs cutting.

categories.name: Responses, reactions, fillers & social phrases
categories.scope: what you say on its own or to keep a conversation going

blocks.label: Yes and no
blocks.rationale: The three ways to answer a yes/no question, which you do in almost every exchange. It's a closed set, so the block stays at three.
blocks.interference: un and uun differ only in length and pitch (a short un against a two-beat, dipping u-un); iya is a firmer no that also corrects or pushes back.

items.use: The casual yes, and also the 'uh-huh' you keep saying while someone talks to show you're following.

examplePolite.ja: はい、行きます。

items.freqNote: うん #49; polite はい #22
items.notes: As a backchannel it shows you're listening, not that you agree; with superiors use hai (ee is the softer conversational polite yes). Trap: un confirms the statement, so to 'ikanai no?' (you're not going?) 'un' means 'right, I'm not going'.

items.use: The casual no to a yes/no question: two beats with a dip in pitch, while a short un means yes.

examplePolite.ja: いいえ、行きません。

items.freqNote: ううん #593; polite いいえ #688
items.notes: A long, flat uun (うーん, #298) means 'hmm'. The romaji is the same but it sounds different. To 'ikanai no?', 'uun, iku yo' means 'no, I AM going'.

items.use: A firmer no than uun: it denies, corrects ('iya, chigau'), or opens a turn with 'well, actually'.

example.romaji: iya, chigau yo. ashita da yo.

examplePolite.ja: いいえ、違います。明日ですよ。
examplePolite.english: No, that's not right. It's tomorrow.

items.freqNote: いや #54, which may also count 嫌 'don't want' written in kana; kanji 嫌 #304
items.notes: This is not the adjective iya 'unpleasant' (D). In polite speech you mostly hear a short ie ('ie, daijoubu desu') or iya itself; full iie mostly answers a direct yes/no question.

blocks.label: Thanks, sorry, please
blocks.rationale: The everyday politeness formulas for thanking, apologising, asking and offering.
blocks.interference: sumimasen apologises and also thanks, while gomen only apologises. onegai is 'please' when you ask for something; douzo is 'please' when you offer it.

items.politeJa: ありがとうございます
items.use: Thanks anyone for anything. Add gozaimasu for strangers, coworkers and anyone older.

example.ja: ありがとう、ほんとに助かった。

examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you, that was a real help.

items.freqNote: ありがとう #128; ありがとうございます #165; clipped ありがと #766
items.notes: The past form arigatou gozaimashita thanks someone for something that's finished, like a meal or a lesson.

items.use: Apologises to friends and family for anything from bumping into them to turning them down; 'gomen ne' is softer.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、遅くなりました。

items.freqNote: ごめん #154; ごめんなさい #254
items.notes: gomen nasai is the earnest middle step: stronger than gomen, less formal than sumimasen.

items.use: Gets a stranger's attention, apologises politely, and thanks someone who went to trouble for you.

example.ja: あ、わざわざすみません。
example.english: Oh, thanks for going to all that trouble.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、これいくらですか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, how much is this?

items.freqNote: すみません #289; spoken すいません #416
items.notes: Often pronounced suimasen. Already polite: with friends say gomen to apologise, arigatou to thank, and nee to get attention.

items.use: Turns any noun into a request ('mizu, onegai') or seals an ask. Said on its own to friends, it's a pleading 'please!'.

example.english: Sorry, can you take care of this?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、これお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you take care of this?

items.freqNote: お願い #258; お願いします #183
items.notes: In shops, 'X o onegai shimasu' is the safe all-purpose way to order.

items.use: Offers something, hands it over, or lets someone go first. It's the same in both registers.

examplePolite.ja: はい、こちらどうぞ。

items.freqNote: どうぞ #140
items.notes: It offers or invites; to ask for something, use onegai (douzo yoroshiku is the set phrase where it softens a request).

blocks.label: Hello and goodbye
blocks.rationale: Fixed greetings for the time of day, first meetings and leaving.
blocks.interference: hajimemashite opens a first meeting and yoroshiku closes it. konnichiwa is for people you aren't close to; with friends, say ohayou in the morning and otherwise just start talking.

items.use: The morning greeting. In shift work (restaurants, TV, some shops) ohayou gozaimasu also opens a shift whatever the hour; elsewhere, after midday, colleagues say otsukaresama desu.

examplePolite.ja: おはようございます、早いですね。

items.freqNote: おはよう #606; おはようございます #583; clipped おはよ #5618

items.use: The daytime hello to neighbours, shop staff and people you don't know well. Friends rarely say it to each other.

example.ja: あ、こんにちは！お買い物？

examplePolite.ja: あ、こんにちは。お買い物ですか？
examplePolite.english: Oh, hello. Are you out shopping?

items.freqNote: こんにちは #537
items.notes: The evening version is konbanwa.

items.use: The everyday goodbye to friends and family; 'mata ne' adds 'see you again'.

examplePolite.ja: では、また明日。失礼します。
examplePolite.english: Well then, see you tomorrow. Goodbye.

items.freqNote: じゃあね #937
items.notes: sayounara sounds final or school-like, and friends almost never say it. Leaving work before others: osaki ni shitsurei shimasu; to coworkers generally: otsukaresama desu.

items.use: Opens a first meeting, before you give your name, and is always followed by yoroshiku.

example.ja: はじめまして、健太です。よろしく！
example.english: Hi, I'm Kenta. Nice to meet you!

examplePolite.romaji: hajimemashite, kenta desu. yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: はじめまして、健太です。よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: How do you do, I'm Kenta. Nice to meet you.

items.freqNote: はじめまして #1596; 初めまして #3524

items.politeJa: よろしくお願いします
items.english: glad to know you; thanks ahead
items.use: Closes an introduction ('please treat me well') and any favour you leave in someone's hands.

example.english: Okay, I'm counting on you tomorrow.

examplePolite.ja: では、明日よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Well then, thank you in advance for tomorrow.

items.freqNote: よろしく #398; よろしくお願いします #516
items.notes: 'X ni yoroshiku' means 'say hi to X for me'.

blocks.label: Got it / say again
blocks.rationale: Saying whether you understood, and asking for a repeat when you didn't.
blocks.interference: wakatta and wakannai differ only in the ending (-tta past vs -nnai negative). nante? asks for the words again, while mou ikkai asks for a full replay.

items.use: Says you've understood, or agrees to a request or plan: the casual 'okay, will do'.

examplePolite.ja: 分かりました、後でやります。

items.freqNote: the tokenizer reduces 分かった to its dictionary form; rank of 分かる #213
items.notes: As a question, 'wakatta?' checks that the other person understood.

items.use: Says you don't understand or don't know, so the other person rephrases or moves on.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと分かんない。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really get it.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと分かりません。

items.freqNote: 分かんない #1567; other forms are folded into 分かる #213
items.notes: For 'I don't know' about a fact, wakannai (polite wakarimasen) is the safer choice; shiranai (shirimasen), said flatly, can sound cold, like 'no idea, not my problem'. shiranai also means you've never heard of it.

items.use: Asks someone to repeat what they just said when you missed the words.

example.english: Sorry, what did you just say?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、今何て言いました？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, what did you just say?

items.freqNote: 何て #834; なんて #84 also counts the 'such as' particle use
items.notes: A bare nante? can sound curt; 'e, nante?' is softer.

items.use: Asks for a replay of what was said, or proposes doing something again.

example.ja: ごめん、もう一回お願い。

examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you say that once more?

items.freqNote: もう一回 #1841; もう一度 #567
items.notes: Polite speech prefers mou ichido to mou ikkai.

blocks.label: Surprise
blocks.rationale: One-word reactions to the unexpected, from puzzlement to disbelief.
blocks.interference: e? reacts to something you just heard, while are? reacts to something you notice. honto? asks whether it's true, while uso! exclaims that it can't be.

items.use: Instant surprise at what you just heard, or a quick 'sorry, what?' when you missed it.

examplePolite.romaji: e? kekkon suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: えっ？結婚するんですか？

items.freqNote: えっ #83; bare え #137
items.notes: A flat, long ee (ええ, #131) is a polite 'yes'; a rising, drawn-out ee?! is stronger surprise than e?. To a superior, say 'sumimasen, mou ichido...' rather than a bare e? to ask for a repeat.

items.use: Asks 'is that true?' about good news, bad news or anything doubtful. Said flat, honto also agrees: 'it really is'.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou desu ka? kekkon suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 本当ですか？結婚するんですか？

items.freqNote: 本当 #199 counts every use; the casual spelling ほんと is #1785
items.notes: honto ni (B) is the adverb 'really, truly'.

items.use: Exclaims disbelief at surprising news. It literally means 'a lie' but accuses nobody, though it's too blunt to say to a superior.

examplePolite.romaji: e, hontou desu ka? kekkon suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、本当ですか？結婚するんですか？

items.freqNote: split across spellings: ウソ #1168, 嘘 #1544, うそ #2305
items.notes: 'uso desho!' is the stronger 'you've got to be kidding'. No polite form: in polite speech say 'e, hontou desu ka?'

items.use: Puzzlement when you notice something is off, missing, or not what you expected.

examplePolite.romaji: are? kagi ga nai n desu kedo...
examplePolite.ja: あれ？鍵がないんですけど…
examplePolite.english: Huh? I can't find my key...

items.freqNote: あれ #98 also counts the pronoun 'that' (J); the clipped あれっ is #18307
items.notes: This isn't the pronoun are 'that thing' (J): here it stands alone, with a rising pitch.

blocks.label: Showing interest
blocks.rationale: Backchannel reactions that show you're following and taking in what's said.
blocks.interference: hee is 'oh, interesting', aa is 'oh, right', naruhodo is 'that explains it', and tashika ni is 'fair point'. Only tashika ni says you've been persuaded.

items.use: Marks realisation or recognition ('aa, sore ka'). Before naruhodo or sokka it shows the penny has dropped.

examplePolite.ja: ああ、あの店ですね。

items.freqNote: ああ #63
items.notes: A bare aa meaning 'yeah' sounds masculine. aa 'like that' is a different word (J).

items.use: Shows interested surprise at something new; draw it out ('heee') for more surprise.

example.ja: へえ、それは知らなかった。

examplePolite.romaji: hee, sou na n desu ka. shirimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: へえ、そうなんですか。知りませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Oh, is that so? I didn't know that.

items.notes: On its own it can sound flippant to a superior; follow it with sou na n desu ka.

items.use: Shows that an explanation has clicked and makes sense to you.

example.ja: なるほど、そういうことか。
example.english: Ah, so that's what it is.

examplePolite.romaji: naruhodo, sou iu koto desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: なるほど、そういうことですか。
examplePolite.english: I see, so that's what it is.

items.freqNote: なるほど #379
items.notes: To a superior it can sound like you're judging them; sou na n desu ne is safer.

items.use: Concedes the other person's point, often before you add your own view ('tashika ni... demo').

example.ja: 確かに、ちょっと高いね。
example.english: True, it is a bit pricey.

examplePolite.romaji: tashika ni, chotto takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 確かに、ちょっと高いですね。
examplePolite.english: That's true, it is a bit expensive.

items.freqNote: 確かに #230
items.notes: tashika on its own means 'if I remember right', which is a different use.

blocks.label: Replies with sou
blocks.rationale: Five fixed replies built on sou. The ending decides whether you confirm, agree, take in news or doubt.
blocks.interference: sou confirms a fact, sou da ne agrees with an opinion, sokka and sou na n da take in news (sou na n da sounds more interested), and sou kana doubts. Drill all five after the same lead-in.

items.use: Confirms that what the other person said is right, usually about you or something you know ('so you're from Osaka?' 'sou').

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu, takai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そうです、高いんですよ。

items.freqNote: そう #31, counting every use including 'that way' (J)
items.notes: Doubled 'sou sou!' is eager agreement; a rising sou? means 'really? you think so?'. sou meaning 'that way' is in J.

items.use: Agrees with an opinion or feeling you share. Drawn out ('sou da nee...', polite 'sou desu nee...'), it buys thinking time before you answer.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ne, takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうですね、高いですね。
examplePolite.english: Yes, it is pricey, isn't it.

items.freqNote: そうだね #850; polite そうですね #539
items.notes: To confirm a fact about yourself, say sou desu, not sou desu ne.

items.use: Takes in new information or an explanation: 'oh, I see', sometimes with a hint of 'oh well'.

example.english: Oh, I see, so it's expensive.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ka, takai n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうですか、高いんですね。

items.freqNote: そっか #482; そうか only reaches #149930 because the tokenizer usually splits it (そう+か)
items.notes: Say it with a falling pitch. A rising sou desu ka? sounds doubtful, and bare sou ka sounds pensive or masculine.

items.use: Reacts to news with interest ('oh, really?') and invites the other person to say more.

example.romaji: sou na n da, takai n da ne.
example.ja: そうなんだ、高いんだね。

examplePolite.romaji: sou na n desu ka, takai n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうなんですか、高いんですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, is that so? So it's expensive.

items.freqNote: rank of the polite そうなんですか #1181; the casual そうなんだ is split by the tokenizer
items.notes: The safest default reaction when someone tells you something about themselves. With yo, 'sou na n da yo' confirms your own news: 'yeah, it is'.

items.use: Softly doubts what the other person just said without contradicting them; said slowly to yourself, it means 'I wonder'.

example.romaji: sou kana, sonna ni takakunai yo.
example.ja: そうかな、そんなに高くないよ。
example.english: You think? It's not that expensive.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ka ne, sonna ni takakunai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そうですかね、そんなに高くないですよ。
examplePolite.english: You think so? It's not that expensive.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer splits そうかな, and polite そうですかね / そうでしょうか are not found; component かな #90)
items.notes: In polite replies, sou deshou ka is the firmer, more formal objection; sou desu ka ne (drawn out: 'sou desu ka nee...') is the gentle one.

blocks.label: Accepting and declining
blocks.rationale: Answers to a request, suggestion or invitation: yes, an eager yes, and the soft no.
blocks.interference: ii yo grants a request and ii ne welcomes an idea. Bare 'ii desu' in reply to an offer means 'no thanks', and chotto... is the polite trailing no.

items.use: Grants a request or permission, or tells someone not to worry ('ii yo, ii yo').

examplePolite.ja: いいですよ、明日行きます。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer mostly splits いいよ and finds it as a unit only at #3841; いい #24 counts every use)
items.notes: In reply to an offer, bare 'ii desu' (often with a hand wave) usually means 'no thanks'; in reply to 'kore de ii desu ka?' it means 'yes, that's fine'.

items.use: Welcomes a suggestion, or praises something someone shows or tells you.

examplePolite.ja: いいですね、明日行きましょう。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer mostly splits いいね and finds it as a unit only at #5365; いい #24 counts every use)
items.notes: ii na (with na) is envy, 'lucky you / I wish', not approval.

items.use: Declines politely: you trail off after chotto instead of saying no, and the listener fills in the refusal.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、明日はちょっと…

items.freqNote: ちょっと #46 counts every use; the refusal is a subset
items.notes: Don't finish the sentence; trailing off is the refusal. When you hear it, take it as a no and don't ask why.

blocks.label: Asking about words
blocks.rationale: The learner's extraction tools: get a word explained, a meaning cleared up, or the Japanese supplied.
blocks.interference: -tte nani? asks what something is, dou iu imi? asks what it means or what someone meant, and nihongo de nante iu? goes from English or a gesture to the Japanese.

items.use: Put any unknown word in front ('X tte nani?') to get it explained. It also asks what a thing is.

examplePolite.ja: それって何ですか？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (って #18 counts every quotative use)
items.notes: nani becomes nan before desu: 'X tte nan desu ka'.

items.use: Asks what a word means, or what someone meant by what they said.

example.ja: それってどういう意味？
example.english: What do you mean by that?

examplePolite.romaji: sore tte dou iu imi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それってどういう意味ですか？
examplePolite.english: What do you mean by that?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; どういう #177, 意味 #287)
items.notes: Said sharply, it means 'what's that supposed to mean?'

items.kana: にほんごでなんていう
items.politeJa: 日本語で何て言いますか
items.use: Point at something or say the English word, then ask this to get a native speaker to give you the Japanese.

example.romaji: sore tte nihongo de nante iu?
example.ja: それって日本語で何て言う？
example.english: How do you say that in Japanese?

examplePolite.romaji: sore tte nihongo de nante iimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それって日本語で何て言いますか？
examplePolite.english: How do you say that in Japanese?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (multi-word frame; 日本語 #3651)
items.notes: Say eigo instead of nihongo to ask for the English.

blocks.label: Getting attention
blocks.rationale: Openers that call someone over, point something out, or stop things.
blocks.interference: chotto matte asks someone to wait, while chotto ii? asks for a moment of their time. nee calls a friend; hora points at something.

items.use: Gets a friend's attention before a question, suggestion or piece of news; doubled 'nee nee' is eager.

examplePolite.ja: あの、明日お時間ありますか？
examplePolite.english: Um, do you have time tomorrow?

items.notes: nee opens a sentence; the ending ne closes one.

items.use: Points something out ('hora, mite'), says 'see, I told you', or hands something over.

examplePolite.romaji: hora, mite kudasai. niji desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ほら、見てください。虹ですよ。

items.notes: It can sound pushy to a superior.

items.politeJa: ちょっと待ってください
items.use: Asks someone to wait or stop, or holds the floor while you think or check something.

example.romaji: chotto matte, hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、話があるんだけど。
example.english: Wait a sec, there's something I need to tell you.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、お話があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, there's something I'd like to talk to you about.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; 待つ #71 counts every form of matsu; ちょっと #46)
items.notes: matte! on its own is the urgent 'wait!'.

items.use: Opens a request, question or interruption by asking for a moment of someone's time, whether a friend's or a coworker's.

example.romaji: chotto ii? hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ちょっといい？話があるんだけど。
example.english: Got a sec? There's something I need to tell you.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ii desu ka? ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっといいですか？お話があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Do you have a moment? There's something I'd like to talk to you about.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; ちょっと #46, いい #24)
items.notes: The usual answers are 'un, nani?' or 'ii yo'. To a boss, say chotto yoroshii desu ka.

blocks.label: Fillers
blocks.rationale: Sounds and words that hold your turn while you think, so a pause doesn't hand it over.
blocks.interference: All five fit the same slot. etto is pure thinking time, ano also softens a request or opens one, maa hedges, nanka makes things vaguer, and nante iu ka hunts for a word.

items.use: Fills the pause while you think of an answer or a word, so you don't go silent.

example.ja: えっと、明日は無理かも。
example.english: Um, let me see... tomorrow might not work.

examplePolite.romaji: etto, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: えっと、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Um, let me see... tomorrow may not be possible.

items.freqNote: えっと #695; えーっと #1373; えーと #5199; ええと #11996, so etto beats the textbook eeto
items.notes: eeto is the slower textbook version; speech mostly uses etto.

items.use: Hesitates before something awkward, or politely gets attention before a question or request ('ano, sumimasen').

examplePolite.romaji: ano, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Um... tomorrow may not be possible.

items.freqNote: あの #66 also counts the demonstrative 'that'; the filler-only form あのー is #1320
items.notes: Before a noun it's the J word 'that': ano hito.

items.use: Hedges or half-concedes ('maa, ii ka', oh well, fine), softening an answer you don't want to commit to.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: まあ、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Well, tomorrow may not be possible.

items.notes: 'maa maa' means 'so-so' or 'now, now'. Opening a polite answer with maa can sound offhand to a superior. A standalone 'maa!' (oh my!) is a dated feminine exclamation you'll hear in dramas.

items.use: A casual filler that makes what follows vaguer or softer ('nanka, tsukareta', I'm kind of tired).

example.ja: なんか、明日は無理かも。

examplePolite.romaji: nanka, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なんか、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Somehow... tomorrow may not be possible.

items.freqNote: the filler なんか is misparsed (#144167); 何か #72 also counts 'something'
items.notes: Overuse sounds young. nanka is also the casual 'something' ('nanka nomu?', want something to drink?) and 'stuff like' ('kore nanka dou?'); only the floating, sentence-opening use is the filler.

items.politeJa: 何て言うんでしょうか
items.use: Buys time while you search for the right word mid-sentence.

example.romaji: nante iu ka, chotto kawatta hito da ne.
example.ja: 何て言うか、ちょっと変わった人だね。
example.english: How should I put it... he's a bit of an odd one.

examplePolite.romaji: nante iu n deshou ka, chotto kawatta hito desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何て言うんでしょうか、ちょっと変わった人ですね。
examplePolite.english: How should I put it... he's a bit unusual.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; the related っていうか is #948)
items.notes: tte iu ka is different: it means 'or rather', correcting yourself.

blocks.label: Comfort and cheer
blocks.rationale: What you say back to someone's news: relief, a shrug, encouragement, and denying a put-down.
blocks.interference: yokatta looks like a past tense but is relief you feel right now. shouganai accepts a bad outcome, while sonna koto nai rejects a negative claim.

items.use: Relief or gladness at an outcome ('yokatta, ma ni atta'). About someone else's news, it means 'I'm glad for you'.

example.english: Phew, I made it in time!

examplePolite.ja: それはよかったですね！
examplePolite.english: Oh, I'm so glad to hear that!

items.freqNote: the tokenizer reduces よかった to its dictionary form よい #120 (いい #24 holds the present tense)
items.notes: It's the past of ii; *iikatta doesn't exist.

items.use: Accepts a setback you can't change and moves on; it also means 'oh well, if I must' when you give in.

example.ja: しょうがない、また明日行こう。
example.english: Oh well, let's go again tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: shouganai desu ne, mata ashita ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: しょうがないですね、また明日行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: It can't be helped. Let's go again tomorrow.

items.freqNote: しょうがない #999; 仕方ない #1770; しかたない #1845
items.notes: shikatanai (or shikata ga nai) means the same and sounds slightly more formal; shaanai is the slangy version.

items.use: Encourages someone before or during any effort, from an exam to a long shift. The usual reply is 'un, ganbaru'.

examplePolite.ja: 明日の試験、頑張ってください。

items.freqNote: 頑張って #736; 頑張る #235; 頑張れ #1637
items.notes: Said to a boss, it can sound a little presumptuous. To someone already struggling, muri shinaide (don't overdo it) is kinder.

items.use: Brushes off a compliment ('your Japanese is so good!'), or reassures someone who's putting themselves down.

examplePolite.romaji: e, sonna koto nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: え、そんなことないですよ。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer splits the phrase)
items.notes: In polite speech you also hear 'sonna koto arimasen'.

reviewSummaries: natural: The casual lines are strong: almost every casual example is something a Tokyo speaker would really say, and every freqRank I spot-checked matched the tool output. The weak spots are the polite counterparts. sou deshou ka, chotto okuremashita, the exclaimed yokatta desu and a politely narrated kagi ga arimasen all sound textbook-stiff or shift the nuance, and the nante iu ka example puts the filler where it makes no sense. Beyond those, several examples copy a neighbour's sentence (iya = uun, sumimasen = gomen) and so never show the use that sets the item apart. Nothing needs cutting; otsukare and daijoubu-as-response are the clearest gaps.

nuance: Overall the block is strong. Glosses, use lines and interference notes are mostly accurate and pragmatically aware (sou desu vs sou desu ne, naruhodo to superiors, chotto... as a refusal, the uun/hmm romaji collision), and every frequency rank checks against the tool. The real gaps are learner traps that were left out: the yes/no answer to a negative question, wakannai as the soft 'I don't know' (shiranai sounds curt), nanka also meaning 'something', and daijoubu desu as 'no thanks'. Beyond those: sumimasen's examples duplicate gomen's, some flag and contrastGroup gaps, three 3-item blocks, and otsukare missing while hajimemashite takes a slot.

form: The form is very clean. The romaji follows the convention throughout (no macrons; long vowels, っ doubling, wa/o/e particles and spacing are all correct), kana and politeJa match, every masu, -te and contraction form is correct, and every example's romaji matches its Japanese word for word. All 49 freqRank values match the tool, and 15 checked alsoIn pointers resolve. The fixes needed are structural: 'ano' collides with J's slug, three prereqs use headwords like 'honto?' instead of slugs, ii-yo and ii-ne carry ranks the tokenizer made misleadingly low, nanka is the only item without a polite example, and several contrastGroups don't match the minimal pairs their blocks' interference text describes. Nothing needs cutting.

categories.name: General verbs
categories.scope: highest-reach verbs; casual = dictionary form, polite = masu form

blocks.label: Be and have
blocks.rationale: The ways to say something is there or that you have it: aru for things, iru for people and animals, motteru for what you own or carry.
blocks.interference: aru vs iru depends on whether the thing is alive (kasa aru / neko iru), and that holds for 'have' too: kyoudai iru? / inu iru? but jikan aru?; motteru is for what's in your possession or on you (kasa motteru?).

items.use: States that a thing, event or amount exists or is available, and is the default 'have' for time, plans and things (jikan aru?), with the thing marked by ga.

example.english: Do you have an umbrella at home?

examplePolite.romaji: uchi ni kasa ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: うちに傘がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have an umbrella at home?

items.freqNote: ある #21; includes auxiliary -te aru and copular de aru
items.notes: The negative is the separate word nai (kasa nai), never *aranai.

items.use: Says where a person or animal is or that they exist (ima doko ni iru?), is the 'have' for people and animals (kyoudai iru?, kanojo iru?, inu iru?), and is the base that -teru is built on.

examplePolite.ja: 今うちにいますか？

items.freqNote: いる #42 merges the verb with auxiliary -te iru; 居る #6802 separately
items.notes: Homophone iru 'need' (要る) is godan: iranai, itte.

items.use: Holding or carrying something, and in the -teru form owning or having it on you (kuruma motteru?), with motte iku / motte kuru meaning take / bring.

example.english: Do you have an umbrella on you?

examplePolite.ja: 今傘持ってますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have an umbrella with you?

items.notes: Owning or having it on you is motteru; bare motsu is 'hold / carry' (motou ka? = shall I carry that?) and also 'last' (ashita made motsu, karada ga motanai).

blocks.label: Do, can, become
blocks.rationale: The structural action verbs — do (suru, casual yaru), can do (dekiru) and become (naru) — that turn nouns and adjectives into events.
blocks.interference: suru and yaru overlap as 'do' (nani shiteru / nani yatteru), but only suru builds noun+suru verbs (shinpai suru, renraku suru); 'can do' for those is X dekiru, not a potential form of suru.

items.use: The all-purpose 'do' and the hinge of every noun+suru verb (benkyou suru, shinpai suru), while X ni suru / -ku suru means 'go with X' or 'make it X'.

example.english: What are you up to right now?

examplePolite.ja: 今何をしてますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you doing right now?

items.freqNote: する #15; also carries every noun+suru compound
items.notes: Irregular: shite, shita, shinai, shiyou.

items.use: Casual-leaning 'do' for activities, hobbies, sports and tasks (yatta!, gitaa yatteru, nani yatteru?); yarimasu is normal in everyday polite talk (watashi ga yarimasu), with shimasu the safer choice in formal settings.

example.ja: なんかスポーツやってる？

examplePolite.ja: 何かスポーツをやってますか？

items.freqNote: やる #45; includes -te yaru
items.notes: yatta! = 'Yay!' for any good news, not only your own success; yaru also means give to pets and plants (mizu yatta?), and -te yaru (doing for someone) sounds rough.

items.english: can do; be ready; come into being
items.use: The 'can' for skills and every noun+suru verb (unten dekiru, nihongo dekiru), with the skill marked by ga; dekita means 'it's ready / done' and also that something new appeared (atarashii mise ga dekita, kareshi dekita?).

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma no unten wa dekimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 車の運転はできますか？

items.freqNote: できる #73 (kana); 出来る #1313 counted separately
items.notes: Only nouns and suru-verbs take dekiru (unten dekiru, never *unten sureru); every other verb uses its potential form: ikeru, taberareru, never *iku dekiru.

items.use: Any change of state, as adjective -ku naru or noun / na-adjective ni naru (samuku natta, genki ni natta), and dou natta? asks how something turned out.

examplePolite.ja: 寒くなりましたね。

items.freqNote: なる #29
items.notes: Past natta reports the new state: samuku natta = it's cold now.

blocks.label: Coming and going
blocks.rationale: The motion verbs for plans and arrivals: go, come, go home, come back, leave, enter.
blocks.interference: iku/kuru follow the speaker's position, so 'I'll come to your party' is iku yo; kaeru means back to home or base while modoru means back to where you just were.

items.use: Going anywhere, asking about plans (iku?) and inviting (ikou), with the destination marked by ni or e; te-form and past are irregular (itte, itta).

example.ja: 明日のパーティー行く？
example.english: Are you going to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーに行きますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going to the party tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 行く #40; kana いく #179 separately; both include -te iku
items.notes: Heading to the listener is iku: ima iku ne = 'coming now'.

items.use: Movement toward the speaker or the place being talked about (kite!, kita!), and it is irregular: kita, konai, kite.

example.ja: 明日のパーティー来る？
example.english: Are you coming to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーに来ますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you coming to the party tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 来る #52; kana くる #429 separately; both include -te kuru
items.notes: The host asks kuru?; the guest answers iku yo.

items.use: Going back home or to your base such as your hometown or country (mou kaeru), and it is godan: kaette, kaetta.

example.english: What time are you heading home?

examplePolite.ja: 何時に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: What time are you going home?

items.freqNote: 帰る #101; homophone 変える (change) #450 separately
items.notes: Looks ichidan but is godan (kaette); kaeru 'change' is ichidan (kaete).

items.use: Returning to where you just were, or to a topic or earlier state (sugu modoru), without the 'home' meaning of kaeru.

example.english: What time will you be back?

examplePolite.ja: 何時に戻りますか？
examplePolite.english: What time will you be back?

items.use: Leaving a place (ie o deru) and coming out or appearing, as in answering the phone (denwa ni deru), getting a fever (netsu ga deta) or being in a show or match.

examplePolite.ja: もう家を出ましたよ。

items.freqNote: 出る #81
items.notes: Its transitive partner is dasu (put out, hand in).

items.use: Going into a room, bath, club or company, and fitting into a container (kaban ni hairu?), with the place marked by ni.

example.english: Have you had your bath yet?

examplePolite.ja: もうお風呂に入りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you had your bath yet?

items.notes: Godan despite the -iru ending: haitte, haitta.

blocks.label: Eat, drink, sleep
blocks.rationale: The body's daily round — eating, drinking, going to bed, getting up, being tired — which comes up in nearly every how's-your-day exchange.
blocks.interference: neru is going to bed, nemuru is actually falling asleep (nerenakatta / nemurenakatta = couldn't sleep); medicine is nomu, never taberu; tsukareta, a past form, is 'I'm tired' now.

items.use: Eating anything and suggesting meals (nani taberu?), and it is the model ichidan verb for pattern drills.

examplePolite.ja: もうご飯を食べましたか？

items.freqNote: 食べる #130

items.use: Drinking anything, taking medicine (kusuri o nomu) and going out drinking (nomi ni iku).

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nani o nomimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何を飲みますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you having to drink today?

items.notes: Medicine is nomu, never taberu.

items.use: Going to bed and sleeping (nanji ni neta?), and also lying down.

example.english: What time did you go to bed last night?

examplePolite.ja: 昨日何時に寝ましたか？
examplePolite.english: What time did you go to bed last night?

items.notes: neteru = is asleep; neta = went to bed.

items.use: Waking up or getting up (nanji ni okita?), and also events happening (nani ga okita?).

example.english: What time did you get up this morning?

examplePolite.ja: 今朝何時に起きましたか？
examplePolite.english: What time did you get up this morning?

items.freqNote: 起きる #329
items.notes: okiteru? = 'are you awake?'

items.use: Getting tired, where the past tsukareta is the normal way to say 'I'm tired' right now.

example.ja: 今日はほんとに疲れた。

examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に疲れました。

items.freqNote: 疲れる #714; 疲れた #1640 also listed as its own entry
items.notes: Present tsukareru says something is tiring (kono shigoto tsukareru = this job wears you out); 'I'm tired' right now is tsukareta, a lasting state is tsukareteru.

blocks.label: Look and show
blocks.rationale: Seeing and letting someone see: look or watch, show, and look for.
blocks.interference: mite (look) and misete (show me) differ by one syllable and reverse who does the looking; 'look for' is sagasu, never a form of miru.

items.use: Looking at something, watching shows and checking messages (mita?), and mite! points something out.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっとこれを見てください。
examplePolite.english: Please take a look at this.

items.freqNote: 見る #55; includes auxiliary -te miru
items.notes: Seeing a person, as in meeting up, is au, not miru.

items.use: Showing something to someone (X ni miseru), and misete is the standard 'let me see' for photos, phones and shop items.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、それ見せてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could I see that?

items.freqNote: 見せる #265; includes -te miseru

items.use: Searching for lost things, people, jobs or places, and X sagashiteru n desu kedo is the standard way to open in a shop.

example.english: I'm looking for my keys right now.

examplePolite.ja: 今鍵を探してます。
examplePolite.english: I'm looking for my keys right now.

items.freqNote: 探す #391; 捜す #708 counted separately
items.notes: Success is mitsuketa / mitsukatta (found it), not sagashita.

blocks.label: Knowing and remembering
blocks.rationale: Verbs for what you know: understand, know, remember, forget — the ones a learner uses about themselves in every exchange.
blocks.interference: wakaranai = I can't understand or work it out, shiranai = I have no information — but when you just can't answer a question (a stranger asks the way), wakarimasen / wakannai is the soft default and shirimasen sounds curt. 'Remember' is oboeteru, not shitteru; both live in the -teru form.

items.use: Understanding or being able to tell (wakaru?, wakaranai), with the thing understood marked by ga, and wakatta doubles as 'got it / OK'.

examplePolite.ja: この言葉は分かりますか？

items.freqNote: 分かる #213; kana わかる #1492 counted separately, so combined use is higher than either rank
items.notes: wakatteru = 'I know already', which can sound irritated.

items.use: Having a piece of information or knowing a person or place, where the positive is always shitteru and the negative always shiranai (never *shittenai).

examplePolite.ja: この言葉は知ってますか？

items.freqNote: 知る #74 (all inflections; 知ってる not found as a unit); 知らない #669 as its own entry
items.notes: Polite shirimasen can sound like 'not my business'; wakarimasen is the safe polite 'I don't know'.

items.use: Getting something into memory (oboeru) and still having it (oboeteru / oboetenai), so 'do you remember?' is always oboeteru?

example.ja: あの人の名前覚えてる？
example.english: Do you remember that person's name?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito no namae o oboetemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの人の名前を覚えてますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you remember that person's name?

items.freqNote: 覚える #255
items.notes: Bare oboeru means 'memorise'; remembering now is oboeteru, and 'oh, now I remember!' is omoidashita, not oboeta.

items.use: Forgetting names, facts and plans and leaving things behind, mostly as wasureta / wasurechatta, plus the reminder wasurenaide ne (don't forget) and a, wasureteta (oh, I'd forgotten).

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito no namae o wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの人の名前を忘れました。

items.freqNote: 忘れる #201
items.notes: Leaving an item behind is also wasureru: kasa wasureta.

blocks.label: Say, talk, ask
blocks.rationale: Speech-act verbs: say, talk, ask or listen, tell, ask a favour.
blocks.interference: English 'ask' splits into kiku (a question) and tanomu (a favour), and 'tell' into iu (words), hanasu (talk about) and oshieru (give information).

items.use: Reporting words with tte or to (nante itta?), naming things (X tte iu), and sou iu / kou iu for 'that kind of'.

examplePolite.ja: 今なんて言いましたか？

items.freqNote: 言う #28; kana いう #167 counted separately; quotative って-forms split off by the tokenizer
items.notes: Pronounced yuu; itta / itte sound the same as iku's, but casual speech often says yutta / yutte, which keeps them apart.

items.use: Talking with someone (X to hanasu), telling about something, and speaking a language (nihongo hanaseru?).

example.english: I'll tell you about it later.

examplePolite.ja: 後で話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll tell you about it later.

items.notes: Quoting someone's exact words is iu, not hanasu.

items.use: Listening (kiite), hearing news (kiita?) and asking someone a question, with the person asked marked by ni.

examplePolite.ja: 友達に聞いてみました。

items.freqNote: 聞く #67; 聴く #1930 separately
items.notes: Bare tomodachi ni kiita usually means 'I heard it from a friend'; kiite mita makes it 'I asked'.

items.use: Giving someone information or know-how, where oshiete is the everyday 'tell me' for numbers, directions and tips.

examplePolite.ja: 電話番号を教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Could you give me your phone number?

items.freqNote: 教える #196
items.notes: Not just 'teach': michi oshiete = 'tell me the way'.

items.use: Asking someone to do something (X ni tanomu) and ordering food or a delivery (nani tanomu?).

example.english: I asked a friend to do it.

examplePolite.ja: 友達に頼みました。
examplePolite.english: I asked a friend to do it.

items.notes: A direct tanomu (yo)! = 'I'm counting on you' leans masculine; to ask a favour yourself say onegai / onegai shimasu — 'X, tanomimasu' is how a boss hands out a task.

blocks.label: Think and feel
blocks.rationale: Verbs for what's going on in your head: an opinion (omou), thinking it over (kangaeru), something on your mind (ki ni naru), a hunch (ki ga suru).
blocks.interference: omou gives a view (... to omou) while kangaeru means working something through (mada kangaeteru); ki ga suru (a hunch, takes a clause) and ki ni naru (it nags at me, takes ga) share ki but differ in particle and verb.

items.use: Attaches with to to any clause to state an opinion or guess softly (ii to omou), and -ou to omotteru states a plan.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ame ga furu to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日雨が降ると思います。
examplePolite.english: I think it will rain tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 思う #33
items.notes: Someone else's view uses omotteru (Tanaka-san mo sou omotteru); nouns and na-adjectives keep da before to: ii hito da to omou, kirei da to omou (never *ii hito to omou).

items.use: Actively thinking something through or coming up with ideas, and the polite way to put off a decision (chotto kangaete mimasu / kangaete okimasu).

examplePolite.ja: それはまだ考えてます。

items.freqNote: 考える #112
items.notes: Hearing chotto kangaete okimasu usually means a polite no; 'I think that ...' is to omou, not to kangaeru.

items.use: Something keeps pulling your attention, as curiosity, interest or worry, with the thing marked by ga (X ga ki ni naru).

example.romaji: ashita no tenki, ki ni naru.
example.english: I'm a bit worried about tomorrow's weather.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no tenki ga ki ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の天気が気になります。
examplePolite.english: I'm a little concerned about tomorrow's weather.

items.freqNote: 気になる #368 as a lexicalized entry
items.notes: Its active partner: ki ni shinaide = don't worry about it.

items.use: Attaches to any clause to mark it as a hunch rather than a claim (... ki ga suru), sounding more intuitive than to omou.

example.romaji: ashita ame furu ki ga suru.
example.english: I have a feeling it'll rain tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ame ga furu ki ga shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日雨が降る気がします。
examplePolite.english: I have a feeling it will rain tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 気がする #554 as a lexicalized entry
items.notes: No to: a clause attaches directly (furu ki ga suru); a na-adjective takes na and a noun takes mitai na (hen na ki ga suru, uso mitai na ki ga suru).

blocks.label: Making plans
blocks.rationale: Arranging to see someone: wait, meet, decide, get in touch.
blocks.interference: 'See a friend' is au with ni, not miru; kimeta (I decided) vs kimatta (it's been settled) is the pair to watch inside kimeru.

items.use: Waiting for someone or something (X o matsu), and matte / chotto matte is the all-purpose 'hold on'.

example.english: I'll wait for you at the station.

examplePolite.ja: 駅で待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll be waiting at the station.

items.freqNote: 待つ #71
items.notes: matteru = 'I'll be waiting' as well as 'I'm waiting'.

items.use: Meeting or seeing a person, planned or by chance, with the person marked by ni (or to for a mutual meet-up).

example.english: What time should we meet tomorrow?

examplePolite.ja: 明日何時に会いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: What time shall we meet tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 会う #110; 合う (fit, match) #563 separately
items.notes: Homophone au 合う = fit / match (saizu ga au).

items.use: Deciding on something (X ni kimeru = go with X) and asking or saying whether a decision is made (kimeta?, mada kimetenai).

example.ja: 週末の予定もう決めた？
example.english: Have you made plans for the weekend yet?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu no yotei wa mou kimemashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末の予定はもう決めましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you decided your weekend plans yet?

items.freqNote: 決める #261; intransitive 決まる #335 separately
items.notes: kimatta = 'it's been decided' (no one named); kimeta = 'I/we decided'.

items.use: Getting in touch by any channel — text, call or message — and the standard way to close a plan (mata renraku suru ne), with renraku shite = let me know.

examplePolite.ja: また連絡しますね。

items.freqNote: 連絡する not found as a unit; rank of the noun 連絡
items.notes: The person contacted takes ni: senpai ni renraku suru.

blocks.label: Buy, use, make
blocks.rationale: Everyday verbs for handling things: buying, using and making them.
blocks.interference: tsukatta (used) and tsukutta (made) differ by one vowel, so they share the kore dare ga ...? frame and are told apart by ear; katte is also the te-form of katsu (win) and of kau 'keep a pet', and the word katte 'selfish / as you like', so context decides.

items.use: Buying anything (X o kau), and nani katta? / doko de katta? is everyday small talk.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, doko de katta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それ、どこで買ったんですか？

items.notes: Negative is kawanai; homophone kau 飼う = keep a pet.

items.use: Using objects, apps, words, money or time, and tsukatte ii? asks to borrow or use something.

examplePolite.ja: これ、誰が使いましたか？

items.notes: tsukatta (used) and tsukutta (made) differ only in the middle vowel.

items.use: Making, cooking or creating anything — food, plans, friends, even time (jikan o tsukuru).

examplePolite.romaji: kore, dare ga tsukutta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、誰が作ったんですか？

blocks.label: Wrong and stuck
blocks.rationale: Reactions when something's off: it's different or wrong, I'm in a bind, I made a mistake.
blocks.interference: chigau is a state (that's wrong / different) and machigaeru an act (I got it wrong): bangou chigau yo vs bangou machigaeta.

items.use: The everyday one-word 'no, that's not it' for correcting someone (far more common than iie in conversation) and the verb for being different (X to chigau); a flat chigau! can sound blunt, so soften with chotto chigau kamo.

examplePolite.ja: 電話番号が違いますよ。

items.freqNote: 違う #94
items.notes: A verb, not an adjective: polite chigaimasu, never *chigai desu.

items.english: be in a bind; be stuck
items.use: Saying a situation causes you trouble, which is the indirect way to object or ask for help (komatta na, komaru n desu kedo).

example.english: That'd be a bit of a problem.

examplePolite.ja: それはちょっと困ります。
examplePolite.english: That would be a bit of a problem for me.

items.notes: komatta = 'I'm stuck (now)'; the past describes the current state.

items.use: Getting something wrong yourself — a number, a word, the way — and the learner's main repair verb (machigaeta, gomen).

example.english: I got the phone number wrong.

examplePolite.ja: 電話番号を間違えました。
examplePolite.english: I got the phone number wrong.

items.freqNote: 間違える #956; intransitive 間違う #711 and noun 間違い #1085 counted separately
items.notes: machigatteru = 'is wrong' (a state); machigaeta = 'I made the mistake'.

blocks.label: Start, stop, keep at it
blocks.rationale: Phases of an activity — starting it, its ending, quitting it — plus ganbaru, the effort of keeping at it.
blocks.interference: owatta = it finished (shigoto owatta, done for the day) while yameta = someone stopped or quit (shigoto yameta, quit the job).

items.use: Starting an activity, hobby, job or meeting (X o hajimeru), and hajimeyou means 'let's start'.

examplePolite.ja: 最近ヨガを始めました。

items.freqNote: 始める #330; intransitive 始まる #435 separately
items.notes: Transitive; the thing itself starting is hajimaru (jugyou ga hajimaru).

items.use: An activity coming to an end (shigoto owatta?), and owatta! also announces that your own task is done.

example.english: Are you done with work yet?

examplePolite.ja: もう仕事は終わりましたか？

items.freqNote: 終わる #190
items.notes: Slang owatta... = 'I'm doomed' (shiken owatta = I bombed the exam); that sense is slang, not 'it finished'.

items.use: Stopping an action, giving up a habit or plan, and quitting a job or school (X o yameru), with yamete! meaning 'stop it!'

example.english: Did you already quit your job?

examplePolite.ja: もう仕事を辞めましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you already quit your job?

items.freqNote: やめる #117 (kana); 辞める (quit a job) #604 separately
items.notes: Written 辞める for quitting a job, やめる for stopping an action; one word by ear.

items.use: Putting in effort or holding out (ganbaru, ganbatta), and ganbarimasu is a standard polite promise to do your best.

examplePolite.ja: 次は頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll do my best next time.

items.freqNote: 頑張る #235; lexicalized 頑張って #736 and 頑張れ #1637 counted separately
items.notes: The bare encouragement ganbatte is drilled as a formula among the social phrases.

blocks.label: Giving and getting
blocks.rationale: The giving triad, where direction picks the verb: away from me (ageru), toward me (kureru), I receive (morau).
blocks.interference: ageru and kureru both translate 'give' but point opposite ways — anything coming to me or my side is kureru; morau makes the receiver the subject and marks the giver with ni.

items.use: Giving from me or my side to someone else (X ni ageru), and kore ageru means 'here, you can have this'.

example.english: I'm giving this to a friend.

examplePolite.ja: これは友達にあげます。
examplePolite.english: I'm giving this to a friend.

items.freqNote: あげる #668 (kana); 上げる (raise) #837 separately; includes -te ageru
items.notes: Offering to a superior with ageru can sound condescending.

items.use: Someone giving to me or my in-group, with the giver marked by ga and the recipient (me) usually left unsaid.

examplePolite.ja: これは友達がくれました。

items.freqNote: くれる #565; includes -te kureru
items.notes: Things given to you are never ageta: tomodachi ga kureta.

items.use: Receiving something, with me as the subject and the giver marked by ni or kara (X ni moratta).

example.english: I got this from a friend.

examplePolite.ja: これは友達にもらいました。
examplePolite.english: I got this from a friend.

items.freqNote: もらう #313; 貰う #11381; includes -te morau
items.notes: moratta and kureta describe the same event from two angles.

blocks.label: Take, cost, call
blocks.rationale: Wide-reach light verbs whose meaning comes from the object: toru (take, pass, get), kakaru (time or money it takes), kakeru (cause trouble, call, spend, put on).
blocks.interference: 'It takes an hour' is kakaru, not toru; kakaru (it takes, ga) and kakeru (spend, call, o) are an intransitive/transitive pair — jikan ga kakaru vs jikan o kakeru.

items.use: Picking up or passing things (sore totte), plus light-verb uses for taking a break, a photo, a seat or a licence (yasumi o toru, shashin toru).

examplePolite.ja: すみません、それ取ってください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you pass me that?

items.freqNote: 取る #228; homophone 撮る (take a photo) #649 separately
items.notes: totte (take) vs tootte (pass through) differ only in vowel length.

items.use: How much time or money something takes (jikan ga kakaru, dore kurai kakaru?), and also incoming calls and locks being on.

examplePolite.ja: どれくらいかかりますか？

items.freqNote: かかる #385 (kana); 掛かる #5316 separately
items.notes: Intransitive partner of kakeru: jikan ga kakaru (it takes) / jikan o kakeru (spend).

items.use: Causing trouble (meiwaku o kakeru), phoning (denwa o kakeru), spending time, locking, and putting on glasses or sauce.

examplePolite.ja: 迷惑をかけてすみません。

items.freqNote: かける #244 (kana, all senses); 掛ける #2742 separately
items.notes: For phoning, casual talk more often says denwa suru: ato de denwa suru ne.
