reviewSummaries: natural: Strong set. The casual examples are natural Tokyo speech, the contrast frames work well (owatta/yameta, kureta/moratta, furu to omou/furu ki ga suru), and every freqRank matches the tool output. The main problems: polite versions were converted mechanically (topic wa plus -mashita ka where natives say -ta n desu ka), 'mata renraku suru' is mistranslated as 'again', 'kore ... ageta' slips on kore/sore deixis, and yaru's use field contradicts its own polite form. One list-wide decision is still open: whether spoken polites use -teimasu or -temasu. No cuts.

nuance: The glosses are mostly accurate, the polite forms are true desu/masu pairs with the same meaning, the ledger pointers check out, and the contrast design is strong (wakaru/shitteru and tsukau/tsukuru built on the same sentence frame). Every item earns its place, so nothing is cut. The main meaning problems: iru's 'have (people)' sense is missing; tsukareru's present tense is misdescribed; the pragmatic claims for yaru, chigau and tanomu are off; dekiru is missing its 'come into being' sense and the *iku dekiru trap; and the wakarimasen vs shirimasen politeness trap needs a block-level note. Coverage gaps worth filling: tsuku, asobu, shinpai suru and kariru/kasu (major); okureru, mitsukeru/mitsukaru, iru (need) and sumu/hataraku/yasumu (minor). 'Coming and going' should be split, since it already has 6 items and grows to 7 with tsuku.

form: The form is clean overall. I checked all 54 freqRank values with the tool and every one matches, including the separate kana/kanji ranks quoted in freqNotes. All 32 ledger pointers and every te-dependents, exit-battery and vocab-trainer pointer I grepped resolve. Romaji follows the convention, kana and politeJa match, conjugations and contractions are correct, there are no duplicate slugs, and all 14 blocks hold 3–6 items. The real fixes are: write 家 as うち where the romaji is uchi (aru, iru), so the audio can't come out as 'ie'; change the broken prereq "kaeru" to kaeru-return; use slugs (teru, te-request, tte-quote) instead of romaji in prereqs; write nante as one word; and add closing punctuation to match category J and kotoba. The rest are small gloss fixes (motsu, tsukareru, chigau, yaru, wasureru), two missing contrastGroups, and a few missing alsoIn pointers.

categories.name: Grammar patterns as vocabulary
categories.scope: attachments bolted onto any verb or adjective

blocks.label: Past, negative, linking
blocks.rationale: The first endings almost every sentence needs: past and negative for verbs and for adjectives/nouns, plus the adjective/noun linking form built on the same -ku stem.
blocks.interference: Verbs and adjectives conjugate differently (neta / isogashikatta, ikanai / isogashikunai), never *isogashii datta; and takai ja nai is a tag ('it's pricey, isn't it?'), never the negative takakunai.

items.use: Puts any verb in the past for what you did or what happened, built with the same sound changes as the -te form (itta, tabeta, shita).

example.english: I went to bed early last night.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は早く寝ました。
examplePolite.english: I went to bed early last night.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer folds た into the verb (standalone た #100752)
items.notes: -ta also covers 'already': mou tabeta? = have you eaten yet? Trap: 'not yet' is mada tabetenai, never *tabenakatta, which means 'I didn't eat (then)'.

items.use: Makes any verb negative for 'don't / won't' (ikanai, wakannai), and is the stem that -nakya, -nakute mo ii and -nai hou ga ii build on.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は行きません。

items.freqNote: ない #43 combines the negative auxiliary and the adjective 'there isn't'
items.notes: Past negative is -nakatta (ikanakatta); casual speech shortens -ranai to -nnai (wakannai). With a rising tone it invites: issho ni ikanai? = want to come? (polite: ikimasen ka?)

items.use: Past tense for descriptions: i-adjectives swap -i for -katta (samukatta, ii -> yokatta), while na-adjectives and nouns take datta (hima datta, ame datta).

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は忙しかったです。

items.freqNote: rank of だった; the tokenizer splits -katta off the adjective, so it has no usable rank of its own
items.notes: Trap: never *takai datta, and in polite speech never *takai deshita; the past goes on the i-adjective itself (takakatta, takakatta desu).

items.use: Negative for descriptions: i-adjectives swap -i for -kunai (takakunai, ii -> yokunai), while na-adjectives and nouns take ja nai (hima ja nai, sou ja nai).

examplePolite.ja: 今日は忙しくないです。

items.freqNote: rank of じゃない, which also counts the tag-question use (ja nai?)
items.notes: Past negative: -kunakatta / ja nakatta (polite -kunakatta desu / ja nakatta desu). Trap: after an i-adjective ja nai is always the tag (takai ja nai = it's pricey, isn't it); more formal polite is -ku arimasen / ja arimasen.

items.use: The -te form of adjectives and nouns, used to link descriptions (yasukute oishii) or give a reason (isogashikute, hima de); negatives use -nakute (jikan ga nakute).

example.ja: この店、安くておいしいよ。
example.english: This place is cheap and the food's good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono omise, yasukute oishii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このお店、安くておいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: This place is cheap and the food's good.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; an inflection the tokenizer splits off
items.notes: Na-adjectives and nouns take de (shizuka de, ame de); ii -> yokute.

blocks.label: Doing and done
blocks.rationale: Four -te auxiliaries that set the shape of an action: ongoing, tried out, finished, done ahead.
blocks.interference: -teru, -chau and -toku are all short contractions on the same -te form; key on the ending: -teru ongoing, -chatta finished, -toku done ahead. Don't mix -toku with -teku (-te iku): kaitoku vs kaiteku. -te miru stays apart as 'try and see'.

items.english: is doing / is in a state
items.use: Attaches to the -te form for an ongoing action (tabeteru), a resulting state (kekkon shiteru, shitteru) or a habit; it is the casual contraction of -te iru.

example.english: I'm writing a report right now.

examplePolite.ja: 今レポート書いてます。
examplePolite.english: I'm writing a report right now.

items.freqNote: rank of contracted てる; full いる #42 also counts the main verb 'be'
items.notes: With change verbs it's a state, not progress: kekkon shiteru = is married. Trap: the negative of shitteru is shiranai, not *shittenai.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to try something out and see how it goes (tabete miru, kiite miru), which also softens plans and suggestions.

example.english: OK, I'll give it a try.

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、食べてみます。
examplePolite.english: OK, I'll give it a try.

items.freqNote: rank of kana みる, mostly the auxiliary (見る #55 is 'see')
items.notes: Not 'attempt and fail': you actually do it to find out.

items.use: Contracted -te shimau, marking something done completely, often with regret or an 'oops' (wasurechatta, tabechatta); -nde verbs take -jau (nonjatta).

example.ja: レポート、もう書いちゃった。

examplePolite.ja: レポート、もう書いちゃいました。

items.freqNote: rank of ちゃう (some Kansai ちゃう 'no, wrong' mixed in); ちゃった #4935, じゃう #9415, full しまう #2285
items.notes: The regret reading is the everyday one: saifu wasurechatta = I forgot my wallet (ugh). Not -cha (= -te wa): kaetchau = I'll end up going home, kaetcha dame = you can't go home. -chaimashita is friendly-polite; with superiors or strangers use -te shimaimashita.

items.use: Contracted -te oku, for doing something now so it's ready later (kattoku) or leaving it as it is (sono mama ni shitoite); -nde verbs take -doku (yondoku).

example.ja: レポート、先に書いとく。
example.english: I'll get the report written first.

examplePolite.ja: レポート、先に書いときます。
examplePolite.english: I'll get the report written first.

items.freqNote: rank of kana おく (mostly the -te oku auxiliary); contracted とく #8852
items.notes: Not -teku (-te iku): kaitoku = write it now so it's done, kaiteku = write it before heading off. Past -toita (kaitoita) sits close to -teta (kaiteta); listen for the o.

blocks.label: Want, can, have done
blocks.rationale: The frames for talking about yourself: what you want to do, what you want others to do, what you can do, and what you've done.
blocks.interference: issho ni ikitai (I want to go) vs issho ni itte hoshii (I want you to go): the -te form hands the action to the other person. -ta koto ga aru needs the past; iku koto ga aru means 'sometimes'.

items.use: Attaches to the verb stem for what you want to do (ikitai, tabetai) and conjugates like an i-adjective (ikitakunai, ikitakatta).

example.english: I want to go with you.

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to go with you.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer folds たい into the verb (standalone たい #5172 badly undercounts)
items.notes: For someone else's wants, quote them (ikitai tte) instead of stating them. Don't offer with -tai desu ka? (nomitai desu ka? sounds nosy); use -masen ka? or ikaga desu ka? instead. The object can take ga: mizu ga nomitai.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to say you want someone else to do something (kite hoshii, yamete hoshii), with the doer marked by ni.

example.english: I want you to come with me.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni itte hoshii n desu kedo...
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行ってほしいんですけど…
examplePolite.english: I was hoping you'd come with me...

items.freqNote: rank of kana ほしい; also counts plain 'want (a thing)'
items.notes: Said straight at someone it presses: soften with n da kedo (casual) or n desu kedo (polite), and to ask a stranger or senior use -te moraemasu ka? instead.

items.use: Turns a verb into 'can': godan verbs change -u to -eru (iku -> ikeru), ichidan verbs swap -ru for -rareru (taberu -> taberareru), suru becomes dekiru; the object often takes ga (nihongo ga hanaseru).

example.ja: 明日のパーティー行ける？
example.english: Can you make it to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni ikemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーに行けますか？
examplePolite.english: Can you make it to the party tomorrow?

items.freqNote: tokenizer keeps potentials as their own verbs: 言える #291, 行ける #985, 話せる #1219; suppletive できる #73
items.notes: Casual speech drops ra in short verbs: mireru, koreru (ra-nuki); polite speech keeps -rareru. wakaru has no potential (wakareru = break up). mieru / kikoeru = it's visible / audible, vs mirareru / kikeru = get to see / listen.

items.use: Attaches to the past form to ask about or state experience (itta koto aru?, mita koto nai); casual speech drops ga.

example.english: Have you ever been to Okinawa?

examplePolite.romaji: okinawa ni itta koto ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 沖縄に行ったことがありますか？
examplePolite.english: Have you ever been to Okinawa?

items.freqNote: rank of fused ことがある; also counts the 'sometimes' use (iku koto ga aru)
items.notes: With the plain present (iku koto ga aru) it means 'sometimes', not experience.

blocks.label: Choosing
blocks.rationale: Noun + particle frames for picking among options (deciding, settling, suggesting loosely) plus the frame for when only one option is left.
blocks.interference: koohii ni suru (I'll have coffee), koohii de ii (coffee will do), koohii demo (coffee or something) change only the particle; -demo after a noun is not 'but': it softens here, but can also mean 'even'.

items.english: X will do, X is fine
items.use: After a noun, settles on it as good enough (mizu de ii, kore de ii?) when ordering, checking or accepting something.

examplePolite.ja: コーヒーでいいです。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits で+いい (いい #24)
items.notes: Can sound like 'it'll have to do'; koohii ga ii is the keen choice. To accept a host's offer, say koohii o onegai shimasu; kore de ii desu ka? (is this OK?) is always safe.

items.use: After a noun, picks it from the options (kore ni suru, raishuu ni suru), the standard way to order or settle a choice.

example.ja: じゃあ、コーヒーにする。

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、コーヒーにします。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits に+する (fused ことにする 'decide to' #886)
items.notes: With a verb it becomes koto ni suru: iku koto ni shita = I decided to go.

items.use: After a noun, offers it as one loose example so a suggestion sounds soft (ocha demo, eiga demo), mostly in invitations.

example.english: Want to grab a coffee or something?

examplePolite.ja: コーヒーでも飲みませんか？
examplePolite.english: Shall we grab a coffee or something?

items.freqNote: rank of でも, shared with 'but' and 'even'; an upper bound
items.notes: Three readings after a noun: a loose example in offers and invitations (ocha demo), 'even' (kodomo demo wakaru, sensei demo shiranai), and 'any-' after question words (nandemo ii). Only at the start of a sentence does demo mean 'but'.

items.use: After a plain verb, says it's the only option left (yaru shika nai, matsu shika nai), for resolve or resignation.

example.english: I guess I just have to do it.

examplePolite.ja: もうやるしかないです。
examplePolite.english: I guess I just have to do it.

items.freqNote: rank of fused しかない; also counts plain 'only X' after nouns
items.notes: After a noun it's plain 'only': kore shika nai = this is all there is. More formal: -shika arimasen.

blocks.label: May and must
blocks.rationale: The permission and obligation ladder on one verb: may, mustn't, must, needn't.
blocks.interference: -nakute mo ii (needn't) gets mistaken for 'mustn't' (-cha dame); anchor both to one verb: kaeranakute mo ii (you don't have to go) vs kaetcha dame (you can't go).

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to ask for or give permission (suwatte mo ii?, tabete ii yo); casual speech often drops mo.

examplePolite.romaji: mou kaette mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: もう帰ってもいいですか？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits て+も+いい (fused てもいい only #56914); いい #24
items.notes: A refusal usually comes as chotto... rather than a flat dame.

items.politeJa: 〜ちゃダメです／〜じゃダメです
items.use: Contracted -te wa dame, used to forbid or warn against something (sawatcha dame); verbs with -nde take -ja (nonja dame).

examplePolite.ja: まだ帰っちゃダメですよ。

items.freqNote: rank of the contraction ちゃ; ダメ #596, いけない #277 (all uses)
items.notes: -cha dame desu is the friendly version; careful speech uses -te wa dame desu, firm rules -te wa ikemasen, and requests to strangers -naide kudasai.

items.use: Attaches to the -nai stem (ikanakya) for what you've got to do; casual speech usually stops there and leaves off ikenai.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ帰らなきゃいけませんね。

items.freqNote: tokenizer often splits the contraction, so this undercounts; なきゃいけない #4891, なくちゃ #9360, なければならない #6186
items.notes: -nakucha and -nai to mean the same and are heard too; -nakya is the most common.

items.use: Attaches to the -nai stem to say something isn't necessary (konakute mo ii, ki ni shinakute ii); casual speech drops mo.

example.ja: まだ帰らなくてもいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to go home yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada kaeranakute mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: まだ帰らなくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't have to go home yet.

items.freqNote: rank of fused なくてもいい; split tokens not counted, so likely an undercount
items.notes: It's the opposite of -nakya: 'don't have to', never 'mustn't'.

blocks.label: Becoming
blocks.rationale: Change-of-state frames on naru and suru: something becomes X, someone makes it X, a skill or habit gradually comes about.
blocks.interference: kami mijikaku natta (it got short) vs kami mijikaku shita (I made it short) differ only in naru vs suru; -you ni naru attaches to verbs, -ku naru to adjectives.

items.use: Marks a change of state: i-adjectives take -ku naru (samuku naru), na-adjectives and nouns take ni naru (genki ni naru, isha ni naru).

examplePolite.ja: 髪、短くなりましたね。

items.freqNote: rank of なる (all uses; change-of-state dominant)
items.notes: ii -> yoku naru: yoku natta = it got better.

items.use: Makes something X on purpose: i-adjectives take -ku suru (yasuku suru, hayaku shite), na-adjectives take ni suru (shizuka ni shite), often as a -te request.

example.english: I got my hair cut short.

examplePolite.ja: 髪、短くしました。
examplePolite.english: I got my hair cut short.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; する #15 counts all doing
items.notes: Common as a request: hayaku shite (hurry up), shizuka ni shite (keep it down). Na-adjective ni suru isn't the choosing ni suru: kirei ni suru = tidy it up, koohii ni suru = I'll have coffee.

items.use: After a plain verb, often a potential, marks a gradual change in ability or habit (hanaseru you ni natta, hayaku okiru you ni natta).

example.ja: ちょっと話せるようになった。
example.english: I can speak a little now.

examplePolite.ja: 少し話せるようになりました。
examplePolite.english: I can speak a little now.

items.freqNote: rank of fused ようになる
items.notes: It implies change over time; for losing an ability say -naku natta (taberarenaku natta).

blocks.label: Too, easy, hard
blocks.rationale: Suffixes on the verb stem that grade how something goes: too much, easy, hard, and the way to do it.
blocks.interference: -yasui and -nikui are opposites on the same stem (kakiyasui / kakinikui), and -yasui here is not 'cheap'; -sugiru makes a verb, -kata makes a noun.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem or adjective stem for overdoing or excess (tabesugita, takasugiru, shizukasugi), and the bare -sugi is common in reactions.

example.ja: 昨日ちょっと飲みすぎた。
example.english: I drank a bit too much last night.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日ちょっと飲みすぎました。
examplePolite.english: I drank a bit too much last night.

items.freqNote: rank of 過ぎる (also 'pass by'); kana すぎる #838, noun すぎ #2478 (tabesugi)
items.notes: Casual reactions use bare -sugi to mean 'so X', not 'too X': oishisugi = so good, kawaisugi = so cute (youth slang; keep it among friends).

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem for 'easy to' (wakariyasui, tsukaiyasui) or 'prone to' (tsukareyasui), and conjugates like an i-adjective.

example.english: This pen is easy to write with.

examplePolite.ja: このペン、書きやすいです。
examplePolite.english: This pen is easy to write with.

items.freqNote: rank of kana やすい, the suffix (安い 'cheap' #1315 is separate); 分かりやすい #3193
items.notes: Not 'cheap': after a verb stem yasui means easy.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem for 'hard to' (kikinikui, tabenikui), a soft way to say something is awkward or inconvenient.

example.english: This pen is hard to write with.

examplePolite.ja: このペン、書きにくいです。
examplePolite.english: This pen is hard to write with.

items.freqNote: rank of kana にくい, the suffix (憎い 'hateful' #3878 separate); 分かりにくい #12919
items.notes: iinikui n da kedo (this is hard to say, but...) is a common lead-in to awkward news.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem to make a noun meaning the way to do it (tsukaikata, yarikata, iikata), which covers 'how do you...?' without new grammar.

example.english: Do you know how to use this?

examplePolite.ja: これの使い方分かりますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know how to use this?

items.freqNote: rank of 言い方, the top -kata compound; やり方 #1241, 使い方 #3636 (方 'kata' #292 mixes 'person')
items.notes: The object takes no: kanji no kakikata (*kanji o kakikata). Suru nouns take no shikata: benkyou no shikata.

blocks.label: Go and do
blocks.rationale: Errand and direction frames on iku and kuru, which say where the trip goes around an action.
blocks.interference: katte kuru (go buy and come back), katte iku (buy on the way, then go), kai ni iku (go out to buy): the same verb on three trips; -te + iku/kuru vs stem + ni. In casual speech katteku (on my way) and katte kuru (go and come back) differ only by the final -ru; listen for it.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for going to do something and coming back (katte kuru, itte kimasu), or for a change that has set in (samuku natte kita).

examplePolite.ja: 飲み物買ってきますね。

items.freqNote: rank of kana くる, mostly the auxiliary (来る #52 is 'come')
items.notes: itte kimasu (I'm off) is this pattern frozen as a set phrase.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for doing something on the way out or taking it along (motte iku, tabete iku), or for a change that will keep going (fuete iku).

example.english: I'll pick up drinks on my way.

examplePolite.ja: 飲み物買っていきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll pick up drinks on my way.

items.freqNote: rank of kana いく, mostly the auxiliary (行く #40 is 'go'); contracted てく #7358
items.notes: Casual speech shortens it to -teku: motteku, katteku.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem for the purpose of a trip (tabe ni iku, ai ni kita) and works with other movement verbs (tori ni kaeru).

example.english: I'm heading out to buy drinks.

examplePolite.ja: 飲み物買いに行きますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm going out to buy drinks.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits に+行く (行く #40 counts all going)
items.notes: Suru nouns drop suru: kaimono ni iku, benkyou ni kita.

blocks.label: Favours
blocks.rationale: The giving/receiving triad that marks who benefits from an action.
blocks.interference: Same act, three viewpoints: tomodachi ga oshiete kureta / tomodachi ni oshiete moratta / tomodachi ni oshiete ageta. Kureru points toward the speaker, ageru away, and morau takes the receiver's view with the giver on ni.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form when someone does something for you or your side (oshiete kureta), and is the base of casual requests (-te kureru?).

examplePolite.ja: 友達が教えてくれました。

items.freqNote: rank of kana くれる, mostly the auxiliary use
items.notes: Leaving it off sounds cold: oshiete kureta thanks the person, oshieta only reports. As a request, -te kurenai? is softer than -te kureru?

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for a favour seen from the receiver's side, with the doer marked by ni (tomodachi ni oshiete moratta); it also frames requests (-te moraeru?).

example.ja: 友達に教えてもらった。
example.english: I got a friend to tell me.

examplePolite.ja: 友達に教えてもらいました。
examplePolite.english: I got a friend to tell me.

items.freqNote: rank of kana もらう (main verb 'receive' and the auxiliary combined)
items.notes: moratta suggests you asked for it; kureta credits the giver's kindness. The doer takes ni with morau but ga with kureru.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for a favour done for another person, outward from the speaker (oshiete ageta, katte ageru).

examplePolite.ja: 友達に教えてあげました。

items.freqNote: rank of kana あげる (main verb 'give' and the auxiliary combined)
items.notes: Offered to someone's face (yatte ageru yo) it can sound condescending; avoid it toward superiors.

blocks.label: Advice
blocks.rationale: The standard ways to give advice, warn against something, and ask what to do.
blocks.interference: Positive advice takes the past -ta (yasunda hou ga ii), negative takes plain -nai (muri shinai hou ga ii), never -nakatta; -tara ii is the softer one and is how you ask: dou shitara ii?

items.use: Attaches to the past form to give firm advice (yasunda hou ga ii), with present meaning despite the past form.

example.romaji: kyou wa yasunda hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 今日は休んだ方がいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa yasunda hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は休んだ方がいいですよ。

items.freqNote: rank of ほうがいい (方がいい #1346); shared with -nai hou ga ii and comparative 'X no hou ga ii'
items.notes: Can sound strong; soften with kamo (yasunda hou ga ii kamo).

items.use: Attaches to the plain -nai form to advise against something (ikanai hou ga ii, muri shinai hou ga ii).

example.romaji: kyou wa muri shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 今日は無理しない方がいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa muri shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は無理しない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's better not to push yourself today.

items.freqNote: rank of ほうがいい, shared with -ta hou ga ii
items.notes: Never *-nakatta hou ga ii: positive takes -ta, negative takes -nai.

items.use: Attaches to the -tara form to ask for advice (dou shitara ii?) or to suggest something gently (kiitara ii yo).

examplePolite.ja: どうしたらいいですか？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer folds たら into the verb (standalone たら #2818)
items.notes: -ba ii (dou sureba ii?) means the same and sounds slightly more careful. Casual suggestions often stop at -tara? or -tara dou?: kiitara? = why don't you ask?

blocks.label: Naming and framing
blocks.rationale: Three ways to talk about a whole idea: an activity you like or find hard (-no), a thing by its name (-tte iu), and a conclusion you want to deny (-wake ja nai).
blocks.interference: -no names the action (iku no ga suki) while wake ja nai denies a conclusion (iku wake ja nai); -tte iu labels a name and becomes to iu in careful speech.

items.use: After a plain verb, turns the action into a noun so you can say you like it, are good at it or find it hard (ryouri suru no ga suki, iku no wa muri).

examplePolite.romaji: ryouri suru no ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 料理するのが好きです。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; の #1 is dominated by the possessive particle
items.notes: 'I like to cook' needs it: *ryouri suru ga suki is wrong. With shumi wa ... and dekiru, use koto instead: shumi wa ryouri suru koto, oyogu koto ga dekiru.

items.use: After a name or clause, labels it (sakura tte iu mise = a shop called Sakura) or asks what something is called (nante iu no?).

example.ja: さくらっていう店知ってる？
example.english: Do you know a place called Sakura?

examplePolite.romaji: sakura tte iu omise shittemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: さくらっていうお店知ってますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know a place called Sakura?

items.freqNote: rank of っていう across all uses (naming, quoting, tte iu ka); って言う #1659; careful-speech という #104, also all uses
items.notes: Careful speech uses to iu (sakura to iu omise). Polite 'what's it called?': nan to iimasu ka? Also a hedge: tte iu ka = or rather.

items.use: After a plain clause, denies a conclusion the listener might draw (kirai na wake ja nai), and often trails off into kedo.

example.romaji: kirai na wake ja nai kedo...
example.ja: 嫌いなわけじゃないけど…
example.english: It's not that I don't like it, but...

examplePolite.romaji: kirai na wake ja nai desu kedo...
examplePolite.ja: 嫌いなわけじゃないですけど…
examplePolite.english: It's not that I don't like it, but...

items.freqNote: rank of fused わけじゃない; わけ alone #272, わけない #449
items.notes: Trap: without ja it flips: iku wake nai = no way I'm going; iku wake ja nai = it's not that I'm going. Na-adjectives take na (hima na wake ja nai); nouns take na casually, to iu in careful speech. Often opens with betsu ni; more formal: -wake ja arimasen.

changelog.change: Punctuation aligned with cat-j/kotoba: final . in romaji and 。 in ja for statements, full-width ？ in ja, comma after jaa and after fronted bare topics (kono mise, kono pen, kami, repooto), … for trailing kedo.

The finalise rules forbid adding items, so the orchestrator must restore them or repoint any F prereqs (likely ou-ka, ou-kana). Likewise not added: nuance's suggestions you-ni-suru, -tara dou?, -te kurenai?, -tsumori and -naide. 3-item blocks are kept.

reviewSummaries: natural: The casual examples are strong: almost all are what a Tokyo speaker would actually say, with natural particle drop and contractions, and the romaji is clean. The weak spots are in the polite pairs (demo changes the meaning; te-hoshii, tte-iu and kute-de sound stiff or odd to a coworker) and in oshieru translated as 'teach' across the favour triad, where everyday speech means 'tell'. The rest is polish: -arimasen vs -nai desu consistency, missing softeners (yo, n desu kedo, sorosoro) and a few listening-trap notes that point at the wrong pair. Nothing to cut.

nuance: This is a strong, accurate draft. Every freqRank I checked matches the tool output, the polite pairs are true register counterparts (except a few pragmatic gaps), and the examples are natural. Every item earns its place, so nothing is cut. The main fixes are missing traps that cause misreadings: demo can also mean 'even' or 'any-', wake nai means 'no way', the negative question works as an invitation, mada -tenai is the 'not yet' answer, and polite -te hoshii desu and -tai desu ka? are pushy. Several alsoIn pointers are wrong or point to nothing. On structure, the 'Wrapping a clause' block isn't grouped by meaning, five blocks have only 3 items, and the volitional -ou/-you set needs checking against the other categories.

form: The forms are clean. Every romaji line follows the convention: no macrons, sou/kinou/koohii/paatii, kaetcha/sawatcha, and joined auxiliaries. Romaji, ja, kana and the polite pairs match sound for sound in all 40 items, conjugations and contractions are right, the 11 blocks hold 3–5 items each, and no slug is repeated. I re-ran every freqRank through freq.py and all of them match; I grepped about 40 alsoIn pointers.
The one systemic defect is prereqs: 27 items list romaji headwords ('-te', '-ta', '-nai', '-tara', '-kedo', '-tte') where the list expects slugs, so those prereqs point at nothing. Other problems: two wrong battery pointers (ta-past #97; nai-negative #99/#100), punctuation that doesn't match cat-j and kotoba (no 。, half-width ?), and membership drift against keep.txt (volitional dropped).

categories.name: Pointing, question & people words
categories.scope: ko/so/a/do series, question words, indefinites, pronouns

blocks.label: this/that: things
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do row for things: near me, near you or just said, far or shared, and which.
blocks.interference: sore vs are: sore is near you or just said, are is far or something we both remember; dore is for three or more, docchi for two.

items.use: Points at a thing near you so you can ask about it or choose it before you know its name; it stands alone and never goes before a noun.

examplePolite.ja: これ、いいですね。

items.notes: Before a noun it becomes kono: kono hon, never kore hon.

items.use: Points at a thing near the listener, and even more often at what they just said, so it is the main way to react to an idea (sore hontou?, sore tte dou iu imi?).

examplePolite.ja: それ、いいですね。

items.notes: Use sore, not are, for something the other person just mentioned.

items.use: Points at something away from both of you or something you both remember, and stands in for a word you can't recall (are, are da yo).

examplePolite.ja: あれはどうなりましたか？

items.freqNote: also counts the surprised 'are?' (G)
items.notes: Calling a person are sounds rude; say ano hito.

items.use: Asks which one out of three or more and takes ga, not wa (dore ga ii?); for a choice between two, use dotchi.

examplePolite.ja: どれがいいですか？

items.notes: dore demo ii = any of them is fine.

blocks.label: Question words
blocks.rationale: The bare wh-words for what, who, when, why and how much; each opens a question on any topic.
blocks.interference: nande (why) and nan de (by what) sound the same, so nan de kita? can mean 'how did you get here?'; a question word never takes wa, and as the subject it takes ga.

items.use: Asks what; before d, t and n sounds it shortens to nan (nan da, nan desu ka, nan de), so you need both forms by ear.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nani suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何するんですか？

items.freqNote: 何(なに) #34; 何(なん) #245; bare なん #97
items.notes: nani ga, nani o, but nan desu ka; the switch has to be automatic. nan no hanashi? = what are you talking about?

items.use: Asks who (dare ga), whose (dare no) or with whom (dare to); the answer takes ga.

examplePolite.romaji: donata ni kikeba ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どなたに聞けばいいですか？

items.freqNote: polite どなた #1577
items.notes: dare desu ka is fine with coworkers; donata is the softer choice with strangers and on the phone.

items.use: Asks when, and with kara or made asks since when or until when (itsu kara?, itsu made?).

examplePolite.ja: いつがいいですか？

items.freqNote: いつ #257; 何時(いつ) #2675 counted separately
items.notes: No ni after itsu: itsu iku?, not itsu ni iku?

items.use: The everyday casual 'why', said alone (e, nande?) or in a question ending in no?, and usually answered with kara; it can sound blunt or accusing, so doushite is softer and the safe choice in polite speech.

examplePolite.ja: どうして来なかったんですか？

items.freqNote: なんで #232; 何で #572 (also includes 'by what means'); polite どうして #170
alsoIn: 05-acquisition-order critique: question words incl. nande omitted
items.notes: By ear, nande iku? sounds the same whether it means 'why are you going?' or 'how are you getting there?', and is usually heard as 'why'; to ask for the route, say dou yatte iku? or nani de iku?

items.use: Asks a price or amount (kore ikura?); ikura demo means 'as much as you like' (ikura demo aru), and ikura -te mo means 'no matter how much' (ikura tabete mo futoranai).

examplePolite.ja: 全部でいくらですか？

items.notes: ikura is for price and amount; for 'how many' the word is ikutsu.

blocks.label: this/that: places
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do row for places: here, where, there by you, over there.
blocks.interference: soko is near the listener, asoko is away from both of you; asoko is the irregular member (not ako).

items.use: Names the place where you are, or 'this part' of something (koko ga muzukashii); takes ni for where things are and de for where things happen.

examplePolite.ja: ここにありますよ。

items.notes: Shop staff say kochira for 'here'; koko is fine in your own polite speech.

items.use: Asks where (doko ni aru?, doko iku?) or which part (doko ga ii?); in casual speech the particle after it is often dropped.

examplePolite.ja: どちらにありますか？

items.notes: doko desu ka is fine in everyday polite speech; dochira is the softer version. dochira also means 'which of two' (docchi): dochira ni? and dochira kara? ask about a place, dochira ga ii? asks for a choice.

items.use: A place near the listener or one just mentioned, and also 'that point' in a discussion (soko ga mondai).

examplePolite.ja: そこにありますよ。

items.freqNote: 底 'bottom' counted separately (#4174)
items.notes: soko is by the listener; a place far from both of you is asoko.

items.use: A place away from both speakers, either in view or one you both know (asoko no raamenya).

examplePolite.ja: あそこにありますよ。

items.notes: The irregular member: asoko, not ako.

blocks.label: this/that + noun
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do row that is always followed by a noun, with the same distances as kore/sore/are.
blocks.interference: kono must have a noun after it (kono mise) while kore stands alone; sono toki is 'then' in a story, ano toki is 'that time we both remember'.

items.use: Goes before a noun to point at something near you or current (kono mise, kono hen = around here) and never stands alone.

examplePolite.ja: この店、おいしいですよ。

items.notes: kono mae usually means 'the other day', not 'before this'.

items.use: Goes before a noun for something near the listener or just mentioned (sono hito, sono toki = at that time), which makes it the main back-reference word in stories.

example.english: That place you mentioned is good.

examplePolite.ja: その店、おいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That place you mentioned is good.

items.freqNote: also counts the hesitation filler sono... (G)
items.notes: Said alone with a pause, sono... is a hesitation filler (G).

items.use: Goes before a noun for something far off, or for something you both remember (ano mise, ano toki = that time).

example.english: That place (you know the one) is good.

examplePolite.ja: あの店、おいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That place (you know the one) is good.

items.freqNote: also counts the hesitation filler ano (G)
items.notes: Said alone, ano... is the 'um, excuse me' filler (G).

items.use: Goes before a noun to ask which one of several, mostly inside set frames (dono hen?, dono hito?, dono kurai?).

examplePolite.ja: どのくらいかかりますか？

items.notes: dono kurai? (how long, how much) is its most useful frame.

blocks.label: People
blocks.rationale: The person words every conversation needs: I, the name suffix, everyone and oneself.
blocks.interference: jibun means 'self' for whoever the subject is, not only 'me'; -san never goes on your own name.

items.use: The neutral 'I', safe for anyone in polite speech, though men usually switch to boku or ore casually; it is dropped whenever context makes it clear and used mainly for contrast or 'me too'.

examplePolite.ja: 私も行きます。

items.notes: Saying watashi in every sentence sounds foreign; drop it unless you're contrasting. In casual speech men usually say boku or ore and women watashi or atashi; with desu/masu, watashi suits everyone.

items.use: Attaches to a name, a job or a shop (tanaka-san, omawari-san, panya-san) as the default respectful suffix, but never on your own name, or on your own family when talking to outsiders.

examplePolite.ja: 田中さんはもう来てますか？

items.freqNote: さん #17 (三 'three' counted separately at #2400)
items.notes: Where English says 'you', use the person's name + san (tanaka-san wa dou?); anata sounds distant or presumptuous. -kun (boys, juniors) and -chan (children, close friends) are the casual alternatives.

items.use: Everyone in the group (minna de = all together); in polite speech minasan addresses or refers to other people.

examplePolite.ja: 皆さんお元気ですか？

items.freqNote: polite 皆さん #332
items.notes: Keep minna when you include yourself (minna de ikimashou); minasan is for others.

items.use: A reflexive 'self' for any person: jibun de (by yourself, on your own) and jibun no (your own).

examplePolite.ja: 自分でやります。

items.notes: In Kansai, jibun can also mean 'you'.

blocks.label: How / this way
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/do manner words plus dou yatte: how something went, how it is done, and 'like that'.
blocks.interference: dou asks for an opinion or report (dou datta?), dou yatte asks for the method (dou yatte iku?); the bare reply sou (sou da ne) is drilled in G, so the so- card here is sou iu.

items.use: Asks for an opinion, a report or a plan in one word (dou?, dou datta?, dou suru?, dou omou?, dou shita no? = what's wrong?), and after a noun it suggests (ashita dou?).

examplePolite.ja: 映画はどうでしたか？

items.freqNote: extra-polite いかが #840
items.notes: Shop staff use the extra-polite ikaga desu ka when offering something.

items.english: that kind of; like that (what you said)
items.use: Refers back to something just said or mentioned (sou iu koto = so that's it, sou iu hito = that kind of person); the same sou follows verbs of thinking and doing (sou omou = I think so, sou yatte = like that).

example.english: Oh, so that's what you mean.

examplePolite.ja: そういうことですか。
examplePolite.english: Oh, so that's what you mean.

items.freqNote: そういう #129; そうやって #919; bare そう #31 is mostly the reply (G)
items.notes: The a- version aa iu / aa yatte (something you both saw) is mostly for recognition; sou works almost everywhere you might say aa.

items.use: Demonstrates a way of doing something while you show it (kou yatte, kou suru to), and kou iu means 'this kind of'.

example.romaji: kou yatte tsukau n da yo.
example.ja: こうやって使うんだよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kou yatte tsukau n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: こうやって使うんですよ。

items.freqNote: こういう #281; こうやって #807
items.notes: kou? with a gesture means 'like this?', the easiest way to check you're doing it right.

items.use: Asks for the method or route (dou yatte iku?, dou yatte tsukuru?), where bare dou would ask for an opinion.

examplePolite.romaji: dou yatte tsukau n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どうやって使うんですか？

items.notes: Alone, dou yatte? works as a quick 'How?'

blocks.label: What kind
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do 'kind' row for describing something or asking what it is like.
blocks.interference: donna (what kind) vs dono (which one); sonna is the neutral 'that kind you mentioned', anna often sounds critical.

items.use: Describes something you are showing or experiencing (konna kanji, konna no hajimete), and konna ni means 'this much, so'.

examplePolite.romaji: konna kanji de ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こんな感じでいいですか？

items.notes: konna ni + adjective is an exclamation: konna ni oishii n da! (I didn't know it was this good!)

items.use: Describes what the other person has or just said, and builds push-back (sonna koto nai = that's not true); alone, sonna! means 'no way!'

examplePolite.romaji: sonna kanji de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんな感じでいいですよ。

items.notes: sonna ni + negative means 'not that much': sonna ni takakunai.

items.use: Goes before a noun to ask someone to describe it (donna hito?, donna kanji?); any particle goes after that noun (donna kanji ga ii?).

example.english: What sort of thing do you want?

examplePolite.romaji: donna kanji ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どんな感じがいいですか？
examplePolite.english: What sort of thing would you like?

items.notes: donna hito? asks for a description; dono hito? asks you to pick one.

items.use: Describes something you both saw or know, mostly in anna hito or anna koto, and is often disapproving.

example.english: I'd like it like that one.

examplePolite.ja: あんな感じがいいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like it like that one.

items.notes: anna hito often sounds critical, like 'someone like that'.

blocks.label: this/that: ways & sides
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do direction row for which way, whose side and which of two, each with a polite -chira form.
blocks.interference: docchi is for two choices, dore for three or more; kocchi and socchi can also mean 'me' and 'you', so listen for people, not places. The -chira forms are what you say to customers and strangers; with coworkers kocchi/docchi + desu is normal.

items.use: Points to a direction, a side or one of two choices (kotchi ga ii), and casually also means 'me, my side' (kotchi wa daijoubu).

examplePolite.ja: こちらがいいです。

items.freqNote: polite こちら #200
items.notes: kochira also introduces people: kochira wa tanaka-san desu.

items.use: Asks which of two, or which direction, and takes ga (dotchi ga ii?).

example.english: Which of the two do you want?

examplePolite.ja: どちらがいいですか？

items.freqNote: polite どちら #1013
items.notes: dotchi demo ii means 'either is fine'.

items.use: The direction or choice on the listener's side, and casually a way to say 'you' without anata (sotchi wa dou?).

examplePolite.ja: そちらがいいですよ。

items.freqNote: polite そちら #1162
items.notes: sotchi wa? means 'and you?', a casual way around anata.

items.use: The direction or thing away from both of you, used mostly for pointing out the way (atchi da yo).

example.english: That one over there looks better.

examplePolite.ja: あちらがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: That one over there looks better.

items.freqNote: polite あちら #1685
items.notes: Learn atchi da yo, 'it's that way', first.

blocks.label: In, on, other
blocks.rationale: Relational nouns that attach to another noun with no to say where something is, or that it is a different one.
blocks.interference: naka/soto and ue/shita come after the noun (hako no naka) but hoka comes before (hoka no hito); ue/shita also mean older/younger.

items.use: Places things in or out of something (kaban no naka, soto de), and X no naka de ichiban means 'the most out of X'.

example.romaji: naka ja nakute, soto ni aru yo.
example.ja: 中じゃなくて、外にあるよ。

examplePolite.romaji: naka ja nakute, soto ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 中じゃなくて、外にありますよ。

items.freqNote: 中 read なか #133; 外 soto #437
items.notes: naka also means 'relationship' (naka ga ii = get along well).

items.use: Places things above or below (tsukue no ue), and gives relative age or rank (futatsu ue = two years older).

example.romaji: ue ja nakute, shita ni aru yo.
example.ja: 上じゃなくて、下にあるよ。
example.english: It's not on top, it's underneath.

examplePolite.romaji: ue ja nakute, shita ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 上じゃなくて、下にありますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's not on top, it's underneath.

items.freqNote: 上 read うえ #321; 下 shita #622
items.notes: shita also means 'tongue' and 'did' (past of suru); context sorts it.

items.use: Comes before no or ni: hoka no means 'another, other' and hoka ni means 'besides, anything else'.

examplePolite.ja: 他のはありませんか？

items.freqNote: plus ほか #1673, 他にも #1824
items.notes: hoka ni wa? is the quick 'anything else?' follow-up.

blocks.label: Person, thing, matter, place
blocks.rationale: The four general nouns that let you talk around any word you don't know.
blocks.interference: mono is a thing you can touch (taberu mono), koto is an act or topic (suki na koto), tokoro is a place or a trait (yasashii tokoro).

items.use: Any person or people, usually with a description in front (ii hito, ano hito), and hito ni yoru means 'it depends on the person'.

examplePolite.ja: 好きな人、いますか？

items.notes: People take iru, not aru: hito ga iru.

items.use: A concrete thing, usually with a description in front, so you can name what you lack the word for (taberu mono, hoshii mono).

example.romaji: suki na mono tanonde ii yo.
example.ja: 好きなもの頼んでいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: suki na mono tanonde ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 好きなもの頼んでいいですよ。

items.notes: mono da at the end means 'that's just how it is' (sou iu mono da).

items.use: An abstract thing such as an act, event or topic (suki na koto, sonna koto), X no koto means 'about X', and it is the base of patterns like -ta koto ga aru.

example.romaji: suki na koto shite ii yo.
example.ja: 好きなことしていいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: suki na koto shite ii desu yo.

blocks.label: Something, someone
blocks.rationale: Question word + ka = some-, used to ask whether rather than what.
blocks.interference: nanika atta? asks whether anything happened (answer un / uun); nani ga atta? asks what happened (answer with the thing).

items.use: Asks whether there is something (nanika atta?) or offers something unspecified (nanika nomu?); in fast speech it becomes nanka.

examplePolite.ja: 何かあったんですか？

items.notes: Casually most people say nanka: nanka atta no? The same nanka is also a filler (G).

items.use: An unspecified person: dareka kita? asks whether anyone came, while dare ga kita? asks who came.

examplePolite.ja: さっき誰か来ましたか？

items.use: An unspecified place, often with the particle after it dropped (dokoka iku?); doko iku? would ask where.

examplePolite.ja: どこか行くんですか？

items.notes: Casually dokoka is said dokka (どっか #788); use dokoka in polite speech.

items.use: An unspecified time, mostly for future wishes and loose plans (itsuka ikitai, itsuka mata).

examplePolite.ja: いつか行きたいですね。

items.freqNote: ５日 read いつか #3202 and 五日 #43449 counted separately
items.notes: itsuka also means 'the fifth (day)'; context separates them.

blocks.label: Nothing, nobody
blocks.rationale: Question word + mo + a negative verb = nothing, no one, nowhere.
blocks.interference: With a negative verb all three mean no-thing, no one, nowhere; when a particle is needed it goes before mo (dare ni mo, doko ni mo).

items.use: With a negative verb means 'nothing, not anything' (nanimo nai, nanimo tabenakatta).

examplePolite.ja: 何もありませんよ。

items.freqNote: 何にも (nan ni mo) #1238
items.notes: The emphatic casual form is nan ni mo (nan ni mo nai).

items.use: With a negative verb means 'no one' (daremo inai), and splits around a particle (dare ni mo iwanai = won't tell anyone).

examplePolite.ja: 誰もいませんよ。

items.freqNote: 誰にも (dare ni mo) #743
items.notes: daremo ga + a positive verb means 'everyone' but sounds formal (daremo ga shitteru); casually say minna shitteru.

items.use: With a negative verb means 'nowhere, not anywhere' (doko ni mo ikanai), keeping ni or de inside.

examplePolite.ja: どこにもありませんよ。

items.freqNote: どこも not found; rank of どこにも
items.notes: dokomo with a positive verb means 'everywhere' (dokomo onaji); casually ni is often dropped with a negative too (dokomo itte nai = haven't been anywhere).

blocks.label: Anything, anyone
blocks.rationale: Question word + demo = any- at all, for the free-choice answers.
blocks.interference: nandemo ii (anything's fine) vs nanimo iranai (I don't want anything): demo usually goes with a positive verb and mo with a negative (nandemo nai 'it's nothing' is the set exception); it is nan-, not nani-, before demo.

items.use: Free choice: anything at all is fine (nandemo ii yo), with a positive verb, unlike nanimo.

examplePolite.ja: 何でもいいですよ。

items.freqNote: 何でも #728; なんでも #3802
items.notes: nandemo nai ('it's nothing') is a set phrase in G.

items.use: Any time at all, the easy yes to a scheduling question (itsudemo ii yo, itsudemo kite).

examplePolite.ja: いつでもいいですよ。

items.use: Any place at all (dokodemo ii yo, dokodemo aru).

examplePolite.ja: どこでもいいですよ。

items.use: Any person at all (daredemo ii yo, daredemo dekiru = anyone can do it).

dropped.reason: All three reviewers cut it. speakNeed 1, spread 2, reach 2; its #63 rank is the interjection 'ah' (G), and the manner frames rank low (ああいう #1183, ああやって #7741). Its prompt is identical to G's aa card, and its prereq pointed to the wrong card. The aa iu / aa yatte recognition point now sits in sou-manner's notes. The How block keeps 4 items.

reviewSummaries: natural: Most casual examples are natural Tokyo speech, and the kosoado and indefinite blocks are idiomatic throughout. Four problems would mislead an audio-first learner. (1) The nande note says nan de iku can't mean 'why', which is wrong: the two are identical in speech. (2) The commas in the -san and minasan examples create a pause that turns a question about someone into addressing them. (3) The dare/donata and nani polite lines are a register clash and textbook-stiff phrasing. (4) The casual forms dokka and nanka should be taught as the default. The rest is polish: the 'casual-only' flags overstate how casual kocchi, docchi and nande are, there are small nuance shifts in the na→desu ne pairs, and aa-manner should be cut as recognition-only.

nuance: Category J is well built overall. The ko/so/a/do rows, the ka/mo/demo series and the hito/mono/koto/tokoro block are meaning-first, the examples are natural, and most traps are noted (kono mae, donna vs dono, nanika vs nani ga). One note is wrong: nande's 'nan de iku = how, not why' teaches the opposite of what a listener hears. The other gaps are pragmatic: the casual 'I' (boku/ore) and the 'you' problem (name + san, not anata) are missing, and donata is shown in the wrong setting. Smaller fixes: the ikura demo / daremo ga glosses, the two-word naka/soto and ue/shita cards, overstated casual-only flags, and cutting aa-manner.

form: Mechanically clean. I checked every freqRank with the tool (all 52+ match), and the alsoIn pointers checked (exit battery, nouns list, vocab-trainer sets and phrase ids, 05 S3 and the critique) all exist. Romaji follows the convention, examples match ja word for word, conjugations are right, and there are no duplicate slugs. All blocks have 3–6 items. The real problems: donna's 'takes ga' claim is false; kou and aa-manner name a prereq that isn't in this category; and sou-manner and aa-manner reuse the exact prompts of G's sou and aa cards. Cut aa-manner and re-head sou-manner as sou iu. The rest is pointer cleanup and small consistency fixes (dou polite, tokoro headword vs rank, itsuka note).

consDropped.reason: True duplicate of G-onegai. Both have the casual headword 'onegai' and both make a request ('X, please' / 'please, I'm asking'). G-onegai is the stronger placement: its polite form is the real register pair (onegai -> onegai shimasu, which also works for asking for things, as in kore onegai shimasu), and it anchors the onegai-douzo contrast group. F-kudasai pairs casual onegai with a different word (kudasai) and is in no contrast group. F4 still has 4 items. Standalone kudasai still appears as the polite form of -te, -naide, chotto matte and ganbatte. Consider adding 'kore kudasai' to G-onegai's notes. With this drop the list has 398 items.

checks.consNotes:
PREREQ FORMAT: I standardised prereqs on slugs (the id minus the category prefix), not romaji. The task text said "exact romaji", but 340+ prereqs are already slugs. The cat-i changelog ("Romaji headwords replaced with slugs ... per form review") and g-review.json (honto? -> honto) both chose slugs. Romaji also can't serve as a key because 5 headwords are shared by two items each: -te (E-te-and / F-te-request), -naide (E-nai-de / F-naide), ano, iya, onegai. I converted the 22 romaji prereqs left in E and F, for example -tara -> tara, -nai -> nai-negative, -tte iu -> tte-iu-called. One judgement call: F-ja-nai-q now points to kunai-ja-nai, the item that teaches -ja nai and warns about the tag reading, instead of nai-negative. I removed the particle prereqs (o, ga, ni, to, no) from 40 H items and from B-no-hou-ga, because particles are not items in this list (they live in kotoba particles). After the fixes every prereq resolves to a slug and the prereq graph has no cycles (checked with a script).

ROMAJI CONVENTION: J used kocchi/socchi/acchi/docchi, which breaks the "t before ch" rule. kotoba's own src/lib/romaji.ts writes っ before ch as 't', and B-metcha already follows it. I fixed romaji, use, notes and contrastGroup on the four items and the mention of the word in J-dore's use. Example sentences are not a fixable field, so the orchestrator needs to change their romaji by hand: J-kocchi "kotchi ga ii na.", J-docchi "dotchi ga ii?", J-socchi "sotchi ga ii yo.", J-acchi "atchi ga ii na.". The J8 block's interference text also needs it ("docchi is for two choices..., kocchi and socchi can also mean..." -> dotchi / kotchi / sotchi). Please also apply \b(ko|so|a|do)cchi -> \1tchi to the use, notes and examples of categories B–G; I only had full text for A, H, I and J, which have no other hits. In romaji and polite fields there are no macrons, no 'wo', no capitals and no kana. Each of these is spelled the same way everywhere: ja nai, n da / n desu, sou na n da, desho? / deshou, honto (casual) / hontou (polite), jaa, iu. The '?' rule is also consistent: '?' only on questions carried by intonation alone, none after ka.

UNFIXABLE VIA FIELDS — SLUG COLLISION: D-iya and G-iya both have the slug 'iya'. This is the same fatal class of bug as the ano collision g-review caught: on import one overwrites the other. Rename one, for example G-iya -> iya-no (nothing references either as a prereq).

CONTRAST GROUPS: no group name was shared across categories. Two I groups were the H groups' names with the words reordered: kuru-iku vs H3 iku-kuru, and kureru-morau-ageru vs H13 ageru-kureru-morau. I unified them under the H names, so each now spans its verb and its -te form layer. I left C2 'tabun-kitto-zettai' and F6 'certainty' separate; they are related (both blocks are labelled 'How sure') but have different forms.

ALSOIN: the I items used '12-list-te-dependents X7' without the '#' that A and H use for the same R/X/H numbering, so I normalised to '#X7'. I also changed '05-acquisition-order: S11 potential' to the 'S3 (...)' style.

LEFT ALONE (style, not spelling): leading-hyphen use differs by category. E hyphenates particle-like enders (-kedo, -kara, -node) while B does not (dake, shika); F writes tte / tte kanji / wake da without a hyphen while E, I and G write -tte / -tte iu / -wake ja nai. This doesn't change the spelling of any word, so I made no change; unify later if wanted. F-to-omou and H-omou overlap but are distinct layers (the 'I think' ending vs the verb), linked by a prereq, so I kept both.

selectorNotes:
407 kept, chosen frequency-first. Per category: A40 B31 C28 D42 E32 F39 G50 H52 I35 J58. All ids were checked for duplicates; 404 matched the scratchpad pool files and the other 3 (B-omotta-yori, I-kute-de, J-tokoro-place) are in the computed pool.

Hardest calls:

1. J is over quota (58 against about 50) because of the family rule. Seven ko/so/a/do series are kept whole (kore, kono, koko, konna, kocchi, kou, kou-iu = 28 items), plus the -ka, -mo and -demo indefinite families (11 items). J-aa-manner (s2 r2 n1), J-aa-iu (#1183), J-dokodemo (#11237*) and J-daredemo (#24037*) are in only to complete their families. To make room, the B -ni series (konna ni, sonna ni, anna ni, donna ni; #1332 to #3341) is cut whole, even though "sonna ni + negative" is idiomatic.

2. Relative time. kinou, kyou and ashita are kept (all in the top 400). The week, month and year rows and ototoi/asatte are cut whole and left to the calendar drill. Each row is a closed family that would split around rank 1100 to 2800. kesa, konban, asa and yoru are also cut, as close to clock times.

3. Adjective contrast pairs pulled in weaker partners: furui #1126, sukunai #1076, yasui #1315, chiisai #879. In exchange, the nagai/mijikai, atsui/samui, jouzu/heta and tokui/nigate pairs are cut whole. The most painful cut is atsui/samui (small-talk staples, n5, but #1030/#1214). Also cut despite good ranks:
   - okashii #359 (overlaps hen)
   - kimochi #231 (a noun)
   - umai #246 (masc; jouzu and oishii cover it)
   - daisuki (narrower than suki)
   - saikou #551, zannen #682, hima #909

4. G social phrases. The universal set is kept, and konbanwa (#1334) stays to keep ohayou/konnichiwa/konbanwa whole. Cut as situation-bound (low reach) despite good ranks:
   - itadakimasu/gochisousama, tadaima/okaeri and itte-kimasu/itterasshai (cut as pairs)
   - moshimoshi #442 (the hardest cut)
   - otsukare, omedetou, ki-o-tsukete, hisashiburi, shouganai, kekkou-desu, yoshi

5. Duplicate placements, with the kept one first:
   - Time: C-toriaezu (dropped A), A-mou-ikkai (dropped G)
   - Degree and stance: B-honto-ni (dropped C), C-mochiron, C-masaka and C-tonikaku (dropped the G/G/E copies), G-tashika-ni (dropped C)
   - Adjectives: D-daijoubu, D-sugoi and D-dame (dropped G)
   - Connectors: E-tame-ni (dropped I), E-tari-tari (dropped I-tari-suru), E-nai-de together with F-naide (dropped I-naide)
   - Endings and patterns: F-n-da-kedo (dropped E), F-tsumori, F-ou-lets and F-ou-to-omou (dropped the I copies), I-ta-hou-ga-ii (dropped F), I-te-kureru (dropped F-te-kureru; F-te-kurenai kept as the request)
   - Verbs: H-ki-ga-suru, H-owaru and H-hajimeru (dropped F/I copies)
   - Responses: G-nanka (dropped J), G-nante (dropped J-nante and I-nante-dismissive)
   - Same word, different jobs, so both kept: sou (3 items), ano, are, iya/iya, kedo and kedo-final, te-and and te-request, tte-quote and tte-heard, tara.
   - Dropped as the same word: F-kara-final, F-noni-final, E-ka-or (F-ka covers the word), F-tara-suggest.

6. Flagged items. darou (masc, #102) is kept on frequency. ore (#44) is cut so boku is the only male pronoun, and atashi is not kept. anata (n2) is cut, so there is no second-person pronoun. The only heavily flagged items are the three slang words: metcha, maji-de and yabai.

7. Kept on merit despite weak or missing ranks (tokenizer splits): tabun, te-mo, nakya, cha-dame, nakute-mo-ii, nagara, tari-tari, nai-de, ii-ne, ii-yo, de-ii, no-koto, ja-nakute, tte-nani, nihongo-de-nante-iu. I-katta-datta, I-kunai-ja-nai and I-kute-de are treated as must-keep core forms.

8. H is at 52, a little above guidance, because the user approved general verbs. The cut verbs that hurt most: ireru, mieru, yobu, sagasu, dasu, kakeru, shinjiru.

407 ids, checked by script with no repeats. Per category: A 40, B 31, C 29, D 44, E 33, F 37, G 52, H 54, I 38, J 49. Speaking-first meant G (reactions and learner repair phrases), H (verbs, as the user asked) and J (pointing and question words) sit at or just above their upper bound. A, C and E were trimmed to pay for that.

Hardest calls:
1. Relative calendar words cut as whole series: kotoshi/kyonen/rainen, raishuu/senshuu/konshuu and the month row, plus asa/yoru/kesa/konban and shuumatsu. They are useful (r3, n4), but they lose to patterns that attach to any verb (-nagara, -uchi ni, -made ni, -chuu, r5), and they fit the calendar systems drilled separately. kyou, ashita and kinou stay. ototoi and asatte were left out as the outer ends of that set.
2. Topic adjectives in D: oishii kept (said at every meal). atsui, samui, itai, nemui, atarashii/furui and nagai/mijikai cut. Contrast pairs kept whole: ii/warui, suki/kirai, hayai/osoi, takai/yasui, ookii/chiisai, omoshiroi/tsumaranai, muzukashii/kantan, hima/isogashii, saikou/saiaku. raku and tsurai cut to make room.
3. Same-word duplicates; one kept each time:
   - B: honto-ni, sonna-ni
   - C: toriaezu, mochiron, tashika-ni, tonikaku, masaka, dekireba
   - D: daijoubu, sugoi, dame, zannen
   - E: tame-ni, tari-tari
   - F: n-da-kedo, tsumori, rashii
   - G: mou-ikkai
   - H: ki-ga-suru, owaru, hajimeru
   - I: volitional, ta-hou-ga-ii, ou-to-omou
   - J: minna
   Different functions both kept: chotto (degree) and chotto... (soft no), iya (adjective) and iya (interjection), ano (filler) and ano (demonstrative), sou in three roles, aa (interjection) and aa (manner), are (pointing word) kept while are? (huh) was cut, demo (but) and -demo (or something), kedo and kara as conjunctions and as sentence endings, -te (and) and -te (request), -tte (quote) and -tte (heard), I-te-kureru (does for me) and F-te-kurenai (request). F-te-kureru was dropped as a near-copy of te-kurenai.
4. Closed families. Kept whole in J: ko/so/a/do for kore, kono, koko, konna, kocchi and kou (aa-manner is weak at n1 but stays for the series), and the full indefinite grid (nani/dare/itsu/doko + ka/mo/demo; itsumo is in A). That grid costs daredemo (#24037) and dokodemo (#11237), but it is one rule. In B, konna ni / sonna ni / anna ni / donna ni are kept whole. The kou iu / sou iu / aa iu / dou iu series was cut whole because konna/sonna covers the same meaning (G-dou-iu-imi stays as a fixed phrase). Give/receive sets kept whole in H and I, plus te-kuru/te-iku, ku-naru/ku-suru, te-mo-ii/nakute-mo-ii/cha-dame, katta-datta/kunai-ja-nai.
5. Register. nande is kept and doushite cut, because doushite becomes nande's polite form; kocchi works the same way with kochira. No second-person "you" (anata, kimi) and only watashi (boku/ore cut). Name + san covers "you" in practice, but this is the call most worth a second look. Only three slang items: metcha, maji de, yabai. Other casual-only items (jan, naa, nanka, nande, kocchi series, mendokusai, datte) are kept with their flags.
6. Cut from G for budget: rituals and narrow replies (itadakimasu/gochisousama, konbanwa, otsukare, mata ne, kochira koso, maa maa, yatta, bikkuri shita, nandemonai, mou ii, are?, da yo ne). Some of these build from items already kept. The near-misses in H were renraku suru, tasukaru, kawaru, tanomu, kizuku and nareru.

No frequency lookups were needed; this used the ranks given in the pool.

408 ids, all unique, checked with a script. Per category: A 42, B 30, C 28, D 39, E 33, F 38, G 51, H 56, I 38, J 53. Every category is within ±30% of its guide. H is at the top of its range because the user said general verbs are good. I made no frequency lookups: this pass only selects ids, and all ranks I cite are the pool's own.

HARDEST CALLS
1. Full families cost slots. J keeps six complete ko/so/a/do series. They are kore, kono, koko, kocchi, konna and kou/sou/aa/dou, so J-aa-manner stays even though it is weak on its own. B keeps all four of konna ni/sonna ni/anna ni/donna ni. J also keeps the whole indefinite grid: nanika/dareka/dokoka/itsuka, nanimo/daremo/doko ni mo, and nandemo/daredemo/dokodemo/itsudemo. daredemo and dokodemo only made it because of the family rule. To pay for this I cut the kou iu/sou iu/aa iu/dou iu series whole: it largely overlaps konna/sonna, and the general item wins. G-dou-iu-imi stays as a separate fixed phrase.
2. Calendar and time-of-day words are cut whole. That covers the senshuu/raishuu/kotoshi/kyonen/sengetsu grid, shuumatsu, asa/hiru/yoru and kesa/konban/yuube. I treated them as part of the calendar system that is drilled separately. kyou/kinou/ashita stay as core time words, but ototoi/asatte are out. This is the cut I'm least sure of; if you want any back, start with kesa, konban, senshuu and raishuu.
3. Duplicates: one placement each when the function is the same. Kept: A-zutto, A-toriaezu, B-honto-ni, J-minna, B-sonna-ni, C-mochiron, G-tashika-ni, C-tonikaku, C-dekireba, D-daijoubu, D-sugoi, D-dame, D-zannen, G-mou-ikkai, E-tame-ni, F-tsumori, F-yotei, F-ou-lets, F-ou-to-omou, I-ta-hou-ga-ii (kept beside its partner I-nai-hou-ga-ii), H-ki-ga-suru, H-owaru, H-hajimeru, E-tari-tari (over I-tari-suru), F-n-da-kedo. D-daijoubu also has to cover the polite 'no thanks' refusal. Both placements kept where the functions differ: tte (quote and hearsay), tara (if and 'why don't you'), te ('and' and 'please'), ka ('or' and question), nai (negative and invitation), te-kureru (request and 'does for me'), sou (three ways), ano (filler and 'that'), aa, chotto (degree and soft no), and iya (G no versus D dislike). Same-function duplicates cut: F-kedo-final, F-kara-final, F-noni-final, I-naide, I-volitional, the C and G masaka (uso covers disbelief) and G-maji (C-maji-de kept). Different-function variants cut only for budget: I-rashii-typical, I-demo-or-something, J-are/G-are-huh (only J-are kept), J-nanka and J-nante.
4. A polite counterpart counts as covered. J-doushite is cut because it is J-nande's polite form, B-totemo is B-metcha's, and F-sou-da-hearsay is F-tte-heard's. Also cut: F-kamo-shirenai (kamo kept), mou-sukoshi (mou chotto kept), F-te-kurenai (te-kureru kept) and the variants nai-to and nakucha (nakya kept).
5. G was the tightest category. Responses, clarifying moves (tte nani, nante, nihongo de nante iu, dou iu imi, nante iu ka) and the tools for each intent come first. Social set phrases are trimmed to 11: arigatou, gomen, sumimasen, jaa ne, yoroshiku, hajimemashite, hisashiburi, ohayou, konnichiwa, otsukare and ganbatte. Cut: household pairs (tadaima/okaeri, itte kimasu/itterasshai), itadakimasu/gochisousama, oyasumi, konbanwa, kocchi koso, omedetou, mata kondo, and the chunks that are just two kept items joined (da yo ne, taihen da ne, dou shiyou).
6. D keeps general evaluative and state adjectives in whole contrast pairs: ii/warui, suki/kirai, omoshiroi/tsumaranai, muzukashii/kantan, hayai/osoi, ooi/sukunai, ookii/chiisai, isogashii/hima, saikou/saiaku and jouzu/heta. Whole pairs cut: takai/yasui (shopping; I-yasui-suffix stays as 'easy to'), tokui/nigate, nagai/mijikai, chikai/tooi, atsui/samui. Physical states like itai and nemui are cut too.
7. Covering every intent:
   - Agree: un, sou, sou da ne, tashika ni, ii yo, ii ne.
   - Refuse: uun, iya, the soft-no chotto, daijoubu, mou ii, muri, dame.
   - Hedge: ichiou, tabun, kamo, kana, n ja nai, tte iu ka, wake ja nai, betsu ni, sou kana.
   - Guess: hazu, mitai, rashii, sou (looks like), desho, kitto, moshikashite.
   - Request: -te, -te kureru, -te moraeru, onegai, kudasai, -naide, sasete, chotto ii.
   - Invite: -nai?, -ou, -ou ka, yokattara, zehi, issho ni.
   - Explain: n da, n da kedo, kara, node, datte, wake da, tsumari, tatoeba.
   - Concede: kedo, demo, noni, -te mo, shouganai, kekkyoku.
   - Advise: hou ga ii and nai hou ga ii, -tara?, -tara ii.
   - Permission and obligation, kept whole: -te mo ii, -cha dame, -nakya, -nakute mo ii.
   - Giving, both sets whole: ageru/kureru/morau and the -te forms of each.
   - Kept as pairs: -te kuru/-te iku and ku naru/ku suru.
8. Smaller calls:
   - Positional words: only naka-soto and ue-shita, the pair ids, because they carry the 'among' and 'older/younger' senses. mae-ushiro and tonari-yoko are cut.
   - Pronouns: watashi only. boku is flagged masculine, anata is little used in speech, and kare/kanojo are cut. sei de/okage de is cut as a pair.
   - Rough, gendered and dialect forms: none kept. Frequent casual or slang items kept: metcha, maji de, yabai, jan, naa, nanka, datte, nande and the kocchi series.
selection.boundaryNotes:
The final count is 406 + 7 added − 13 removed = 400. F-kedo-final is in both the remove list and dupResolutions, so it counts once. Category totals after the changes: A 40, B 27, C 27, D 44, E 31, F 36, G 49, H 54, I 40, J 52.

DUPLICATES. Only one pair is the same word doing the same job: E-kedo and F-kedo-final. A trailing "kedo..." is just E-kedo with the second clause left unsaid, and F-n-da-kedo already covers the "the thing is..." lead-in. Mention the trailing use in E-kedo's example. The other 13 base pairs do different jobs, so both stay:
- A-tokoro (aspect) / J-tokoro-place (place, side)
- B-chotto (degree) / G-chotto-soft-no (refusal move)
- D-iya (dislike) / G-iya (no, well)
- E-tara (if) / F-tara-suggest (why don't you)
- E-te-and / F-te-request
- E-tte-quote / F-tte-heard
- E-ka-or / F-ka
- E-nai-de (without) / F-naide (please don't)
- F-no-question / I-no-nominalizer
- F-nai-invite / I-nai-negative
- sou in three roles (F-sou-looks, G-sou, J-sou-manner)
- G-ano / J-ano
- G-aa / J-aa-manner (kept for the kou/sou/aa/dou family)
Three of the adds share kana with base items but do different jobs: I-yasui-suffix (easy to) vs D-yasui (cheap), G-are-huh (huh?) vs J-are (that), and I-demo-or-something (ocha demo nomu?) vs E-demo (but).

SWAPS AND ADDS:
- I-tara-ii replaces F-tara-ii-na. -tara ii covers "dou shitara ii?" (what should I do?), which matters more for a learner, and "-tara ii na" (I hope) is the same pattern plus naa. Carry the "I hope" sense into I-tara-ii's example.
- -yasui (#1141) and -nikui (#2419) go in as a contrast pair. Both are productive r5 patterns: wakariyasui, kikinikui.
- -kata (way of doing) covers yarikata and tsukaikata. Its rank, #292 for 方(かた), also counts the "person" sense.
- -demo (or something) is the soft-suggestion tool for invitations.
- are? (#98, mixed with あれ "that") is a top confusion reaction.
- kakeru (#244) covers denwa kakeru, meiwaku kakete gomen and jikan kakeru. It is the strongest verb missing; selectors called it a painful cut. That takes H to 54 (guidance about 45), which fits the user approving general verbs.

CUTS:
- B konna ni / sonna ni / anna ni / donna ni, cut as a whole family. Their ranks, checked with the tool, are #1783, #2089, #1332 and #3341. konna/sonna/anna/donna stay in J. anmari covers the negative "not that much" and sugoku the exclamation, so the four slots buy higher-reach patterns.
- B-totemo (#617): it is already metcha's polite field. Keep it there, and consider making sugoku's polite field "totemo / sugoku" so the plain "very" stays reachable without the slang item.
- E-dakedo (#192): it is covered by demo (#32) and kedo, and its polite form desu ga is the same.
- E-sorekara (#2967): de/sorede, ato and -te kara cover it.
- E-tte-iu-ka (#948*): it overlaps G-nante-iu-ka.
- G-dou-shiyou (#655): it is built from dou + shiyou.
- G-ii-na: it is ii + naa, and ii yo / ii ne stay.
- G-oyasumi (#1575, r1): a household or chat set phrase, cut because G was the most over-quota category (49 against about 40).
F ends up under its guidance (36 against about 50) and I over (40 against about 35). -tara ii and -demo could reasonably be filed under F.

NEXT ADDS IF THE USER WANTS MORE: H-ireru (#222), the D-jouzu (#1309) / D-heta (#1475) pair, C-zehi (#1143, goes with yokattara), and D-atarashii (#301) with furui as a pair.

All ranks cited above come from freq.py output, apart from tte iu ka, whose rank is the pool's own.

B: Indefinites nanimo/daremo + negative, nandemo (#728), hoka (#613) -> J
